item.title: Give your SEO access without handing over your passwords
item.description: Search Console, GA4, Business Profile, WordPress, and Shopify all let you invite an SEO by name. Which role to pick for each, and how to take access back.
item.content:encoded:
Give your SEO access without handing over your passwords

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 28, 2026

The first week of an SEO engagement is mostly logins. The fastest way through it is the one that causes trouble later: emailing your own username and password. Every tool an SEO needs lets you invite a person by email, give them a role, and remove them in one click when the work ends. Here is the role to pick in each one.

Why a shared password costs more than it saves

A shared login is your identity. Anything done under it looks like you did it, two-step verification codes go to your phone at awkward hours, and when the engagement ends the only way to close the door is to change a password that your own staff also use. An invitation ties every action to a named person and ends with a single click. It also keeps the account yours if the relationship sours, which is the case nobody plans for.

Ask your SEO for the Google account or email address they want invited, then use the roles below.

Google Search Console: a full user is usually enough

Search Console has owners and users. In Settings, then Users and permissions, an owner can add a full user, who sees all the data and can take some actions, or a restricted user, who sees most data and can change nothing. A full user covers nearly all audit and indexing work.

Grant owner only when the SEO has to manage other users or settings. Google treats a delegated owner the same as a verified owner except for one thing: a verified owner proved ownership with a token on your site, such as an HTML file or a DNS record. That token outlives the person. Google's help page warns that removing an owner from the property leaves their tokens in place, and while a token remains, that person can verify again and walk back in. When an SEO who verified the property leaves, remove the file or DNS record they added, and only theirs, since one token can also verify Merchant Center or Google Workspace.

A property must always keep at least one verified owner. Make sure that owner is you or someone on your staff.

Google Analytics: Analyst for reading, Editor only for setup

GA4 has five predefined roles, each including the permissions of the one below it:

  • Viewer sees settings and data and can build personal explorations.
  • Analyst can also share explorations with other users of the property.
  • Marketer can also create and change audiences, events, key events, and attribution settings.
  • Editor has full control of settings at the property level, without managing users.
  • Administrator has full control, including who else gets access.

Analyst covers reporting. Marketer fits an SEO who needs to mark a form submission as a key event. Editor is for someone fixing a broken tracking setup, and Administrator rarely belongs to anyone outside the business. Grant access at the property level unless the SEO works on every property in your account, because account-level access flows down to all of them.

GA4 also offers two data restrictions you can add to any role: No Cost Metrics and No Revenue Metrics. If your SEO has no need to see what you spend on ads or what you earn per order, switch those on.

Google Business Profile: Manager, never primary owner

From Business Profile settings, then People and access, an owner can invite someone as an Owner or a Manager. Google says managers have mostly the same access as owners: they edit business information, reply to reviews, post updates, add photos and products, and download performance data. They cannot add or remove people or delete the profile. That is the right fit for nearly all local SEO work.

The primary owner is the one account that can hand the profile to someone else. Keep it in the business. A primary owner cannot remove themselves until they transfer the role, so a profile whose primary owner is a departed agency is a profile you will spend weeks recovering. Google also applies a seven-day waiting period to every new owner or manager, during which they cannot delete the profile, remove other people, or transfer primary ownership. Plan around that week rather than discovering it on deadline.

The person you invite needs their own Google Account, and Google Groups cannot be added.

WordPress: a named account, removed afterward

WordPress ships with five roles. An Editor manages every post and page, including other people's, but cannot touch plugins, themes, or site settings. An Administrator can do everything, including installing code.

Content work fits Editor. Most SEO plugin settings, redirects, and sitemap options sit behind Administrator, so technical SEO usually needs it. Create a separate administrator account in the SEO's own name and email, never your own login. That keeps their changes traceable in any activity log and lets you delete the account, and reassign its content to you, on the last day.

Shopify: a collaborator account with a request code

Shopify gives outside help its own door. A collaborator account reaches only the sections of the admin you approve, and it does not use up one of your staff seats. Under Settings, then Users and permissions, then Collaborators, you can require a collaborator request code, so only people you have given the code can even ask for access. Shopify's help center says the code requirement is on by default. Generating a new code invalidates the old one, which is a tidy way to stop stray requests after a project.

When the request arrives, approve only what the work needs. Product editing and online store themes cover most SEO tasks. Orders, customers, payments, and finances usually do not belong in the request.

The day the work ends

Access granted this way comes back in a few clicks per tool:

  • Remove the person from Search Console, and delete any verification file or DNS record they added.
  • Remove them in GA4 at both the account and property level, wherever they appear.
  • Remove them from People and access on every Business Profile, and confirm the primary owner is still yours.
  • Delete their WordPress account and assign its content to a staff user.
  • Remove the Shopify collaborator and generate a new request code.

Keep a short list of every invitation you send during the engagement. Offboarding then becomes reading that list back.

item.title: When Google's AI does the booking, be bookable
item.description: Google's AI Mode now books restaurant tables in nine countries and is testing tickets and local appointments. How a local business becomes one it can book.
item.content:encoded:
When Google's AI does the booking, be bookable

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 28, 2026

A diner types "find me a table for four near Clarendon at seven on Friday, somewhere quiet with good pasta" into Google's AI Mode. Google searches several reservation services at once, checks which places actually have a table, and hands back a short list with buttons that complete the booking. A restaurant that only takes reservations by phone is not on that list, however good its reviews are.

How the feature grew

Google introduced agentic restaurant reservations in AI Mode in August 2025, first for people enrolled in its Labs experiments in the United States. The companies Google named as partners at the time included OpenTable, Resy, and Tock for dining, Ticketmaster, StubHub, and SeatGeek for events, and Booksy for local appointments such as hair and beauty.

In November 2025 restaurant booking opened to everyone in the United States without the Labs sign up, while event tickets and local service appointments stayed in Labs. In April 2026 Google took restaurant booking to eight more markets: Australia, Canada, Hong Kong, India, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa, and the United Kingdom. Each time the mechanics were the same. Google queries the reservation platforms it works with, compares live availability, and links the guest to complete the booking on the partner's system.

The plain requirement: live availability on a platform Google reads

The AI can only offer a slot it can see. For a restaurant, that means taking online reservations through a platform Google works with and keeping its availability current there. For a salon, barber, spa, or similar appointment business, it means an online booking system with real calendar slots, which is where a partner like Booksy fits. Event venues need their inventory on a ticketing partner.

If you already use one of these platforms, check that your listing there is complete: the correct business name, address, cuisine or service type, price range, photos, and a calendar that reflects reality. A platform profile that shows no availability because nobody maintains it reads the same as no profile at all.

Your Google Business Profile still decides who gets considered

Booking sits on top of ordinary local search. The AI first decides which businesses match the request, using the same signals that drive the local map results: category, location, hours, reviews, photos, and what the web says about you. Then it checks who can be booked. The groundwork is the same as always:

  • Pick the most specific primary category and keep hours, including holiday hours, correct.
  • Add your reservation or booking link to the profile, so it points at the platform holding your availability.
  • Describe the experience in words a request might use: quiet, private room, gluten free, walk ins welcome, parking.
  • Answer reviews that mention the things people ask for, because those descriptions feed the matching.

The new Business Profile performance reports show whether booking clicks are rising after you make these changes.

Test it the way a customer would

Open AI Mode and ask for your kind of business the way a real customer would, with a day, a time, a party size, and a reason. Try three or four variations. Note whether you appear, whether you appear as bookable, and who appears instead. Repeat the same questions monthly. If a competitor across the street keeps getting the booking, compare their platform profile and their Business Profile with yours line by line; the difference is usually visible.

What this does not cover yet

Appointment and ticket booking were still Labs features in the United States at the last public update I can confirm, and Google has not opened flight or hotel booking in AI Mode. Contractors, clinics, and law offices are not in this booking flow at all. For them, the work remains being the business the AI names and links to, which my guide to service area businesses on Google covers.

Questions owners ask about AI bookings

Do I have to switch reservation systems?

Only if yours is not one Google reads. Ask your provider directly whether it supplies availability to Google's booking features before you change anything.

Does Google charge me for an AI Mode booking?

The booking completes on the partner's system, so any fee is whatever your reservation platform already charges under your agreement with it.

item.title: Selling inside AI assistants: the real state of play
item.description: Where buying inside ChatGPT and Google AI Mode actually stands for a small online shop in late 2026, which programs need a waitlist, and what to fix first.
item.content:encoded:
Selling inside AI assistants: the real state of play

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 28, 2026

Every week a shop owner asks me how to get a buy button inside ChatGPT. The honest answer changed twice in the last year, and most of the advice still circulating describes a program that has since been reorganized. Here is where buying inside AI assistants actually stands, and the work that pays off no matter which program wins.

What OpenAI launched, and what it changed

In September 2025 OpenAI announced Instant Checkout, which let a person buy from a merchant without leaving the ChatGPT conversation. It ran on the Agentic Commerce Protocol, an open standard OpenAI built with Stripe, and Etsy sellers were first in line. For a few months the pitch was simple: list your products, and shoppers can pay right there in the chat.

In March 2026 OpenAI changed course. A company spokesperson told reporters that "Instant Checkout is moving to Apps, where purchases can happen more seamlessly," meaning checkout now happens inside a merchant's own ChatGPT app or on the merchant's site. The protocol survived, but its job moved toward product discovery: feeding live product data into ChatGPT so it can recommend and link to you. Large retailers with their own ChatGPT apps get the in-chat purchase. A small shop gets found, then sends the buyer to its own checkout.

How a small shop gets into ChatGPT shopping

OpenAI's merchant documentation describes a structured product feed with titles, descriptions, images, prices, and availability. Every purchasable variant needs its own row with a stable parent ID and its own variant ID, and the feed has to carry your real seller name and working links to your shipping and return policies. Onboarding is by application through OpenAI, rather than self serve. Shopify and similar platforms handle much of this for their merchants, so check your platform's sales channel settings before you hire anyone to build a feed by hand.

Product pages still matter when no feed exists. ChatGPT's shopping answers draw on what it can read about you on the open web, so the same clean product pages that work in Google work here.

Google's version runs through Merchant Center

Google took a different road. Its Universal Commerce Protocol is an open standard for agentic commerce, and its first job is direct buying inside AI Mode in Google Search and on Gemini on the web. The shopper pays with Google Pay using details saved in Google Wallet, while the merchant stays the seller of record.

The details matter for a small shop. According to Google's Merchant Center help, the feature covers eligible products in the United States, Canada, and Australia, and it is open to select merchants through an early access interest form. A product shows the Buy button only when its listing carries the native_commerce attribute with checkout eligibility set. The merchant also needs a Google Pay and Wallet Console account, and a payment provider can handle that onboarding. Google lists multi item carts, loyalty account linking, and order tracking and returns as roadmap items, which tells you how early this is.

Your Merchant Center feed is the foundation for all of it. If your feed is messy today, the buy button is not your next step. My guide to Merchant Center free listings covers the feed errors to fix first.

What to do this quarter

None of this requires you to bet on a winner. The same five pieces of work help in ChatGPT, in AI Mode, and in plain Google Shopping:

  • Clean your product data: one variant per row, real stock levels, prices that match the page, and images of the actual item.
  • Publish shipping, returns, and contact pages at stable addresses, written plainly enough that a machine can quote them.
  • Mark up product pages with structured data that matches the visible page. My schema guide for small businesses has the code.
  • Join the waitlists that fit your market, and read the requirements before you apply rather than after.
  • Tag the traffic. OpenAI suggests a utm_medium=feed parameter on feed links, so you can tell ChatGPT shoppers apart in analytics.

Advice to refuse

Be wary of anyone selling guaranteed placement inside ChatGPT or a buy button in AI Mode. Neither OpenAI nor Google sells placement, Google's checkout is invitation only, and OpenAI moved in chat purchases to merchant apps that most small shops do not have. A vendor who promises either is selling something that does not exist on the terms described. My list of SEO and AI search advice to refuse has more of these.

Questions shop owners ask

Do I need my own ChatGPT app to sell there?

Only for purchases that complete inside the chat. Discovery and links to your own checkout come from a product feed and from pages ChatGPT can read.

Will Google charge a fee for AI Mode checkout?

Google's help pages describe the program and its requirements but do not set out a fee schedule for small merchants. Read the current terms in your Merchant Center account before you apply.

item.title: Who Wrote Your Reputation and What AI Search Believes
item.description: I wrote most of my own reputation across thirty years online, and AI search believes it and shows the receipts. An owner audit of praise and provenance.
item.content:encoded:
Who Wrote Your Reputation and What AI Search Believes

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 27, 2026

Search my name and the record glows. Three decades of work surface in the answers, stated with confidence and sourced to pages that describe a seasoned expert. Then click the citations. Ninety five percent of the stellar material traces back to my own hand: sites I own, articles I wrote, interviews I gave, words I published about myself. I stand as the worked example of a reputation the owner wrote personally, and AI search has made that example impossible to hide and worth studying line by line.

The vacuum law

An online record abhors a vacuum, and AI search fills empty space with whatever strangers left behind. An owner who stays silent gets described by a stale directory stub, a furious review from 2016, a namesake in another state with a court record, an ex employee settling a score in a forum thread. Populating the record personally is necessary and legitimate work. I came online in 1993 and spent thirty years answering, in public and under my own name, every question a client could ask: the services, the methods, the credentials, the failures and the corrections. That abundance gives the engines material, and material becomes the answer. The owner who declines to write a record still gets a biography. Strangers hold the pen.

The provenance ceiling

Self corroboration convinces the engine completely. The engine counts sources, weighs consistency, and repeats the record back as fact. The discerning human doing due diligence runs a different audit: click each citation and check the byline. Every road in my record runs back to a property I own or a venue that printed my words. Provenance sets a ceiling on that record because publisher and subject share a name, and experienced buyers read bylines before they read claims. Deals die at that ceiling silently. The prospect praises the materials, says the timing feels off, and hires the competitor a stranger vouched for. The engines believed me at full volume. The human believed me at a discount the size of my authorship share, and my authorship share is 95 percent.

Three kinds of receipts

Receipts come in three kinds, ranked by how hard they are to forge. The first kind is what I say about myself: my pages, my profiles, my stated record. This kind is the foundation and the cheapest evidence in the pile, discounted on sight by anyone who has bought professional services before. The second kind is what venues under my control repeat: my other sites, my newsletter, my columns placed under my own byline, my show. Repetition across my own properties reads as breadth to an engine. To a human it reads as one voice holding several microphones. The third kind is what independent parties stake their own names on. A named client in a named testimonial risks personal standing. A referral spends the referrer's credibility with a friend. A marketplace history backed by paid transactions and verified reviews carries a platform audit behind every star. Coverage an editor chose to run answers to judgment I do not control. The third kind compounds because strangers signed it, and strangers can stop signing the moment the work slips.

The audit I run on myself

Once a quarter I ask the engines who I am, then I click every citation and count the hands. One hand is mine. Several hands belong to outlets that printed my submissions. The hands that matter belong to people with no obligation to me who attached their names to my work anyway. Then I run the subtraction test: strip away every page I wrote or control and see what remains standing. What remains is the reputation strangers will defend in a room I never enter. Any owner can run this audit in an afternoon. The arithmetic is brutal and clarifying, and it converts a vague anxiety about credibility into a number with a direction.

The working instruction

Keep writing the record. The vacuum law grants no retirement, and a silent year hands the pen back to strangers. Spend equal effort earning the third kind. Deliver work that gives a client a result worth signing, then ask for the named testimonial while the result is fresh and the gratitude is specific. Treat marketplace history as an asset with a balance: every completed transaction and verified review raises the share of the record a platform has audited. Give reporters and podcasters material with evidence attached, because an independent voice repeats what it can check. And refuse the counterfeit of the third kind. Bought roundups, generated reviews, and planted praise imitate independent receipts and devalue genuine ones on contact; my guide to SEO advice to refuse names those schemes and the penalties they carry. Thirty years of my own handwriting taught the machines to believe me. The signatures of strangers decide whether humans follow, so I spend my effort collecting signatures I cannot write.

item.title: SEO and AI search advice your business should refuse now
item.description: A field guide for owners: the search tactics to decline, the plausible ones that waste money, and the schemes that end with a site removed from Google.
item.content:encoded:
SEO and AI search advice your business should refuse now

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 27, 2026

Every week a business owner forwards me a pitch that promises search visibility in the age of AI answers. Some of those pitches waste money. A few waste something harder to replace: the trust Google and the answer engines place in a domain. I sort the pitches into three tiers, and I advise my clients to refuse all three, at three different speeds.

Tier one: decline politely

These offers burn budget and return reports. Content sold by volume, priced per post and aimed at a word count, produces pages no customer would quote and no engine will cite. Keyword ranking reports sold as the deliverable measure positions on results pages your customers no longer read. Directory submission blasts and citation packages from 2011 still circulate with new labels. Trophy keyword campaigns chase phrases with national competition while your buyers search with a city in the query. None of this damages a site outright. All of it converts a marketing budget into paperwork.

Tier two: decline firmly

These offers sound modern, and that is the danger. A vendor proposes an llms.txt installation as an AI visibility strategy, as if a courtesy file were a ranking factor. Another sells placements in listicles assembled to be cited, roundups where every entry paid for its chair. A third offers review generation, phrased carefully, at scale. A fourth promises schema sorcery: markup layered onto ordinary pages until the code describes a business far more impressive than the one your customers meet. Each tactic has the shape of a mechanism and the record of a fad. Answer engines cite sources with a history of being right in public. Purchased applause leaves a paper trail, and the trail is the tell.

Tier three: end the relationship

These offers end businesses' presence in search entirely. A proposal to show AI crawlers different text than human visitors is cloaking with a new audience, and Google removes sites for it. An expired domain offered as your new home brings someone else's history, and sometimes someone else's penalties, into your name. Fake locations, fake practitioners, and a network of friendly sites exchanging links all belong to the same family: fabricated evidence of a reputation. The engines audit evidence for a living now. When the audit lands, the penalty lands on the domain, and a new domain starts from zero in an era when zero is a long way down. Any consultant who proposes tier three has told you exactly how the engagement ends.

The sixty second test

Run every pitch through three questions before money moves. First: show me a client you kept through a Google update, and let me call them. A record survives updates; a scheme rents the calm between them, and the calm always ends. Second: what happens to my domain if Google disagrees with this tactic? The honest answer names a risk and a recovery. The dishonest answer changes the subject to rankings. Third: put in writing what you refuse to do. Every consultant I respect keeps a refusal list, and the list is longer than the menu. A vendor who will do anything you can pay for has told you who absorbs the penalty when the audit arrives. It will not be the vendor. Domains are expensive to rebuild and impossible to rush: a new one earns trust at the speed trust is earned everywhere else, one kept promise at a time, in public, on the record.

What to buy instead

Buy the record. Publish under real names, with real experience, on a site that answers customer questions in the words your best people use across the counter. Google's quality guidelines give that record a name, E-E-A-T: experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness, earned in public and assessed in the open. Keep the information current: Google's AI reads today's pages today, while the standalone chatbots answer from a memory months old, so a business that updates its facts competes where freshness counts. When an AI answer gets your business wrong, correct the record at the source; my guide to correcting AI answers walks through that work. Refuse the three tiers, fund the record, and let your competitors rent the shortcuts. One more refusal belongs on the list, and it is the easiest to keep: refuse to panic. Every update produces a week of frightened buying, and the frightened buy the tiers. The record compounds quietly through all of it.

item.title: Nobody Mentions You: The AI Search Problem Owners Miss
item.description: A flawless website stays invisible in AI answers when nobody else on the web mentions the company. Earned mentions, purchased applause, and agency questions.
item.content:encoded:
Nobody Mentions You: The AI Search Problem Owners Miss

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 27, 2026

A business can do everything right on its own website and still vanish from AI answers. The site loads fast, the facts stay current, the pages answer real customer questions, and the engines name the competitors anyway. The missing ingredient sits outside the site entirely: other people, on other sites, talking about the company. AI answers run on corroboration, meaning independent sources repeating a name until the name counts as established fact. A business nobody mentions gives the engines nothing to confirm, and an unconfirmed business gets left out of the answer.

Zero for twelve

I measured this failure in my own practice this week. A regional retailer with several stores asked where it stood in AI search, so I ran a baseline: the questions its buyers actually ask, put to ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Google AI Mode, twelve answers in all. The parent company appeared in zero of the twelve. Its stores appeared again and again, often at the top of the answer. The evidence under those answers ran to review roundups, map and directory listings, and customers discussing their purchases in public forums. Every one of those sources talks about the stores. Almost nothing on the web talks about the company that owns them, so the engines describe the parts and skip the whole. The website held up fine under inspection. The silence sat elsewhere, and no redesign reaches it.

How an answer gets assembled

An owner hears the word mention and pictures a press clipping. In this context a mention means any independent page naming your business in its own words: a review roundup that includes your store, a trade directory entry, a partner page listing you as a supplier, a local news story, a customer thread comparing you with a rival. Your own site counts as testimony from the interested party. Search engines and answer engines both learned long ago to discount testimony and weigh independent repetition. One voice making a claim is advertising. Several unrelated voices making the same claim reads as evidence, and evidence is what an answer is built from. This is why a mediocre site with a loud public record can outrank a polished site in an AI answer, and why the polished site's owner feels cheated. The contest moved off the page years ago. Much of the industry still bills for the page.

What earns mentions

Earned mentions grow out of work other people find useful enough to cite. A retailer that publishes the region's honest price comparison, a contractor whose guide becomes the reference other sites point to, a clinic that answers the question every patient asks: each gives strangers a reason to repeat the name. Local press covers openings, expansions, milestones, and owners who make themselves available as expert sources on deadline. Partners name the suppliers and collaborators they rely on, on pages their own customers read. Directories earn their keep when real customers actually use them, which means the map listings and trade directories in your category deserve current facts, correct names, and photographs a person took. Reviews complete the picture when they come from real transactions, asked for at the counter at the moment of satisfaction and answered in the customer's own words. Every route on this list shares one property: somebody with no obligation to you decided your business was worth a sentence. That sentence is the asset. It compounds, it survives redesigns, and it transfers across every engine that reads the public web.

The purchased version of the same hunger

The hunger for mentions is legitimate, and vendors know it, so they sell the shortcut: placements in roundups assembled for citation, citation packages by the hundred, review generation phrased to sound organic. I catalogued those offers in my guide to SEO advice to refuse, and they belong in the tier an owner declines firmly. Bought applause carries its paperwork with it: disclosed payments, identical phrasing across dozens of sites, roundups where every entry paid for its chair. Engines audit evidence for a living, and a stack of purchased mentions reads as a stack of purchased mentions. Worse, the bought version crowds out the earned one in the budget. Money spent renting applause is money absent from the work that earns it, and the rental expires while the record would have stayed.

Questions to ask before you pay for AI visibility

Three questions separate a mention strategy from a mention purchase. First: show me the independent sources that will talk about my business, and tell me why each one would. A serious answer names publications, directories, partners, and communities, with a reason each would care. A count of placements is a confession. Second: show me my answer presence measured, the same buyer questions on the same engines last quarter and this quarter, with the names that appeared in order. Visibility in AI answers is measurable, and anyone selling it should already own the ruler. Third: put in writing what you refuse to do in my name. The refusal list protects your domain long after the engagement ends, and a vendor without one will eventually buy you the kind of attention that ends in a penalty. Ask all three before money moves, and write the answers into the agreement.

item.title: Service-area businesses on Google Business Profile
item.description: How a business that travels to customers should set up its Google Business Profile: removing the address, choosing service areas, and the phone number.
item.content:encoded:
Service-area businesses on Google Business Profile

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 26, 2026

A plumber, a roofer, a mobile dog groomer, or a pest control company does its work at the customer's door. Google calls these service-area businesses, and it treats them differently from shops: no public street address, a list of areas served instead, and a stricter eye on the details that remain. Most of the trouble I see with these profiles comes from three fields, the address, the areas, and the phone number, so this guide works through each one.

Which kind of business you are

Google recognizes three setups. A storefront serves customers at its address. A service-area business goes to its customers and has no premises where customers are received. A hybrid does both: a showroom or office that customers visit during posted hours, plus crews that travel. A tile company with a showroom is a hybrid; an electrician working from a home office is a service-area business.

Pick the one that matches how customers meet you, because the rest of the profile follows from it. A home-based business that lists its house as a storefront invites strangers to the door and tells Google something it can check and will eventually doubt.

Remove the address when customers don't come to you

Google's service-area help page is direct about it: if you don't serve customers at your business address, remove the address from the profile and enter only your service area. The address still exists in Google's records for verification and for placing you on its internal map. It just stops showing to the public.

Two addresses never qualify. Google's guidelines rule out a rented mailing address where the business doesn't operate, and they rule out P.O. boxes and remote mailboxes. A service-area business can list a so-called virtual office only if staff are actually there during business hours. A coworking desk you visit once a month fails that test.

Choose service areas you can serve

A profile can hold up to 20 service areas, set as cities, postal codes, or other named areas. Google's own tip is that the whole area shouldn't stretch beyond about two hours of driving time from where the business is based. Treat that as an outer limit.

Service areas describe where you work, and they carry little weight in where the profile ranks. Map results still weigh the distance between the searcher and the business location Google holds on file, so a company based in one suburb won't start ranking across a whole metro by listing twenty towns. What wins the farther towns is the website: a useful page for each area where you have real jobs, real photos, and real reviews to show.

Use a phone number that belongs to this business

The guidelines ask for a number that connects to the individual business location, a local number in place of a central call-center line whenever possible, and a number under the business's direct control. Premium-rate numbers aren't allowed at all.

This is where I find the quietest damage. A business with one number on its profile and another on its website may have two perfectly legitimate lines, and it still gives Google, directories, and AI tools two answers to the simplest question about the business. Pick one primary number, put it on the profile, the website header, and the contact page, and keep tracking numbers out of the primary slot.

Keep the name clean

Service-area businesses are tempted to add the city or the service to their name: "Smith Plumbing Denver Emergency Drain Cleaning." Google's guidelines say plainly that unnecessary information in the business name isn't permitted and can lead to suspension. The name on the profile should match the name on the truck, the invoice, and the state registration.

Verification is the gate

Until a profile is verified, nobody can change it, owner or manager. A profile that has never been verified can show in public with outdated details that nobody is able to correct. If your profile is in that state, verification comes before every other fix. For service-area businesses that usually means a video showing the vehicle, tools, and proof of management; my video verification guide covers what to film.

What competitors' listings tell you

Look up the businesses that outrank you and note what they show. Competitors set up as storefronts or hybrids display a street address, and a true service-area business shouldn't add one to match, because it has no premises for customers to visit. A true service-area business competes on what it can prove: reviews that mention the towns and jobs, photos from real sites, prompt answers to questions, and location pages that read like the work of someone who has been there.

A short checklist

  • Business type matches how customers meet you: storefront, service area, or hybrid.
  • Address removed from public view if customers never come to it; no mailboxes or unstaffed offices.
  • Service areas limited to places you serve, within about two hours of your base.
  • One primary local number, the same on the profile and the website.
  • Business name exactly as it appears on signage and paperwork.
  • Profile verified, with at least two people holding access.

Questions service businesses ask

Will removing my address hurt my rankings?

Google still knows where the business is based and uses that location. Removing the address from public view follows Google's guidance for businesses that don't receive customers, and it protects the privacy of a home address.

Can I have a profile in every town I serve?

No. One business gets one profile per real location where it operates. Extra profiles at virtual addresses are a common cause of suspensions.

Should my website list my address?

If you work from home, list the areas you serve and your phone number instead. Your legal notices and invoices can carry the mailing address.

item.title: Google Merchant Center free listings for small shops
item.description: How a small shop gets its products into Google's free listings: the Merchant Center feed, required attributes, shipping, returns, and the errors to fix first.
item.content:encoded:
Google Merchant Center free listings for small shops

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 26, 2026

Plenty of small store owners assume Google Shopping is only an ad product. Free listings, the unpaid half, shows products from any eligible store at no cost, and many of the shops I audit have never switched it on or have a feed full of errors nobody has read. For a shop with a few dozen to a few thousand products, it's some of the cheapest visibility left in search.

Where free listings appear

Google's Merchant Center help page lists the places: the Shopping tab, product rich results in Search with price, availability, and reviews, Google Images and Lens (including Lens results for similar products), YouTube in some countries, Maps, the products section of a Business Profile, and Gemini. The page is careful to say eligibility doesn't guarantee your products will show. Free listings compete on relevance and data quality, and incomplete data loses.

Setting it up

You need a Merchant Center account, a verified and claimed website, and a product source. On Shopify, WooCommerce, BigCommerce, and most hosted platforms, the Google sales channel or an official app builds the feed from your catalog and keeps it current. New Merchant Center accounts are opted in to free listings by default; on an older account, look for the free listings card under Marketing methods and confirm it's on.

A store without a platform integration can upload a spreadsheet feed, but a manual spreadsheet goes stale the first time a price changes. I prefer an automated feed, or, for a small static catalog, letting Merchant Center read the structured data already on the product pages.

The attributes that decide eligibility

Google requires an ID, title, link, image link, price, description, and availability for every product. Depending on the product, it also wants the condition, the brand, a GTIN or manufacturer part number, and whether the item is a multipack or bundle. Clothing needs color, size, age group, and gender.

The GTIN, the barcode number, causes the most confusion. If you resell branded goods, the manufacturer's GTIN belongs in the feed and helps Google match your offer to the product. If you make the products yourself, there's no GTIN to supply, and you mark that the identifier doesn't exist instead of inventing one.

Shipping and returns

In the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, Germany, and several other countries, shipping settings are required. Google also asks for a return policy, ideally set in Merchant Center. These details appear on the listings, and a shopper comparing two stores at the same price will pick the one with free returns shown. Set them once at the account level and they apply to every product.

Fix the Needs attention tab first

The Products page in Merchant Center has a Needs attention tab. That tab is the whole job for the first week. The usual problems I find:

  • Price mismatch. The feed says one price and the page shows another, often because a sale ran on the site and the feed didn't update.
  • Availability mismatch. Products listed in stock that the site says are sold out.
  • Image problems. Promotional overlays, watermarks, or placeholder images.
  • Missing identifiers. Branded products with no GTIN.
  • Policy issues. Restricted products, or a website missing contact details and a return policy.

Each of these has a cause in the store setup. Fixing the cause once beats fixing products one at a time every week.

Write titles for shoppers

The product title in the feed is the line a shopper reads in the results. Lead with what the product is, then the attributes people search by: brand, material, size, color, model. "Walnut cutting board, 18 x 12 inch, end grain" will match more searches than "The Hearthside." Your on-site title can keep the brand flourish while the feed title does the describing.

Connect the pieces

Google's help page recommends linking your Business Profile and any third-party platforms you sell through, and keeping Merchant Center data consistent with your store. Consistency runs in both directions: the product page's structured data, the feed, and the visible page should all carry the same price and availability. When they agree, Google has one answer. When they don't, it has to choose.

How to tell it's working

Merchant Center's performance reports show clicks and impressions from free listings separately from ads. In Search Console, the Performance report's search appearance filter separates merchant listings and product snippets. Give it a few weeks after the errors clear, then compare clicks by product category to see which parts of the catalog Google is showing and which it isn't.

Questions about free listings

Do I need to run Shopping ads?

No. Free listings work on their own. Ads are a separate, paid choice in the same account.

How long until products show?

Google reviews products after the feed is submitted, which can take a few business days. Errors you fix are rechecked on the next feed update.

Do free listings help in AI answers?

Google's help page lists Gemini among the surfaces, and accurate product data is what any shopping assistant needs. Clean feed data is the price of entry.

item.title: The FTC fake review rule for small businesses
item.description: The FTC's rule on consumer reviews took effect October 21, 2024. What it bans, what it allows, and how to ask customers for reviews without risk to you.
item.content:encoded:
The FTC fake review rule for small businesses

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 26, 2026

Reviews drive local search, and for years the rules around them were scattered across platform policies and general consumer protection law. Since October 21, 2024, the United States has had a specific federal rule: the Federal Trade Commission's Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials, 16 CFR Part 465. It lets courts impose civil penalties for knowing violations. Most honest businesses already comply, but a few common habits sit close to the lines, and those are what this guide covers.

This is a practitioner's summary, not legal advice. If you've received a letter from the FTC or a state attorney general, talk to a lawyer.

What the rule prohibits

The FTC's own question-and-answer page groups the rule into a handful of sections:

  • Fake or false reviews and testimonials (section 465.2), including reviews from people who never used the product and reviews that misrepresent the reviewer's experience.
  • Paying for reviews of a particular sentiment (465.4). Incentives become a problem when there's an express or implied requirement that the review be positive, or negative about a competitor.
  • Undisclosed insider reviews (465.5). Reviews by officers, managers, employees, or agents, and in some cases their relatives, need a clear disclosure of the relationship.
  • Company-controlled review sites (465.6) presented as independent.
  • Review suppression (465.7), such as legal threats, intimidation, or false accusations used to get reviews removed.
  • Fake social media indicators (465.8), like bought followers or views, when the business knew or should have known they were fake.

What you can still do

You can ask every customer for a review. The FTC says the rule exempts generalized requests to purchasers to post reviews about their experiences, and offering an incentive to everyone who responds doesn't change that, as long as the incentive doesn't depend on what the review says.

The incentive question has a second layer. Google's own guidelines for Business Profiles go further than the FTC and prohibit offering incentives for reviews on Google at all. A gift card for every reviewer may be legal under the rule and still get reviews removed or a profile penalized on Google. When the platform's rule is stricter, the platform's rule is the one that governs your listing.

Review gating

Review gating means asking customers how their experience was and sending only the happy ones to Google or Yelp, while routing unhappy ones to a private feedback form. The FTC's guidance says the rule doesn't contain a specific prohibition against asking only customers you expect to be satisfied, and in the same answer it warns that the practice can still violate the FTC Act if it misleads people about how the business is rated. Google's review policy forbids selectively soliciting positive reviews.

My advice is simpler than either text: send the same request to every customer, with one link, and handle complaints in your reply to the review. Many reputation tools still ship with gating switched on by default, so check yours.

Employees and family

Staff and relatives are the easiest source of early reviews and the most common source of trouble. Under the rule, a review by an officer or manager that doesn't disclose the relationship is a problem, and a business that asks employees to write reviews has duties to keep those reviews disclosed. Google, for its part, removes reviews that come from conflicts of interest. The cleanest policy is that employees don't review the business they work for.

Responding to bad reviews

The suppression section targets threats and false accusations meant to get a review taken down. Replying publicly, offering to make things right, and reporting a review to the platform when it breaks the platform's rules are all ordinary practice. Threatening a customer with a lawsuit over an honest negative review, or claiming a review is fake when you know it's real, is where the rule bites.

Testimonials on your own website

The rule covers testimonials too. Quotes on your site should come from real customers, reflect what they said, and not be edited to change the meaning. If you show only your best reviews, don't present the page as a complete or independent rating. When you pay or comp someone for a testimonial, disclose it next to the quote. And never add review star markup for reviews of your own business that you collected and display yourself; Google treats those as self-serving and won't show them.

A compliance checklist

  • One review request, sent to every customer, with no screening question in front of the link.
  • No incentives for Google reviews; any incentive elsewhere offered to everyone and not tied to sentiment.
  • No reviews from owners, staff, or relatives, or a clear disclosure where the platform allows them.
  • No bought followers, likes, or views.
  • Bad reviews answered in public, reported only for real policy violations.
  • Website testimonials sourced, unedited in meaning, and disclosed when compensated.

Questions about reviews and the rule

Does the rule apply to a small local business?

Yes. It applies to businesses of any size that sell to consumers in the United States.

Can I ask a happy customer in person to leave a review?

Yes. Asking is fine. The risk comes from a system that asks only the happy ones and steers everyone else away.

Can I buy reviews from a service that promises they're real?

No. A review written to order by someone who wasn't your customer is a fake review under the rule, whatever the seller calls it.

item.title: Black Friday sale pages that keep their rankings
item.description: Build one Black Friday URL and reuse it every year: what Google advises for sale pages, when to publish, what to do in January, and how to track the results.
item.content:encoded:
Black Friday sale pages that keep their rankings

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 26, 2026

Every November I find shops publishing a brand-new Black Friday page at an address like /black-friday-2026, while last year's page sits forgotten at /black-friday-2025 with all the links people gave it. The new page starts with nothing, and Google has to find it, crawl it, and decide what it's worth in the few weeks that matter. One permanent address fixes that, and it's the advice Google itself has given.

What Google has said

In July 2021, Alan Kent of Google's Search Relations team published a post on deal pages that restated the earlier Black Friday advice in a short list: create dedicated pages for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, reuse the same URL each year, create the pages early so Google can index them, link to the sale page from the home page, and include a high-quality image. The same post added that the page title should carry the event description, the page should have text that describes the event, and if the deals are revealed on the day, the page should go up early with general information and be recrawled after the update.

That post is five years old, and it's still the most specific official statement on sale pages I can find. The reasoning hasn't aged: a page that has existed for years has links, history, and a place in the index that a new page has to earn from scratch.

One URL, updated every year

Choose an address with no year in it, such as /black-friday/ or /sale/black-friday/. Put the year in the title and the heading, where shoppers want to see it, and change it each autumn. The address stays put. If you have old yearly pages, redirect each one to the permanent address with a 301 so the links pointing at them still count.

Cyber Monday is a separate search with its own audience, so it can earn its own permanent page. A single combined page works too when the offers are identical. What fails is a new page per year per event, which turns one strong page into eight weak ones over four years.

When to publish

Google Trends shows searches for Black Friday building for weeks before the day, every year. Publish the page, or refresh last year's, by early November. If you can't reveal the deals yet, say what's coming: which departments, when the sale opens, how to get notified. That gives Google something real to index. On the day the deals go live, update the page and request recrawling of that URL in Search Console's URL Inspection tool.

Link to the page from the home page and the main navigation while the sale runs. That link is the strongest signal you can send about which page matters this month.

What goes on the page

Write a few paragraphs a shopper would read: what's on sale, the dates, shipping cutoffs for delivery before the holidays, the return window for gifts, and how the discount is applied. Then link to the actual sale products and categories. A page that's only a banner and a countdown clock has nothing for a search engine or an AI assistant to quote.

Prices belong on the product pages. If those pages carry merchant listing structured data, the sale price can appear in Google's shopping results. Check that the price in the markup matches the visible price on the day the sale starts; when they disagree, Google has two prices and no reason to trust either.

After the sale

Don't delete the page in December, and don't redirect it to the home page. Keep it live with a short note that the sale has ended, a sentence about when it returns, an email signup if you have one, and links to current offers. Take it out of the main navigation, but leave it linked from somewhere on the site, such as a sales or offers hub, so it stays crawlable.

The page will rank for little in March. What matters is that in November it wakes up with years of history behind it instead of none.

Measure it the same way each year

In Search Console, filter the Performance report to the page's URL and compare the same date window around Black Friday each year. Because the address never changes, the comparison is simple. That's another quiet benefit of one permanent URL: yearly pages make the history impossible to read. Keep a note of the dates the page was refreshed and the deals went live, so a jump or a dip can be traced to something that happened.

Questions about holiday sale pages

Should the year be in the title?

Yes. Shoppers search for "Black Friday 2026" and expect current deals. Put the year in the title and heading, and keep it out of the URL.

What about other seasonal sales?

The same rule fits any sale that returns: a back-to-school page, a spring sale, an anniversary event. One permanent address per recurring event.

My platform made a new page every year. What now?

Pick the strongest one, usually the oldest or the one with the most links, move it to a year-free address, and redirect the rest to it.

item.description: Why a local business should claim its Apple Maps place card and its Bing Places listing, what each one feeds, how to set them up, and keeping them consistent.
item.content:encoded:
Apple Maps and Bing Places: local listings past Google

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 26, 2026

Local SEO conversations start and end with the Google Business Profile, and for good reason. But every iPhone owner who asks Siri for a nearby locksmith, taps a business in Apple Maps, or opens directions from a text message is reading Apple's data. Every search in Bing, and the local results that Microsoft's products draw from it, reads Bing's. Both listings are free, both take an afternoon, and most of the small businesses I check have claimed neither.

Apple: the place card

Apple's listing for a business is called a place card. It shows the name, hours, phone, website, photos, and actions such as booking or ordering. Apple describes Business Connect as a free platform for controlling how a business shows up across Apple Maps, Wallet, and other Apple apps. The old businessconnect.apple.com address now forwards to business.apple.com, where Apple has folded the tool into a wider product called Apple Business that also covers devices and email for small companies. The Maps part works the same way: claim the location, prove you run it, and edit the card.

What you can manage on the card:

  • Logo, header image, and photos.
  • Hours, including special hours for holidays.
  • Actions that let people order, reserve, or book from the card.
  • Showcases, Apple's term for short promotions and seasonal offers.
  • Insights on how people found and used the card.

Claiming on Apple

Sign in at business.apple.com with an Apple Account, ideally one tied to the business email instead of someone's personal ID. Add the company, search for the location, and claim it. Apple verifies the business before you can edit. For a business with many locations, Apple offers bulk tools and works with listing-management services that push data to it.

Apple Maps has long shown ratings and reviews from partner services such as Yelp alongside its own, so a business with a poor profile on a partner site may see that reflected in Maps. Check what your card shows before assuming it matches Google.

Bing: Places for Business

Microsoft relaunched Bing Places for Business in October 2025. Management moved to bing.com/forbusiness, existing accounts were moved over automatically, and a recommendation tool now flags missing fields such as photos, hours, and category details. Listings are free and appear in Bing Search and Bing Maps. Search Engine Journal's report on the launch noted that Microsoft plans deeper links to Copilot; I treat that as a plan until Microsoft documents it.

The fastest route is the import from Google. Bing can read an existing Google Business Profile and copy the name, address, hours, and phone. That's a good start only when the Google profile is already correct, because the import copies mistakes as faithfully as facts. Check the category afterward, since Google and Bing don't use the same category lists.

Why these two matter for AI answers

AI assistants answer local questions from whatever business data their systems can reach. Bing's index feeds a number of them, and Apple's data feeds Siri and Apple Maps on every iPhone. If Google says you close at 6 and Apple says 5, an assistant has two answers to pick between, and a customer may drive across town to a locked door. Consistent data across the three big map providers removes the conflict before any AI system has to resolve it.

Keep one master record

Keep a single document with the business name exactly as registered, the address or service area, the primary phone number, the website, the hours, and the categories. Every listing gets copied from that record, never from another listing. When something changes, update the record first and then each listing on the same day: Google, Apple, Bing, and then the directories and review sites that matter in your trade.

That same record pays off when a business changes its name or moves, which is when listings drift most. My guide to changing a business name without losing search covers that case in detail.

A quick audit you can do today

  • Search for your business in Apple Maps on a phone. Note the hours, phone, website, and category.
  • Search for it on bing.com and in Bing Maps. Note the same details.
  • Compare both with your Google profile and your website's contact page.
  • Claim whichever listing you haven't, and correct every difference.
  • Put a reminder in your calendar to recheck all three before each holiday season.

Questions about Apple and Bing listings

Does claiming these help my Google rankings?

Not directly. They get you found by people who don't use Google, and they make your business data agree everywhere, which helps every system that compares sources.

Do I need a paid listing service?

Not for one or a few locations. Both platforms are free to use directly. Services earn their fee when you manage dozens of locations.

What if someone else already claimed my listing?

Both platforms have a dispute or ownership-request process. Start it from the listing itself and keep proof of the business, such as a utility bill or registration, ready.

item.content:encoded:
Glossary of SEO and AI search terms

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 6, 2026 · Updated October 26, 2026

The vocabulary of search and AI visibility, one or two sentences per term. Every entry carries an anchor, so a link can point straight at the definition you need. To find every page that discusses a term, use the index.

301 redirect
A permanent forwarding instruction from an old address to a new one, which passes nearly all of the old page's ranking signals along.
AEO (answer engine optimization)
Shaping pages so that systems which reply with an answer rather than a list of links, from featured snippets to voice assistants to chatbots, can lift a passage and credit it.
AI Overviews
The generated summaries Google places on many results pages, citing the sites they borrowed from. AI Mode extends the idea into a back-and-forth conversation.
AI share of voice
The share of relevant buyer questions where an AI assistant names your brand, measured against the competitors it names instead, tracked with the same question set every month. Method in measuring share of voice in AI answers.
Alt text
Words attached to an image in the markup that describe it for people using screen readers and give crawlers a clue about the picture's subject.
Anchor text
The visible, clickable wording of a hyperlink. When it names the destination's topic, both readers and crawlers know what they'll find.
APO (Automatic Platform Optimization)
Cloudflare's WordPress feature that stores complete pages at the edge so even the first byte arrives quickly. Included with Cloudflare's Pro plan and above, or $5 a month on the free plan, per Cloudflare's pricing.
Astroturfing
Posting praise for a product while pretending to be an ordinary customer, often from new or borrowed accounts. Reddit moderators remove it on sight; see Reddit and AI answers.
Bing Webmaster Tools
Microsoft's no-cost dashboard for owners, covering crawl, index, and keyword data from Bing, whose index also supplies Copilot and several other assistants.
Canonical tag
A line in a page's head nominating which address should represent a set of duplicate or close copies. Google weighs it heavily but may overrule it.
CDN (content delivery network)
A network of servers spread around the world that keeps copies of a site's files and hands them to each visitor from somewhere nearby.
Client-side rendering (CSR)
Building a page in the visitor's browser with JavaScript, so the HTML the server sends starts nearly empty. Crawlers that skip scripts see little or nothing. See SEO for AI-built websites.
CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)
The Core Web Vital that scores how far things jump around on screen during loading. Aim for 0.1 or lower.
Collaborator account
Shopify's door for outside help: a partner reaches only the admin sections the merchant approves, without taking a staff seat. A request code keeps strangers from asking. See Give your SEO access.
Comparison cohort
A fixed group of pages evaluated across reporting periods so changes in the page inventory can be distinguished from changes in performance. See Search Console comparisons.
Core update
A broad change Google makes to how it ranks everything, several times a year. Pages can rise or fall without anything being wrong with them; Google lists each one on its Search Status Dashboard.
Core Web Vitals
Three experience scores Google tracks, LCP, INP, and CLS, taken from Chrome users over a rolling four weeks.
Crawl budget
The practical ceiling on how much of a site a search engine will fetch in a given stretch of time. A concern for very large sites and those spawning endless URL variants.
Crawler
Software that requests pages on its own to read them, such as Googlebot, Bingbot, GPTBot, or ClaudeBot. People also say bot or spider.
Custom extraction
A crawler feature that pulls a chosen piece of every page, by XPath, CSS selector, or regex, into a column, so one crawl can audit headings, schema types, or tracking codes sitewide. Recipes are in custom extraction.
Delegated owner
A Search Console owner added by another owner rather than by placing a verification token on the site. Same powers as a verified owner, and the access ends the moment an owner removes it. See Give your SEO access.
Digital PR
Earning coverage and mentions on other people's sites, newsletters, and shows by giving writers something worth using. The sentences those mentions contain now feed AI answers; see digital PR for AI search.
E-E-A-T
Experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness: the qualities Google's quality raters look for in a page and its author, with trust counted as the most important.
Earned media
Coverage a business didn't pay for and doesn't control: a reporter's article, a reviewer's post, a mention in someone else's newsletter.
Entity
A single real-world thing, whether a company, person, place, or product, that search engines and AI models recognize as one concept however a page happens to phrase its name.
Faceted navigation
Category filters for attributes like color, size, or price. Left open to crawlers, the combinations can balloon into millions of addresses.
Field data
Speed and responsiveness figures gathered from actual visits, as opposed to one synthetic test run on a single machine.
Free listings
Unpaid product results Google shows across Shopping, Search, Images, Lens, and Maps, fed by a store's Merchant Center data. See Merchant Center free listings.
GEO (generative engine optimization)
Work aimed at how generative AI tools portray and cite a company or a page. In practice it overlaps almost entirely with AEO and AI SEO.
Google Business Profile
The free Google listing that puts a business on Maps and in local results, carrying its hours, categories, photos, and reviews.
GTIN (Global Trade Item Number)
The barcode number a manufacturer assigns to a product, such as a UPC or EAN. Resellers put it in their product feed; makers of their own goods mark it as not applicable.
hreflang
Markup that pairs each language or country edition of a page with the audience that should see it.
HSTS
A security header telling browsers to reach a site only over HTTPS for a set period, so no visit ever falls back to an unencrypted connection.
Hybrid business
A business that both receives customers at a posted address and travels to them, such as a tile showroom with installation crews. Its profile shows the address and a service area. See service-area businesses.
Index
The store of pages a search engine considers eligible for results. Nothing ranks until it's in there.
IndexNow
A shared ping system: when a page appears, changes, or disappears, the site tells Bing, Yandex, and other members right away instead of waiting for a recrawl.
INP (Interaction to Next Paint)
The Core Web Vital that times the gap between a tap, click, or keystroke and the screen's visible response. Aim for 200 ms or lower.
JSON-LD
Google's preferred way to write structured data: a JSON object inside its own script element, kept apart from what visitors see.
LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)
The Core Web Vital that times how long the biggest image or text block in the opening view takes to finish drawing. Aim for 2.5 s or lower.
llms.txt
A suggested standard: a Markdown summary kept at the top level of a domain, pointing language models to the pages most worth reading.
Material connection
The FTC's term for any tie between a brand and the person endorsing it, such as payment, free product, or employment. In the United States it has to be disclosed clearly wherever the endorsement appears.
Meta description
The short summary written into a page's code that search engines often show beneath the title in results. It invites the click rather than setting the rank.
Near-duplicate
Two pages whose text is almost, but not exactly, the same, such as product variants or city pages built from one template. Crawlers can flag them by similarity score; see near duplicates and H1s.
Niche edit
A paid link inserted into an article that's already published and indexed, rather than a new article written for the purpose.
noindex
A directive, set in a meta tag or a response header, asking search engines to keep a page out of results.
Open Graph tags
The og: meta tags in a page's head that set the headline, summary, and image Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack, and most messaging apps show when someone shares the link. See social share cards.
Orange cloud
Cloudflare's icon for a proxied DNS record, meaning visitors pass through Cloudflare's network, with its caching and protection, on the way to the site. A gray cloud means DNS only.
Orphan page
A page nothing else on the site links to. Only a sitemap entry or an outside link can lead anyone to it.
Permalink
The permanent address of a single post or page. In WordPress, the Permalinks settings screen decides its pattern; the post name pattern produces readable addresses.
Place card
Apple Maps' listing for a business: name, hours, phone, photos, and actions such as booking, managed through Apple's business tools. See Apple and Bing listings.
Placed article
An article published on another site through a paid arrangement, usually carrying a link back. Google expects the link to be marked rel="sponsored"; see why I turn down backlink work.
Prerendering
Generating a finished HTML copy of a JavaScript page ahead of time and serving it to crawlers or visitors, so the content is readable without running scripts.
Primary owner
The single account on a Google Business Profile that can transfer the profile to someone else. It should belong to the business, never to a vendor. See Give your SEO access.
Pull request
A proposed change to a code repository, shown line by line for review before it's merged. SEO fixes made this way are recorded, reviewable, and easy to undo; see SEO in your Git repository.
Reddit Answers
Reddit's own AI search, launched in December 2024, which summarizes discussions from across the site in reply to a question.
Redirect chain
Several redirects strung together before the visitor arrives. Every extra step costs time and can weaken the signals passed along.
rel="sponsored"
A link attribute that tells Google a link was paid for, so it passes no ranking credit. Google's spam policies ask for it on every paid or sponsored link.
Rendering
Running a page's scripts to produce what a browser finally shows. Anything that exists only after this step can escape crawlers that skip it.
Review gating
Screening customers before asking for a public review, so only satisfied ones reach the review site. Google's policies forbid it, and the FTC warns it can mislead. See the FTC review rule.
Rich results
Search listings dressed up with extra details drawn from structured data, like star ratings, prices, or breadcrumb trails.
robots.txt
A plain text file at the top of a domain that tells bots which folders to stay out of. It governs fetching; keeping a page out of results takes noindex.
Scaled content abuse
Google's spam policy against publishing many pages mainly to manipulate rankings, whether people, AI, or both produce them. The main target of Google's 2026 spam updates.
Schema markup
Structured data written in the Schema.org vocabulary to spell out the people, organizations, places, and products on a page.
Search Console
Google's free owner dashboard: clicks and impressions, index status, Core Web Vitals, and alerts about problems it detects.
Server-side rendering (SSR)
Assembling the complete HTML on the server so a crawler gets every word in the first response, no scripts required.
Service-area business
A business on Google that travels to its customers, such as a plumber or mobile groomer, and hides its street address from the public profile. It verifies by showing its tools, vehicle, and nearby street markers. See video verification.
Single page application (SPA)
A website that loads one HTML shell and swaps content in with JavaScript as people click, instead of loading a new page for each address. Many AI app builders produce them.
Site reputation abuse
Placing a third party's low-value pages on a trusted site to borrow its standing in search, such as coupon or gambling sections rented out under a respected domain. Against Google's spam policies.
Soft 404
A URL that answers with a success code yet shows an empty or not-found page. Google files it with the real 404s.
Spam update
An improvement to the automated systems Google uses to detect pages that break its spam policies. Sites caught by one usually drop sharply and quickly.
Title tag
The headline written into a page's code that search engines usually show as the clickable link in results and browsers show on the tab.
Topic cluster
One hub page that defines a subject, plus a set of pages that each answer a single buyer question in full, all linked together. See topic clusters for AI search.
Vibe coding
Building software by describing what you want to an AI tool and accepting what it writes, with little reading of the code itself. Andrej Karpathy coined the phrase in February 2025.
Video verification
Google's way of confirming a Business Profile from a single unedited phone recording of at least 30 seconds that shows the location, the business, and proof the owner runs it. Explained in my video verification guide.
White label
A service delivered under someone else's brand: an agency resells the work, and its client never sees the vendor's name.
XML sitemap
A machine-readable list of the addresses a site wants crawled, often with the date each last changed.
