item.title: XML sitemaps that tell the truth
item.description: What an XML sitemap should hold in 2026: canonical URLs that answer 200, honest lastmod dates, no priority games, and how I audit one against a crawl.
item.content:encoded:
XML sitemaps that tell the truth

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 24, 2026

An XML sitemap is a list you hand to search engines that says, in effect, "these are the pages I want found, and this is when each one last changed." Search engines treat it as a hint, never an order, and they decide how much to trust it by checking it against what they actually find. A sitemap that lists redirects, duplicates, and dates that change every night teaches them to ignore it. A sitemap that matches the site exactly earns the opposite. Most of the sitemaps I audit fall somewhere in between, and the fixes are almost always about honesty rather than tags.

What a sitemap is for, and what it can't do

A sitemap helps discovery. It's most useful on large sites, new sites with few links pointing in, sites with pages that sit deep in the navigation, and sites that publish or change often. On a twenty page site where every page is linked from the menu, Google will find everything without one, though a sitemap still costs nothing and gives you a tidy report in Search Console.

What a sitemap can't do is make a page indexable. If a page is thin, duplicated, blocked, or canonicalized somewhere else, listing it in the sitemap doesn't overrule any of that. It just adds a line to the Page indexing report explaining why the URL you submitted wasn't indexed. If your real problem is pages that are discovered and then left out, that's a quality and duplication question, and my guide to reading the Page indexing report is the better starting point.

The one rule: list only the URLs you want in search

Every URL in the file should pass four tests at once:

  1. It answers 200. Not a 301, not a 404, not a soft 404 that says "no results" with a 200 status.
  2. It's the canonical. The page's own canonical tag points to itself, exactly as written in the sitemap: same protocol, same host, same trailing slash.
  3. It's indexable. No noindex in the robots meta tag or the X-Robots-Tag header.
  4. It's crawlable. robots.txt doesn't block it.

That rules out a lot of what plugins and platforms put in by default: tag archives you've set to noindex, paginated listings, internal search results, attachment pages, staging hostnames, and the http or non-www versions of URLs. The sitemap and the canonical tags have to agree. When they contradict each other, you've sent two signals and asked Google to pick one.

Honest lastmod dates

Of the optional tags, lastmod is the only one that still matters. Google has said it uses lastmod when the dates are consistently and verifiably accurate, and Bing has written publicly that it leans on lastmod to decide what to recrawl. The key word is accurate. A lastmod should change when the main content of the page changes: a rewritten section, a corrected fact, new prices. It shouldn't change because the footer copyright year rolled over, a sidebar widget updated, or the site was rebuilt.

The common failure is a generator that stamps every URL with the build time. Every page claims it changed today, every day, and the search engine learns that this site's dates mean nothing. On this site, each page's source carries an updated date that I change by hand when the content changes, and the build writes that date into the sitemap, the visible "Updated" line, and the structured data. One date, set on purpose, appearing in three places that agree.

The tags to leave out

priority and changefreq are in the original protocol, and Google ignores both. You can leave them in without harm, but I take them out, because every field in a file should mean something, and these give people the false comfort of having "prioritized" pages that no crawler is listening to.

The same goes for most of the image sitemap extension. Google retired the image caption, title, geographic location, and license tags in 2022. Only the image location is still read. Image entries are worth including for images that matter in search, such as products, diagrams, and original photography, and not worth bloating the file with every icon and spacer.

Size limits and sitemap index files

One sitemap file can hold up to 50,000 URLs and be up to 50 MB uncompressed. Past either limit, split it into several files and list them in a sitemap index file, then submit the index. You can gzip the files to save bandwidth; the size limit applies to the uncompressed version.

Splitting is useful well below the limit. On a programmatic site of more than 20,000 pages, I gave each content type its own sitemap, so Search Console reported indexing for each group separately, and a problem in one template stood out instead of hiding in a site-wide average. The price index case study shows how that played out. Split by template or section, not alphabetically or at random, because the point is to make the reports readable.

Telling search engines where it lives

  • robots.txt. Add a line such as Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml. It must be an absolute URL, and it can sit anywhere in the file. Every crawler that reads robots.txt finds it there, including ones you'll never submit to by hand.
  • Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools. Submit it once in each. You don't need to resubmit after every change; they fetch it again on their own.
  • No more pings. Google retired its old sitemap ping address in 2023, so scripts that still call it are doing nothing. For Bing and the other engines that support it, IndexNow is the way to announce changed URLs quickly.

One ordering detail I care about: if you announce new URLs with IndexNow, do it after the new sitemap is actually live, not the moment you push. On this site, the IndexNow job waits until the public sitemap matches what the release meant to publish, because an announcement about a page that's still deploying wastes the crawl.

How I audit a sitemap

I compare three lists: what the sitemap says, what a crawl finds, and what Search Console reports. In Screaming Frog, I run a normal crawl with the option to crawl linked XML sitemaps switched on, then look at the Sitemaps tab. Three filters do most of the work:

  • Non-indexable URLs in sitemap. Redirects, errors, noindexed pages, and canonicalized pages that shouldn't be listed. Each one is a broken promise.
  • URLs not in sitemap. Indexable pages the crawl found that the sitemap forgot. Often a whole post type or a newer section the generator wasn't told about.
  • Orphan URLs. Pages in the sitemap that nothing on the site links to. Search engines can find them, but an orphan with no internal links rarely ranks. Usually the fix is a few good internal links, sometimes it's deleting a page nobody meant to keep.

Then I open Search Console's Sitemaps report to confirm the file was read without errors, and filter the Page indexing report to submitted URLs only. The gap between "submitted" and "indexed" for each sitemap is the clearest single measure of how much of your intended site Google has accepted.

I also open the file in a browser and read it. A sitemap with a stylesheet attached shows as a readable table instead of raw XML, which makes it easy to spot a staging hostname, a duplicated section, or a run of identical dates at a glance. The sitemap for this site works that way.

Common mistakes I find

  • Two sitemaps from two plugins, both submitted, listing different versions of the same URLs.
  • An old sitemap still submitted in Search Console from a previous platform, full of URLs that now redirect.
  • Development or staging hostnames inside the production file.
  • The sitemap itself blocked in robots.txt, or served with a noindex header that some crawlers read as a reason to drop it.
  • Trailing slash or capitalization mismatches between the sitemap and the canonical tags.
  • A cache layer serving a sitemap that's weeks old, so new pages never appear in it.

None of these is dramatic on its own. Together they make a sitemap that search engines treat as noise.

Questions people ask about sitemaps

Does a sitemap help me rank?

Not directly. It helps search engines find and recrawl pages. Ranking comes from what's on the pages and who links to them.

Do AI search tools read XML sitemaps?

Many of the crawlers that feed AI answers read robots.txt and follow its sitemap line, and Bing's index, which several AI tools draw on, uses sitemaps and IndexNow. An accurate sitemap is part of being easy to read for every kind of machine, alongside an llms.txt file.

Should I list PDFs in my sitemap?

Yes, if they're useful documents you want found in search and they answer 200 at a stable address. Leave out drafts and duplicates of HTML pages.

How often should the sitemap update?

Whenever a page is added, removed, or meaningfully changed. Generate it from the same source as the site, so it can't fall behind.

If your sitemap and Search Console disagree and you can't tell why, that's the kind of thing I sort out in a crawling and indexing engagement. The bigger picture of crawl health is in my site-wide technical SEO work.

item.title: The show notes cascade: podcasting as an AI search strategy
item.description: Every podcast episode publishes its show notes into hundreds of trusted directories, and AI answers cite those copies. How to write notes that get quoted.
item.content:encoded:
The show notes cascade: podcasting as an AI search strategy

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 24, 2026

Most podcasters treat show notes as a courtesy, a few lines typed after the episode is edited and forgotten by morning. I treat them as the most widely republished writing I do. Every episode I release copies its notes, word for word, onto hundreds of podcast indexes and directories, each one a page on a domain that search engines and AI assistants already trust. When someone later asks a machine about my subject, the answer often comes back built from sentences I wrote once, in a notes field, months earlier.

How the cascade works

A podcast is distributed by a feed, and the feed is promiscuous. Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Podcast Index, Pocket Casts, Castbox, TuneIn, Podcast Addict, and a long tail of smaller directories and apps all read the same feed and republish what it carries: the episode title, the audio, and the full text of the show notes. Nothing about this requires outreach, pitching, or a link building campaign. Syndication is simply how the medium works, and it has quietly become an answer engine optimization channel hiding in plain sight.

The second half of the mechanism is newer. Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, ChatGPT, and Perplexity answer questions by gathering text from pages they can reach, and directory pages are easy for them to reach. A claim that appears in your notes therefore exists in hundreds of places at once, stated the same way everywhere, which is precisely the pattern these systems read as settled fact. Repetition used to be what links did for a page. Now the words themselves do it, and show notes repeat more faithfully than almost any other format on the web.

The morning the machine quoted me to myself

On October 24, 2026, I searched Google for what I think about a television show I have covered on my own podcast, The Chris Abraham Show. AI Mode answered with my position, quoting my show notes for season 11, episode 3 nearly word for word: what I came for, what I stayed for, the themes I keep returning to. My essay on the same subject sat at the top of the ordinary results below it. Nobody had written about my opinion except me. The answer engine found my own sentences, syndicated across the podcast directories and my episode pages, and handed them back as the authority on the question.

That is the proof of concept in miniature. The query was about me, but the machinery does not care whose name is in the question. Ask what a company thinks about its own industry, what a founder believes about her market, what a consultant recommends about his specialty, and the same sources get consulted. If your positions live in your show notes, they are positioned to be quoted. If they live only in the audio, the machines mostly cannot use them, because an answer engine quotes text.

Write the notes for citation

Once you see the cascade, the writing rules follow from it. Write every episode's notes as if a directory reader, and then a machine, will repeat them without you in the room.

  • Use full entity names. Write the whole name of every person, company, show, and product, spelled the way it should be quoted. A first name alone cannot be connected to you, and a misspelling repeated in two hundred places is a misspelling with authority.
  • Phrase claims the way they should come back. If you hold a position, state it in one clean, quotable sentence inside the notes. The engines lift sentences, not vibes. My guide to correcting AI answers starts from the same principle: answers are built from sentences found somewhere, so make sure the findable sentences are yours and are right.
  • Include the canonical links. Link each claim to the page on your own site that owns it. Directories carry links unevenly, but the ones that survive point the engines, and the occasional human reader, at your canonical version.
  • Say who is speaking. Name the host and guests with their roles and affiliations. Attribution is what turns a floating opinion into a position a named expert can be cited for.

Front load what matters

Platform notes do not all survive intact. Spotify trims episode descriptions at roughly 4,000 characters, and different directories cut or compress at their own limits. So put the citable material first: the episode's actual subject, the named people, the position sentences, and the key links, all before the credits, the chapter markers, and the housekeeping. Think of the first screen of notes as the press release and everything after it as the appendix. What travels is what appears early, so the sentences you most want quoted should be the sentences every copy is guaranteed to carry.

Keep a mirror you own

Directories are landlords. They can trim your text, surround it with their own recommendations, or disappear, and you hold no deed to any of it. So the cascade needs a home base: a site you control that republishes every episode with the full notes, a transcript, and one permanent page per episode. My own show's website is the worked example I point clients to. It carries the complete notes with no character cap, full transcripts that give the engines thousands more quotable words per episode, and an llms.txt file that hands AI crawlers the whole catalogue in plain text. My guide to what belongs in an llms.txt file covers that format. The directories supply the reach. The mirror supplies the canonical record the reach points back to.

Every episode is a page that stays

A blog post fights for attention in the week it ships and then sinks into the archive. An episode behaves differently. It is a dated, permanent landing surface in every directory at once, still indexed and still quotable years later, and each new episode adds another one without disturbing the rest. A season of weekly episodes is fifty new surfaces a year, each carrying your names, your links, and your stated positions. That compounding is why I call podcasting an investment rather than a content chore: the production cost is paid once, and the citation surface keeps appreciating as the catalogue grows.

Measure the position queries

None of this counts until you check what the machines actually say. Monthly, run a fixed set of position queries: what does this person think about that subject, who offers this service in this place, what is the difference between these two approaches. Record which sentences come back, which sources get cited, and whether your phrasing survives the round trip. My guide to measuring AI share of voice describes the method I use. When an answer quotes your notes verbatim, the cascade is working. When it quotes a competitor's framing instead, you have found the next episode to record and the next notes to write.

Where I fit

I run this play on my own show before I recommend it to anyone, and I build the same machinery for clients: notes written for citation, a mirror site with transcripts and permanent episode pages, and a monthly set of position queries that proves whether the answers are moving. If you want the baseline first, my AI visibility audit runs your money queries through the major answer engines and reports what they say about you today. Book a thirty minute call on my calendar to talk about your show or your site, or write to me through the contact page if you would rather start in writing.

item.title: Measure seasonal local SEO before the busy weeks arrive
item.description: Build a seasonal local SEO baseline using comparable dates, fixed map grids, website inquiries, and store records before demand changes the numbers.
item.content:encoded:
Measure seasonal local SEO before the busy weeks arrive

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 24, 2026

A seasonal business can double its search traffic while its local visibility gets worse. Demand rises, customers search more often, and the totals look encouraging. I build the comparison before the rush so the owner can distinguish seasonal demand, changes in search visibility, and the inquiries that actually reach the business.

Choose the selling window first

Start with the dates that matter commercially. A holiday retailer might earn a large share of its revenue in a short period; a landscape contractor may have several weather dependent peaks. Ask the owner when customers research, when they buy, and when the business has capacity to serve them. Those can be three different windows.

Record the comparison rule before seeing the results. Calendar dates help with fixed holidays. Matching weekdays helps when weekend shopping dominates. For a movable holiday, days before the event may be more useful. Keep more than one view when necessary and explain the reason. Choosing whichever comparison looks best after the season makes an impressive chart and a poor decision tool.

Preserve a baseline for each location

Save the current profile details, the location landing page, the main search queries, and the available performance exports. Record the period covered and the export date. A business with several stores needs separate rows for each actual location, because a strong branch can hide deterioration at another.

Include store opening dates, changes in hours, promotions, major website releases, and advertising activity. These notes explain discontinuities that a search chart cannot. Keep source exports intact and do calculations in a separate working sheet. If a metric changes definition or disappears, retain the old record and explain the break instead of quietly splicing unlike series together.

Keep demand and visibility in separate columns

Search Console shows how the website performed in Google Search. Compare relevant queries and landing pages, then examine clicks, impressions, click through rate, and position together. A larger total can reflect more searches, broader query coverage, or better visibility. The shape of the change matters.

Google's traffic diagnosis guidance includes examining seasonality and using Google Trends. Treat that as context for the market rather than a count of your customers. Compare brand searches with broader product or service searches. A successful radio campaign may increase people searching for the store by name without demonstrating stronger discovery for unfamiliar customers.

Freeze the map measurement setup

A local ranking grid samples results from defined points around a location. To compare runs, preserve the coordinates, spacing, query wording, tool settings, and reporting method. Save the raw observations when the tool allows it. A different grid covers a different market and can change the apparent result without any business improvement.

Decide how to handle missing results and the tool's ranking limit. A business absent from the measured depth is unobserved beyond that limit; assigning it an arbitrary position can distort an average. Report the share of sampled points where the store appears in the chosen visible range, alongside the map itself. This is a repeatable sample, not a promise of what every shopper sees.

Define customer actions accurately

Business Profile reports include several kinds of interactions, and the available metrics vary. Google's documentation defines calls as clicks on the profile's call button. That count does not establish that somebody answered or that a sale followed. Direction requests likewise do not establish a visit.

Keep those actions separate from answered calls, qualified website inquiries, bookings, and recorded sales. Profile performance can also include activity associated with Google Ads. Note advertising changes when interpreting the series. A simple report with honest labels is more useful than a blended “leads” total assembled from actions with very different meanings.

Use an example that exposes the uncertainty

Imagine an illustrative store with website search clicks rising from 1,000 to 1,500 across comparable selling windows. Its share of sampled map points in the top three falls from 60 percent to 45 percent. Meanwhile, qualified inquiries rise from 40 to 44. Traffic grew by 50 percent, but inquiries grew by 10 percent and the measured local footprint weakened.

Those figures do not identify the cause. They suggest questions: did demand expand faster than the store's reach, did traffic shift toward informational pages, did opening hours constrain conversions, or did inquiry tracking change? The next investigation should follow the discrepancy. Declaring a blanket victory would hide the commercially useful part of the report.

Schedule repairs around operational capacity

Use quieter weeks for substantial location page work, tracking repairs, and changes that require careful review. Agree a release cutoff with the owner before peak trading. Keep a path for urgent corrections, especially inaccurate customer information or a broken purchase route. The cutoff is an operating decision tied to the business, not a universal SEO rule.

During the rush, use a small dashboard: important search trends, the fixed local sample, profile actions, qualified inquiries, and trading notes. Assign someone to check that phones, forms, directions, and hours still work. A ranking improvement has little value when a customer cannot get through to the store.

Finish with a decision for the next season

After the peak, compare the agreed windows and identify what deserves investigation or investment. Separate confirmed technical improvements from commercial outcomes and unresolved explanations. Preserve the same measurement setup for the following season, adding annotations when the business changes.

item.title: Search Console comparisons that support better decisions
item.description: Compare Search Console periods with consistent filters, matched weekdays, and page groups so seasonal demand and changing query mixes do not distort the result.
item.content:encoded:
Search Console comparisons that support better decisions

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 24, 2026

An upward line can conceal a weak month. A downward line can follow a useful expansion into new searches. I want a comparison that identifies which pages changed, which searches changed, and what decision the evidence supports. A percentage on its own leaves too much room for a confident explanation that the data never established.

Write the question before choosing the dates

Decide whether you are checking a release, reviewing a month, or investigating a loss. Each calls for a different comparison. A monthly review needs a view of the whole property. A product-template change needs the affected product pages, with an unchanged group beside them where the site has a suitable comparison. Keep the release date in the notes so later readers can distinguish the work from the measurement window.

Record the property, search type, country, device, page filter, query filter, dates, and export date. Save the original exports. Another person should be able to reopen the report and understand what you selected.

Match the calendar to the business

I start a routine comparison with two complete 28-day periods. Each contains four of every weekday. That is a reporting choice, and it removes one source of noise for businesses whose weekday and weekend traffic differ. It does not remove holidays, promotions, school schedules, or changes in demand.

For seasonal work, add the comparable period a year earlier and explain any holiday shift. Google's traffic-drop guidance recommends looking across 16 months and checking search demand in Google Trends. Trends supplies context about interest; it does not tell you how many visits your website should have received. Avoid using an unfinished day or preliminary data as the endpoint of a performance claim.

Keep a stable group of pages

Compare pages that existed in both periods separately from newly published pages. Otherwise a larger site can appear to have improved its existing material when the extra clicks came from additions. For a migration, preserve the mapping from old addresses to new ones before grouping results. Explain which addresses you treated as the same content.

Separate brand searches from the service or product searches relevant to acquiring customers. Define the brand spellings you included. A query filter creates a particular view of the data; describe that view rather than presenting it as the whole market.

Read the metrics together

Google defines click-through rate as clicks divided by impressions. Average position summarizes the highest result from your site across the observations in the selected view. Neither number is a permanent rank for a keyword. Device, country, page, and query groups help explain changes that the property total hides.

Consider an invented example. An established page receives 100 impressions at position 2. It then starts appearing for another 100 searches at position 20 while retaining its original visibility. The combined average becomes 11. Reporting that change as a nine-place collapse would misdescribe what happened. The page gained exposure to a second set of searches.

Calculate the click change in absolute numbers as well as percentages. A move from two clicks to four is a 100 percent increase and two additional clicks. Both statements belong in the report. Calculate a combined CTR from total clicks divided by total impressions, rather than averaging the percentages of rows with different impression counts.

Give the reader a compact evidence record

  • Scope: the property, filters, and page group.
  • Window: two complete periods, with calendar differences explained.
  • Result: clicks and impressions in each period, absolute changes, and percentage changes.
  • Explanation: the pages and query groups responsible for most of the movement.
  • Limit: what remains unresolved, and the next check that will resolve it.

A useful conclusion sounds like this: in this hypothetical comparison, existing service pages lost 30 clicks, new guides added 45, and the property gained 15 overall. The service-page loss still needs investigation. That gives the owner a task the headline total concealed.

Separate a release check from a growth claim

My guide to verifying an SEO fix covers whether the intended change reached the pages. This comparison answers a later question about search performance. A successful deployment and a rise in clicks are separate observations. Concurrent campaigns, seasonality, competitors, and other releases can affect the second.

I bring this reporting discipline to SEO audits: preserve the baseline, identify the affected group, and explain what the next decision rests on. An owner should be able to challenge the conclusion using the evidence delivered with it.

item.title: How to choose the next SEO fix when developer time is scarce
item.description: Choose the next SEO task using business value, affected pages, evidence, dependencies, and effort, then keep a clear record of what shipped and what changed.
item.content:encoded:
How to choose the next SEO fix when developer time is scarce

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 24, 2026

An audit can produce a hundred findings while the development team has room for two changes. The useful question is which two deserve the available time. Counting warnings will not answer it.

I organize that decision around the pages the business depends on, the strength of the diagnosis, and the work required to deliver a change. A priority list is a set of choices under constraints. It should explain why something moves first and what evidence would change that choice.

Identify the pages that matter to the business

Begin with a short inventory of useful destinations: the services people inquire about, products currently available to buy, location pages for operating branches, and articles that support a real customer decision. Ask the owner which actions make those pages valuable.

Traffic alone can mislead. An old article may bring many visits without producing relevant inquiries, while a specialist service page attracts a small audience with a strong reason to call. Avoid inventing a monetary value for either. If conversion evidence is absent, record the owner's explanation and label it as a business judgment.

Use Search Console to examine search visibility alongside that inventory. Google's introduction to Search Console describes its crawl, indexing, and performance reports. Those reports supply observations about search; they do not establish the value of a lead or identify every cause of a change.

Separate active failures from improvement opportunities

A broken inquiry form on an important service page needs a different conversation from a title that could be clearer. Likewise, an accidental exclusion affecting a whole product category deserves investigation before a cosmetic improvement to an infrequently used archive.

Use three practical queues:

  • Restore: an important customer action or access path has failed.
  • Investigate: evidence suggests a material problem, but the cause or scope remains uncertain.
  • Improve: the current experience works, and a bounded change could make it more useful.

These queues prevent an attractive improvement from displacing an unresolved failure. They also avoid treating every suspicion as an emergency. A sudden graph change may justify checking the data before changing the website.

Compare candidates without false precision

For each candidate, record five fields: business relevance, affected population, confidence in the diagnosis, implementation effort, and dependencies. Use plain descriptions. “Shared template serving the current product catalog” is more informative than an unexplained impact score of nine.

Confidence concerns the explanation, not the confidence of the person presenting it. A reproducible failure with a known template cause is different from a correlation between a release and falling visits. Give the second case an investigation task that could confirm or reject the theory.

Effort includes review, release coordination, content preparation, and verification. A ten minute code edit that needs a vendor's approval and an overnight maintenance window is not a ten minute delivery. Ask the developer for an estimate before ranking the task as an easy win.

A simple high, medium, or low label can help sort a discussion, provided its meaning is written down. Avoid multiplying arbitrary scores into a precise looking return forecast. The ordering is a decision aid, not a prediction of future rankings.

Work through a small hypothetical backlog

Imagine a supplier with one developer afternoon available. Three findings arrive: the quote form fails on mobile, twenty product pages have similar descriptions, and an old archive has short meta descriptions. These are invented examples, not reported client results.

The quote form belongs in Restore if testing reproduces the failure. Fixing it protects the customer action that existing visits are supposed to support. The product descriptions need more context: do the products serve different needs, and is important specification information absent? That may become an editorial assignment before any code work is required.

The archive descriptions can wait unless someone establishes a stronger business reason. A crawler highlighting them in red does not change that. The outcome of the afternoon should be a repaired and verified quote path, plus a clearly assigned investigation of the product pages.

If the form failure turns out to be a test configuration problem, revise the queue immediately. Good prioritization leaves room for new evidence rather than defending yesterday's order.

Make each selected task small enough to finish

Turn “improve product SEO” into a bounded assignment: inspect one product family, identify missing information, decide which template fields are needed, and verify the revised output on named examples. The next task depends on that result.

Assign one owner and specify the closing evidence. A title change needs the expected title on the relevant production URLs. A redirect repair needs the intended destination and response behavior for the agreed source set. A form repair needs a successful submission and confirmed receipt, following the page to inbox inquiry test.

Do not require a ranking increase to close a development ticket. That would leave a technically complete change permanently open while search performance moves for many reasons. Track implementation and business measurement in separate fields.

Review the queue after each release

Keep a compact change log: what changed, where, when, who checked it, and what remains unknown. If the evidence reveals a wider issue, expand the next task with that evidence. If a hypothesis fails, remove it from the implementation queue.

Review outcomes over a period appropriate to the question, acknowledging seasonality and other releases. A clean before and after crawl establishes changed technical behavior. It does not isolate the cause of every later traffic movement. The guide to verifying SEO repairs covers that distinction.

The deliverable is a short list somebody can act on: an owner, a reason, a prerequisite, and a test for each item. That is what I expect from a technical SEO audit and from ongoing SEO support. Progress becomes easier to assess when the queue records decisions instead of accumulating warnings.

item.title: Google Business Profile video verification: plan the take before you press record
item.description: Passing Google Business Profile video verification the first time: what Google wants on camera for storefronts and service areas, and what to do if it fails.
item.content:encoded:
Google Business Profile video verification: plan the take before you press record

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 24, 2026

For a lot of businesses, the only verification option Google offers now is a video recorded on a phone. It looks easy, and it fails for reasons that are easy to avoid: the street wasn't clear, the sign didn't match the profile, or nothing on screen proved the person filming runs the place. Google judges one continuous take, so every one of those mistakes means starting over. This is the checklist I work from, built on what Google's help pages say as of October 2026.

You don't pick the method

Google decides which verification methods a profile gets, and its help page says plainly that they "can't be changed." Depending on the business type and region, the menu can include phone or text, email, a postcard, a live video call with a Google representative, or a recorded video. If the recorded video is the only choice on your screen, that's the one to prepare for.

The rules for the recording itself

  • One continuous take of at least 30 seconds. Google wants it unedited, unique, and complete, with no breaks.
  • Recorded live on a phone, through the Business Profile. Footage shot earlier and uploaded later doesn't count, and neither does anything from a desktop.
  • Nothing sensitive. Keep bank, tax, and ID numbers, other private details, and other people's faces out of the frame. Film before opening or when the shop is empty.

In the app, the path is Get verified, then Business video. Google reviews the upload in up to five business days.

What a storefront or hybrid business has to show

Google treats a storefront as a business that serves customers in person at an address with permanent signage. A hybrid business does that and also travels or delivers. The video needs three things, in this order.

  1. Where you are. Start outside with a street sign, the building number, a neighboring business, or a landmark, so a reviewer can match the spot on Google Maps.
  2. That the business exists there. Pan to the storefront and the sign. Google requires the business name printed on a permanent fixture, a signboard, wall, or window, and it must match the name on the profile. A banner zip-tied to a fence doesn't qualify, and neither does a sign still carrying an old trade name.
  3. That you manage it. Unlock the door, walk in, and show something only staff can reach: the register or point-of-sale screen, the kitchen, the stockroom.

Google's own advice is that a business without permanent signage should be set up as a service-area business instead.

What a service-area business has to show

Plumbers, cleaners, mobile groomers, and every other business that goes to its customers verify differently, and Google says a service-area business shouldn't show its address on the profile at all.

  1. Where you operate from. Street signs or landmarks at the business address. If you work from home, Google says the signs and landmarks in your immediate neighborhood are acceptable. It specifically warns against filming empty land or places with no clear markers.
  2. That the business exists. Professional tools, equipment, stock, a branded vehicle, business cards, or branded uniforms.
  3. That you run it. Perform a piece of the service, or unlock the branded van and show what's inside. Google also accepts a business permit, invoice, or utility bill in the business name, held to the camera with the account numbers covered.

Rehearse it, then record it once

Walk the route before you record, with the phone in hand and the app closed. Decide where you'll start, which sign you'll hold on for a few seconds, which door you'll unlock, and which document you'll show. Do it in daylight. Hold each proof steady long enough to read; a quick swipe past the sign is as good as no sign. Narrating as you go ("this is the corner of Main and Fifth, here is the sign, here is the register") costs nothing and leaves the reviewer less to guess.

Before you start, open the profile and compare it against what the camera will see. The business name, the address, and the category on the profile should match the sign, the building, and the work. A profile name stuffed with keywords that appear on no sign is a mismatch the video will expose.

If the video fails

Google tells you why it rejected the video and offers a Review issues button. The replacement has to include everything from the first recording plus whatever was missing, so record the whole sequence again, start to finish, with the gap fixed. Read the reason closely before trying again; a second video with the same flaw will fail the same way. Google's help page also suggests trying another verification method, if one is offered, before contacting support.

When the reason makes no sense, or the profile fails again and again, the trouble usually sits in the profile itself: a name that doesn't match any document, an address Google associates with another business, a category that doesn't fit what's on camera, or a history of edits that made the listing look unstable. Those need fixing before the next video, or every recording will hit the same wall.

Don't edit the profile mid-verification

Google's help page warns that changing the business name, address, or category while a postcard is on its way makes the code stop working. The same logic applies to every method: an edit hands Google a new set of facts to check. Settle the details first, verify, and make any planned changes afterward, one at a time.

How I help with stuck verifications

I take on profiles that keep failing verification, along with suspensions, duplicates, and listings stranded with a former agency. I start by reconciling the profile against the real business and its paperwork, then script the video with the owner so the single take shows everything Google asks for. Google makes the decision, and no one can promise its outcome, but a prepared take removes the avoidable reasons to fail. item.title: Reading the new Google Business Profile performance reports
item.description: Google is testing a rebuilt Performance section for Business Profiles. How to read each new report, Overview first, and what the numbers mean.
item.content:encoded:
Reading the new Google Business Profile performance reports

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 24, 2026

Google is testing a rebuilt Performance section inside Google Business Profile, with an Overview that leads with recommendations and separate sections for Engagement, Reviews, Audience, and Search trends. The test arrived about a day after Google launched its new Business Home portal, and it changes what an owner should look at first. I covered the announcement in my weblog post on the rebuilt scoreboard and promised a full guide to reading the new reports. This is that guide, section by section, in the order I read them myself.

First, check whether you have it

Open your Business Profile and choose Performance. If the page opens with recommendations and the five new section names, your account is in the test and everything below applies to the screens in front of you. If it still shows the familiar single page of totals and charts, you are on the old reports and nothing is wrong with your account.

The rollout is gradual and account by account. Search Engine Roundtable reported the test on October 23, 2026, after Jaikishan Raturi of Wisevu and Syed Amir shared screenshots and video of their accounts, and noted that Barry Schwartz did not yet have it in his own account that day. There is no setting to request and no form to submit. While you wait, capture one screenshot of your old totals as a baseline. Old and new figures may not line up neatly, and a saved baseline settles arguments that memory always loses.

Overview: start with the recommendations

The Overview is the summary screen, and its most useful addition sits at the top: a short list of recommendations drawn from your profile's completeness and recent performance. Read that list before any chart on the page. It is Google's own prioritised worklist for this profile, and it tells you what the platform currently thinks is unfinished, stale, or worth confirming.

A new recommendation usually means one of two things: Google changed what it wants from profiles, or your details drifted out of date as hours, services, and attributes changed in the real business. A recommendation that disappears means the gap it named has closed. Work the list from the top, but verify every item against the business itself before accepting it. A recommendation is a prompt, not an order, and the owner who knows the shop floor outranks the algorithm's guess. Where a suggestion is wrong for your business, decline it and move on with a clear conscience.

Engagement: actions, counted honestly

Engagement gathers the actions people took from your profile: the calls, messages, direction requests, website visits, and bookings your listing produced. Look first at the direction of the totals across a whole quarter rather than any single week. Local demand moves with weather, holidays, school terms, and road works, and a quarter smooths most of that noise into a line you can actually read.

A rise means more searchers reached the point of acting, which is the only point that pays. A fall means less until you have run the interpretation check two sections below, because some of those actions now happen somewhere else. Before blaming the market, compare each action against the channel that receives it. If calls fall, ring the number on your own profile and confirm it connects to the right desk. Broken plumbing hides inside report totals far more often than lost demand does, and it is cheaper to fix.

Reviews: read below the star rating

The Reviews section breaks the detail out instead of compressing everything into one average: how many reviews arrived, how the ratings spread, and the words themselves, close enough to read in place. Look first at the distribution and the pace. Ten reviews carrying two furious outliers tell a different story than a smooth average suggests, and a steady trickle of recent reviews outweighs a proud total gathered years ago.

Then read the text as field research. A cluster of new reviews after a menu change, a hire, or a remodel is your customers writing the changelog. Phrases that repeat across reviews are the phrases the next searcher will meet, so note them exactly. Answer every review briefly and without argument, especially the unfair ones, because the reply is written for the reader who comes after. Then fix the operational thing the complaints repeat. Owners tend to read reviews as reputation. Read them as the cheapest customer research you will ever be handed.

Audience: who is finding you

Audience gathers the people behind the views into one place, so you can see who the profile reaches instead of guessing from the totals. Look first for a match or a mismatch: whether the audience arriving looks like the customers you actually want to serve. A profile can be busy and wrong at the same time, and busy wrongness still costs you the hours spent answering it.

A widening audience after a new service, a move, or a name change usually means the profile started matching new searches, which is growth you can plan around. A narrowing one can mean a competitor opened closer to your best customers, which is a different problem entirely. Hold the audience picture next to your service list and your service area. If strangers keep arriving for something you do not sell, your categories or services are promising it on your behalf. Correct the listing before you correct the customers.

Search trends: the customer's own words

Search trends shows the searches that led people to your profile and how those searches are moving over time. Look first at rising terms you did not plan for, and at your core money terms if they start slipping down the list. Both ends of that movement are instructions, one about what to add and one about what to defend.

Searchers rename things before businesses do. When a trade term gives way to a plain phrase, the market is rewriting your signage in its own vocabulary, and the profile that answers in that vocabulary wins the next visit. Mirror the winning words in your services, your business description, and the local pages of your website, spelled the way customers spell them. Retire the phrases nobody types anymore, however fond the founder remains of them. Sentiment is not a search strategy.

Falling interactions are not falling demand

The old reports trained owners to treat every interaction as demand arriving at the door. That link is weakening. AI answers now resolve questions that used to end with a tap on your profile: the hours, the price range, whether you stock the thing, whether people rate you well. The customer still buys. The tap just happens inside the answer instead, or never happens at all.

An October 2026 analysis of three American florists found profile interactions down 26 percent year over year, with website clicks down 30 percent, calls down 21 percent, and direction requests down 15 percent, while the shops traded on. Three shops make a small sample, so treat those figures as a direction rather than a measurement of your market. Still, the direction matches what I see across accounts: when interactions fall while revenue holds, demand did not vanish. The answer moved upstream. Your job shifts from winning the tap to being the business the answer names, which is why I track AI share of voice alongside these reports every month. Never judge a month by interactions alone again.

A monthly routine that takes twenty minutes

Pick one morning a month and give the reports twenty honest minutes, in this order. First, the Overview, clearing or consciously declining each recommendation. Second, Engagement, comparing the month with the month before and with the same month last year. Third, Reviews: the count, the average, the pace, and the three phrases customers repeated most. Fourth, Audience, in a single line about whether the people arriving are the people you want. Fifth, Search trends, choosing one rising term to adopt and one fading term to retire.

Write those five lines down in the same place every month. Reports reward memory, and a profile read monthly for a year teaches more than any single deep dive performed in a panic. End the routine by choosing exactly one action for the month ahead. A reading that produces nine worries produces none of the fixes, and the reports will be there next month to grade the one you picked.

Mistakes owners make with the old reports

Most of these will survive the redesign, so retire them now. Judging by days, and reading one rainy Tuesday as a trend. Comparing December with January and calling the difference decline. Chasing views, and celebrating impressions while calls and bookings quietly thin out. Treating a drop in calls as lost customers before checking the AI answers, the phone number, and the calendar for an explanation. Never capturing a baseline, so every redesign leaves the owner arguing with a memory. And reading the reports only when something already feels wrong, which guarantees the numbers arrive attached to a bad mood and get believed for the wrong reasons.

Where I fit

Reading these reports well is judgement work, and it sits inside the local search work I do for clients: profile upkeep, a steady review rhythm, and a monthly read of what Google and the AI answers are telling the market about a business. If the new layout has reached your account and you want the first read done properly, book a thirty minute call on my calendar and bring your Performance screen with you. I will read it with you from the top, and you will leave knowing which numbers deserve action and which deserve a shrug. item.title: Spam link spikes and the disavow file: when to act at all
item.description: A burst of junk backlinks rarely needs a response. When Google says the disavow tool fits, how to build a careful file, and the mistakes that cost rankings.
item.content:encoded:
Spam link spikes and the disavow file: when to act at all

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 24, 2026

Sooner or later a backlink tool shows a chart with a cliff in it: hundreds of new links in a month from domains nobody recognizes, scraped directories, foreign casino pages, and strings of nonsense. The instinct is to fight back with a disavow file. Usually the right response is to write the spike down, check one or two things, and leave it alone. Sometimes it isn't, and the difference matters.

What Google does with junk links

Since the Penguin 4.0 update in 2016, Google has treated most manipulative links by discounting them rather than punishing the site they point to. Its people have repeated the point for years. In April 2024 John Mueller said Google ignores link spam and that links pointing at pages returning 404 count for nothing at all. In April 2025, speaking at a Search Central event, he went further: Google has no internal concept of "toxic backlinks," the disavow tool is not routine maintenance, and he would reach for it only with a manual action in hand.

Google's own help page for the tool says the same thing in drier language. Most sites don't need it. It is meant for a site with a considerable number of spammy, artificial, or low quality links that have caused a manual action or are likely to cause one. And it is labeled an advanced feature, because a careless file can hurt a site's performance in search.

Why spikes look scarier than they are

Third party backlink tools count everything they find, and they find a lot of garbage. Scraper sites copy pages wholesale with the links intact. Automated directories list every domain they can reach. Spam networks link to well known sites to look legitimate. None of that was your doing, and Google has had about two decades of practice ignoring it. A "toxicity" score in a commercial tool is that tool's opinion, built on its own crawl, and Google doesn't share it.

Spikes also coincide with real traffic losses often enough to be framed for them. This year a client's tool showed close to nine times the usual monthly count of new referring links in the same weeks that branded searches fell. The links were real and ugly. They were also not the only thing that changed that month, so they went into the investigation as one hypothesis with a test, rather than as the answer.

When a spike deserves attention

  • Search Console shows a manual action for unnatural links to your site. This is the case the tool was built for.
  • Someone bought links in your name. A previous agency, an old owner, or an overeager employee paid for placements, link exchanges, or private blog network posts. Google's spam policies treat those as link schemes whoever arranged them.
  • The pattern is targeted. Hundreds of exact match commercial anchors pointing at one money page look like an attempt to trip a filter, which is different from random scraper noise.
  • The links point at real pages and the timing fits a loss that survives every other test. Even then, the disavow is a contained experiment, not a cure.

If none of those apply, record the spike with its dates and sources in your SEO log, keep an eye on Search Console, and spend the hours on something that moves rankings.

Build the file from Google's data first

Start with the Links report in Search Console, which shows the linking sites Google itself knows about, and use third party exports only to fill gaps. Review the list by domain, not by URL, and sort it into three piles: plainly manipulative, plainly fine, and unsure. Only the first pile goes in the file. The unsure pile stays out, because a wrongly disavowed link from a real publication throws away value you can't easily get back.

Before disavowing a link you arranged, try to get it removed. Google asks for that first, and if you're filing a reconsideration request after a manual action, documented removal attempts are part of a credible case.

The file format, exactly

  • A plain text file with a .txt extension, encoded in UTF-8 or 7-bit ASCII.
  • One entry per line: a full URL, or a whole domain written as domain:example.com. Subfolders can't be disavowed on their own.
  • Lines starting with # are comments and are ignored. Use them to date each batch and note why it's there.
  • At most 100,000 lines, comments and blank lines included, and 2 MB. Each URL can be up to 2,048 characters.
# Reviewed 2026-10-24: paid placements from a former vendor, removal requests unanswered
domain:cheap-article-network.example
domain:spun-directory.example
# A single page on an otherwise legitimate site
https://news.example/sponsored/old-placement.html

Uploading, replacing, and undoing

Only a property owner can upload, and the tool works with URL prefix properties, not Domain properties, so verify the right one first. A list applies to that property and its child properties, and the http and https versions need their own lists. Each upload replaces the previous file entirely, so always edit the current file rather than uploading a fresh one with only new entries; errors are flagged immediately and leave the old list in place. A button cancels every disavowal for the property. Google says changes in either direction take a few weeks, and disavowed links keep appearing in the Links report afterward, which surprises everyone the first time.

Mistakes I clean up

  • Disavowing the whole export. Someone uploads a tool's full "toxic" list and quietly throws away links from local news, suppliers, and universities.
  • Losing the old file. A new upload replaces the old one, so years of careful entries vanish when someone starts over.
  • Forgetting a migration. The old domain's file doesn't follow the site to a new domain or protocol.
  • Treating disavow as the fix for a traffic drop while the real cause sits in templates, indexing, or redirects.

How I handle link reviews

I don't sell link building, for reasons I explain in why I turn down backlink work, and I don't sell disavow files by the thousand lines. I review the profile against Search Console's data, keep the file conservative, and treat links as one hypothesis among several, as in the clinic migration, where I rebuilt an inherited file to keep legitimate domains. If a spike landed in the same month as a traffic loss, start with a technical SEO audit that finds the cause before anyone uploads anything.

item.title: Your website form says success. Did anyone get the inquiry?
item.description: Trace a test inquiry from landing page to form, confirmation, inbox, and reporting. Find delivery failures and false conversion counts before buying traffic.
item.content:encoded:
Your website form says success. Did anyone get the inquiry?

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 20, 2026

A visitor can press Send, see a reassuring message, and still fail to reach your business. Conversely, a real inquiry can arrive without appearing in your analytics report. Before treating a shortage of leads as a search problem, test the entire contact route and write down where the evidence stops.

Choose one journey and agree on the test

Begin with a landing page that matters commercially. Follow its contact button as an ordinary visitor would, using a phone as well as a desktop when possible. Include any intermediate service page, embedded scheduler, or external booking screen. A homepage contact link may work while the button on a course or product page points to an obsolete destination.

Tell the person receiving inquiries that a test is coming. Use clearly labeled test content and an address you control. Agree whether the test may create a CRM record or trigger an automatic reply. If the route creates a paid reservation or another commitment, use the provider's supported test environment or stop before that action. Testing should produce identifiable evidence without confusing staff or customers.

Distinguish five different events

A useful investigation separates the stages that dashboards often collapse into one conversion:

  1. Contact intent: the visitor follows a contact or booking link.
  2. Submission attempt: the visitor presses the form's submit button.
  3. Accepted request: the form system confirms that it has accepted the information.
  4. Business delivery: the intended inbox or CRM receives a usable record.
  5. Qualified conversation: staff confirms that the inquiry is relevant and can be followed up.

These events need different evidence. A button click proves interest in a route, not that a message arrived. A confirmation screen alone does not prove inbox delivery. A delivered message is not automatically a sale. Name the stage in the report so nobody mistakes a convenient measurement for the business outcome.

Check the visitor experience before inspecting tags

Look for the defects a customer encounters: the wrong form, a missing service option, a keyboard covering a required field, validation that clears the message, or a confirmation with no explanation of what happens next. Verify the destination of each priority call to action. Repeated buttons may share styling while leading to different places.

Try a deliberate validation failure as well as a successful submission. Leaving a required field empty should not produce the same success event as a completed request. Refresh the confirmation page and revisit it directly. If either action adds another apparent inquiry, the report may be counting page visits rather than accepted submissions. Record the behavior before changing the setup.

Follow the message into the business

Record the submission time and check the form provider's record where available. Ask the recipient to confirm arrival in the expected inbox, not just in a forwarding account or spam folder. Check that the reply address works and that the message includes the context needed to respond. A notification without a usable sender or service reference can leave staff unable to help.

For a CRM connection, verify the actual record and assignment. An integration can accept a submission yet fail to assign it to the current owner. For an external scheduler, inspect the confirmed appointment in the scheduling system. Treat mail delivery, integration delivery, and notification delivery as separate checks whenever they are separate systems.

If something fails, preserve the test reference and the available error evidence. The next fix might belong to the website, mail service, form provider, or CRM administrator. Repeatedly changing SEO metadata will not repair a broken delivery connection.

Check what analytics actually records

Observe the test in your analytics debugging tools and compare it with the business record. Document what triggers the event: a click, a browser callback, an accepted response, or a confirmation view. Pick one primary success definition for the route and check that a single submission does not count several times through overlapping tags.

Repeat under the consent choices your site offers. A customer may successfully contact you while analytics remains unavailable. Keep consent behavior intact and explain the resulting measurement limit. Do not force a match between inbox totals and recorded analytics events by ignoring visitors' choices.

Keep names, email addresses, message text, and other identifying details out of analytics events and URLs sent to analytics. Google's guidance on avoiding personally identifiable information describes this requirement. Use a nonpersonal form label or service category when appropriate, and inspect the payload rather than assuming a plugin is configured correctly.

Keep a small evidence sheet

For each tested route, record the starting URL, destination, device, time, consent state, expected recipient, observed confirmation, actual receipt, and analytics behavior. Add a status such as passed, failed, or unverified. Use unverified when you lack access to a system; a missing permission is not proof that the system failed.

Retest the failed route after its repair with another labeled submission. Include at least one unsuccessful attempt to confirm that validation no longer produces a false success. Save the outcome and tell the receiving team which test records can be removed. Repeat the essential checks after a redesign, form replacement, or change of destination.

Decide whether the next problem is visibility or follow-up

Once delivery works, review a suitable period of actual inquiries with the business owner. Separate spam, duplicate contacts, unsupported requests, and suitable prospects. If suitable inquiries arrive but remain unanswered, the bottleneck is follow-up. If the route works but relevant visitors rarely reach it, investigate the landing pages and search visibility. The diagnosis should determine the work.

item.title: Moving a website? Check its images and PDFs before closing the old host
item.description: Keep images, PDFs, and share cards working during a website move. Inventory old media URLs, test the new files, and find references to the retiring host.
item.content:encoded:
Moving a website? Check its images and PDFs before closing the old host

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 15, 2026

A website can finish its move while its pictures are still living in the old house. Every article loads, the new domain works, and the migration looks complete until somebody cancels the previous hosting account. Then the photos, brochures, and link previews disappear together. Media deserves its own inventory and its own acceptance check.

Make a second list for files

The familiar migration spreadsheet maps old pages to new pages. Add a separate sheet for images, documents, and other files. Google's site move guidance explicitly includes hosted images and downloads in the move. That matters because a page address and the files used by that page can belong to different servers, accounts, and caching systems.

Start with the old site's crawl, the media library or storage export, and any list of downloads linked from the content. Include files referenced in templates as well as files an editor inserted into an article. A crawl of visible links alone may miss a social image declared in metadata or an alternative image used on a narrow screen.

I provide a media migration inventory worksheet in CSV format. Its example rows are fictional. Replace them with the old file address, its new destination, the page that uses it, and the checks that establish whether the move is complete. Keep the worksheet private if the real inventory contains unpublished documents.

Record what the file is supposed to be

A successful request does not prove the file is right. An image URL can return an HTML error page with a successful status. A brochure link can open a different brochure from three years earlier. Record the expected file type and, where useful, its dimensions, page count, or another detail that distinguishes it from a placeholder.

ItemCheckEvidence to keep
Article imageThe intended image opens at the new address.Response type, dimensions, and a visual check.
PDF downloadThe document opens and contains the expected version.Document title, version date, and referring page.
Share cardThe page points to the correct public image.Metadata URL, image size, and a preview check.
Responsive imageEach offered image variant can still be fetched.The complete source set and its destinations.

Separate copying from updating references

There are two jobs. First, put the intended files somewhere the new site controls. Second, change the references that still ask for them at the previous location. Finishing the first does not finish the second. Search the repository or exported content for the retiring hostname, upload directory, and media delivery domain. Include any encoded versions your content system stores.

Look at image elements, responsive source sets, CSS backgrounds, document links, structured data, Open Graph images, and social card metadata. Check generated pages as well as source files: an import script may keep rebuilding the old addresses after a manual correction. Google's image guidance describes how standard image markup helps discovery; this inventory also checks whether that markup reaches a surviving file.

Decide what happens at the old address

If the media URL changes, decide how visitors and existing links should reach the replacement. For a permanent move, Google's redirect guidance favors a permanent server redirect where possible. Map a file to its actual replacement rather than sending every missing image or download to the home page. A replacement page is a different thing from the image or document a browser requested.

Write down who controls the old hostname and how its redirects will be served after the old application closes. A redirect rule inside an account you are about to cancel will not provide continuity. If a particular hosting plan cannot keep those addresses working, resolve that limitation while the old service is still available.

Check original artwork before resizing

A technically valid social card can still crop a face, stretch a square cover, or replace distinctive original artwork with a generic image. Compare the new card with the original. Decide whether the image should fill its frame or sit inside it with space around it, then inspect the result at the size a person will see. The social share card guide covers the metadata and preview side.

When a source file is small, record that fact instead of treating an enlarged copy as a new high-resolution original. Keep the source and the transformed output separately. That makes a later correction possible without downloading an already compressed derivative and processing it again.

Test the dependency you intend to remove

Before shutting anything down, use a controlled test to find requests to the old media host. A developer can block that hostname locally in a test browser and load representative pages on the new site. Compare the network requests with the inventory. This is a diagnostic exercise in a test session, not a request to change public DNS or interrupt the live service.

Repeat it for a short article, an image heavy page, a page with a PDF, and a link shared on a social platform. Then run the wider crawl to find exceptions outside the sample. A cached picture in one browser is weak evidence that an external dependency has gone.

Sign off the files as well as the pages

Close each inventory row with the destination checked, the references updated, the old address decision recorded, and any unresolved exception assigned to a person. Keep the date and the deployment being tested. That gives the owner a concrete basis for deciding when the old hosting can be retired.

item.title: Internal linking: stitching your pages into a useful website
item.description: Build useful paths through your existing pages with contextual links, clear anchor text, working section targets, and an internal linking worksheet.
item.content:encoded:
Internal linking: stitching your pages into a useful website

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 15, 2026

A visitor arrives on one page. That page can either end the visit or give them a sensible next step into the rest of your work. Internal linking is how individual pages become a website: a connected body of explanations, services, examples, and answers. The opportunities are often already there, waiting for a sentence that joins them.

Start with the destination, then find its neighbors

Choose a page that deserves to be found: a service with a clear offer, a substantial guide, or a category that helps a buyer narrow the choices. Read it first. Write down which questions it answers and who would benefit from reading it. Then look for other pages where those questions arise naturally.

For example, an article about missing product specifications creates a reason to explain how JavaScript rendering works. A page about moving an old blog creates a reason to visit a redirect guide. The connection follows the subject and the reader's next question. A shared keyword alone is not enough to establish that relationship.

Use a crawl and a content inventory together

A crawl shows the pages reachable through the paths it followed. A CMS export, sitemap, or approved list of production URLs can expose pages absent from that crawl. Compare the lists and investigate the difference. A page missing from a crawl may be orphaned, blocked, redirected, or simply outside the crawl's settings; the label needs checking before it becomes a task.

Record the pages worth retaining and the destinations visitors should reach from them. The internal link planning worksheet has columns for source, target, placement, anchor wording, reason, and verification. Its sample addresses are invented. A working copy should describe real paragraphs on real pages, not a list of hoped for keywords.

Write the sentence before inserting the link

A useful editing test is to read the paragraph aloud with the link treated as ordinary text. Does the sentence still make sense? Does the phrase describe what somebody will find? If the destination takes a whole explanation to justify, move the link to a place where the subject is already being discussed.

Google's link guidance favors descriptive, concise, relevant anchor text and contextual connections between pages. It does not prescribe a magic number of links. In practice, I look for an actual reason for every addition. The destination's topic matters more than fitting an exact phrase into every sentence.

Where the reader isA useful next destinationPossible anchor wording
A migration overviewA detailed media move checklistcheck images and PDFs before retiring the old host
A service descriptionA relevant account of completed workhow the event links investigation unfolded
A diagnostic guideA service that handles the same problemindependent SEO review of the release
A long reference pageA specific section of another guidethe section on checking destination URLs

Give anchors real targets

The word anchor can mean the text someone clicks, or a named section inside a page. Both deserve attention. A link to a whole page should point to the intended production URL. A section link adds a fragment such as #checking-destinations, which should match an actual element ID on that destination.

A section link helps someone arrive at the relevant part of a long document. It does not create a separate article. Keep the identifier stable when a heading is edited, and check it after a template or CMS change. A working page address with a missing fragment can still drop the visitor at the top, far from the promised answer.

Check the markup and the route

Google's crawlable link examples use anchor elements with valid href values. Inspect what your template emits, especially when navigation depends on JavaScript. A card that reacts to a click can look like a link without providing the same route in the HTML. The repository guide explains how to trace that behavior back to the component.

Follow each proposed destination and record its final address. Avoid sending a new link through an old redirect when the final page is known. Check that the destination is the intended version and that its indexing signals agree with its role. Adding more routes to an accidental duplicate only adds another problem to untangle.

Keep hubs and editorial links doing useful jobs

A hub gives people an overview of related material. A contextual link helps at the moment a particular question arises. They can support each other: a clear index introduces the topic, while the detailed pages provide the next connections. The topic cluster guide covers choosing distinct questions for those pages.

For a shop, think about routes between categories, subcategories, and products as well as editorial content. Google's ecommerce structure guidance discusses linking through that hierarchy. The practical question is whether a shopper can navigate to the relevant item without having to guess the phrase your search box expects.

Verify additions before reporting results

Keep a before-and-after record of the changed source pages. Check that the links appear in the agreed locations, open their destinations, and land at the expected sections. Crawl again with comparable settings to inspect incoming links and changes to discovery. If you changed a shared component, sample its different uses rather than assuming one good page represents them all.

After the links are live, watch the destination pages over time and keep other changes in the record. Discovery and a successful fetch can be observed separately from indexing or traffic. This makes the result useful even when search takes time to respond, because the team can see exactly which connections were added.
