item.title: Why your SEO should work in your Git repository, with AI at their side
item.description: An SEO using OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, or GitHub Copilot can trace search problems to the files that cause them. What repository access and review should mean.
item.content:encoded:
Why your SEO should work in your Git repository, with AI at their side

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 11, 2026 · Updated October 15, 2026

Most SEO stops at the admin screen: plugin settings, a crawler export, a spreadsheet of recommendations. Your website doesn't live in the admin screen. If it was built by developers, it lives in a code repository, and that's where its search problems are caused and where they get fixed. An SEO who can work in the repository, with an AI coding assistant doing the heavy reading, fixes causes instead of reporting symptoms. That's how I work, and here is what it means for you.

What a repository is, in plain English

A repository is the master copy of your site's code, with its entire history. Almost every team now keeps it in Git, the version control system Linus Torvalds and the Linux community created in 2005, usually hosted on GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. Older systems such as CVS and Subversion did the same job before Git took over.

The history is the point. Every change is recorded with who made it, when, and why. Changes are proposed as pull requests that someone reviews before they go live, and any change can be rolled back. That's exactly the discipline SEO changes have usually lacked.

Plugins and crawlers report. The code is where it's fixed.

Yoast is a fine plugin and Screaming Frog is the best crawler I own. Both tell you what's wrong on the pages they can see. Neither can tell you why a template produces the problem, and neither can change the template. On a site built with Next.js, Nuxt, Astro, Shopify themes, or a headless CMS, there may be no SEO plugin at all. The titles, canonicals, structured data, redirects, robots rules, and sitemaps are all code.

When the SEO can read that code, the work changes:

  • One fix instead of a thousand. A duplicate title on 3,000 product pages is one line in one template.
  • Redirects where they belong: in the framework's configuration or the host's rules file, tested before launch.
  • Structured data built into components, so every new page gets it automatically.
  • JavaScript problems traced to the line. When content only appears after a scroll or a click, the cause is in a component, and that's where to look.
  • No lost work. Every SEO change has a commit, a reviewer, and a way back.

What AI coding assistants add

A medium sized site can have thousands of files. Reading them used to be the developer's job alone. Now AI coding assistants such as OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot can read an entire codebase, explain how it's organized, trace a problem to the files that cause it, and draft the change. GitHub describes Copilot planning changes, editing code, running tests, and reviewing pull requests. Claude Code works the same way from a terminal.

That puts an SEO who knows what to look for within reach of answers that used to take a developer a week. Two examples from my own client work:

  • During a clinic's move from WordPress to Next.js, a read-only analysis of the repository with an AI coding assistant found thousands of image references still pointing at the old media library and traced them to a handful of central files. The developer got a short, concrete plan.
  • For a local business on Sanity, Vercel, and GitHub, I made the metadata changes myself in a pull request the developer reviewed and merged.

The assistant is fast, tireless, and sometimes confidently wrong. The skill is knowing what search engines need, asking the right questions of the code, and checking every answer. AI doesn't replace that judgment; it multiplies it.

How I work in a client's repository

I work primarily with Codex and Claude Code, and also use Copilot. The repository, the written brief, and the checks carry the work between assistants, so the process does not depend on a single AI provider.

  1. Read-only first. I start with read access, map the templates and routes, and compare the code to what crawlers actually see.
  2. Findings tied to files. Every issue comes with the file and line that cause it, so your developer can act without guessing.
  3. Small pull requests. When you want me to make changes, each one is a separate branch with a clear description, reviewed by your developer before it merges.
  4. Nothing reaches production without your approval, and no passwords or API keys go into the code or into an AI tool.
  5. Verified on the live site after deploy, with a crawl and Search Console.

Questions to ask any SEO you're about to hire

  • Can you read the site's templates, or only the pages they produce?
  • Will you hand the developer findings tied to specific files?
  • Can you open a pull request, and will you follow the team's review process?
  • How do you use AI tools on the code, and how do you check what they produce?
  • What access do you need, and what will you never touch?

Work with me

I've built websites since 1994 and practiced SEO since 1998, and today I work the way modern sites are built: in the repository, through pull requests, with AI coding assistants doing the heavy reading under my direction. If your site lives in GitHub and your SEO lives in a spreadsheet, send me the site or see my sitewide technical SEO, JavaScript SEO, and technical audit services. item.title: Topic clusters for AI search, without your pages competing with each other
item.description: Plan a hub page and one page per buyer question so AI fan out searches find a match for every subtopic, and keep your pages from competing for one query.
item.content:encoded:
Topic clusters for AI search, without your pages competing with each other

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 14, 2026

A topic cluster is one hub page that defines a subject and routes readers, plus a set of pages that each answer one buyer question in full, all linked to each other. AI search rewards the shape because Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode break a question into subtopics and run a separate search for each one. Every subtopic page you publish is another chance to be the page that search returns. The discipline that makes it work is one page per question, and no two pages answering the same one.

Why the shape suits AI search

Google's documentation says AI Overviews and AI Mode may use a "query fan-out" technique, issuing multiple related searches across subtopics and data sources to build a response. Elizabeth Reid, Google's head of Search, described it when AI Mode launched in May 2025: the system breaks a question into subtopics and runs many queries at once. A buyer's one question becomes a dozen narrower searches behind the scenes.

A single long page that covers everything competes in each of those searches with one URL and a diluted focus. A cluster puts a page with a clear, specific answer in front of each subtopic search. To be eligible as a supporting link, Google's guidance adds, a page only has to be indexed and eligible for a snippet in ordinary search. The cluster changes how many questions you can be the best answer to.

Start from questions, not keywords

I build a cluster from the questions buyers ask, in their own words. The best sources are the Search Console query report for the pages you already have, the first lines of inbound emails, notes from sales calls, and the open questions in an AI share of voice question set. Group the questions by what the buyer is trying to decide. Each group that needs more than a few paragraphs to answer properly becomes a page.

Keyword tools still help with volume and wording, and they come second. A cluster planned from a keyword export tends to produce pages that differ by one modifier and answer the same thing, which is how a site ends up competing with itself.

One page per question

When two pages on your site answer the same question, search engines have to pick one, and they often alternate between them or choose the one you'd rank lower. Google's canonicalization guidance exists for exact and near duplicates; the softer version, two different pages chasing one intent, gets no such help. The fix is a decision for each pair: merge them and redirect the weaker URL, or rewrite one so it answers a different question.

I enforce this mechanically on my own sites. The script that builds them refuses to publish a page that shares more than 15 percent of its phrasing with another page on the same site, or a sentence of ten words or more that already appears elsewhere. A human editor misses overlap across eighty pages; a check that runs on every build doesn't.

Build the hub to route, and the spokes to answer

The hub page defines the subject in its first paragraph, says who it's for, and links to every spoke with anchor text that names the question the spoke answers. Google's starter guide asks for exactly that: link text that tells people and Google something about the page it points to. A hub that tries to answer every question itself becomes the long page the cluster was meant to replace.

Each spoke opens with a direct answer in two or three sentences, then supports it. Every section should make sense if it is the only part an AI system lifts. Spokes link back to the hub and to the other spokes a reader would naturally need next, and nowhere else by habit.

A cluster on this site

My AI search service page is the hub for one cluster. Its spokes each answer one question: whether a site is ready (the AI search readiness checklist), how to fix a wrong answer (correcting AI answers), how to earn the mentions answers repeat (earned mentions), what llms.txt does, and how to measure share of voice. None of them answers another's question, and each links back to the hub.

Check the cluster every quarter

Open Search Console's performance report, filter to the cluster's pages, and look at the queries. When two pages draw impressions for the same query, one of them is drifting into the other's territory. When a page draws queries you never planned for, the buyers are telling you what the next spoke should be. Add it, link it from the hub, and keep the rule of one question per page.

item.title: Social share cards: Open Graph tags and images that fit
item.description: How Open Graph and X card tags control the preview when a link is shared, why square images get cropped, the 1200 by 630 standard, and refreshing old previews.
item.content:encoded:
Social share cards: Open Graph tags and images that fit

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 14, 2026

When someone pastes your link into Facebook, LinkedIn, X, Slack, or a text message, the preview that appears is built from a few tags in your page's head. Those tags decide the headline, the summary, and the picture. When they're missing, the platform guesses, and it guesses badly. When they're present but the image is the wrong shape, the platform crops it, and the crop usually cuts off the part that mattered.

The tags that build the preview

The Open Graph protocol, which Facebook introduced and almost every platform now reads, asks for four properties on every page:

  • og:title: the headline as it should appear in the preview.
  • og:type: what the page is, usually website or article.
  • og:image: the full address of the preview image.
  • og:url: the page's canonical address, which the platform treats as its permanent ID.

Add og:description and og:site_name as well. Then describe the image with three structured properties: og:image:width and og:image:height in pixels, and og:image:alt, which the protocol defines as a description of what is in the image, not a caption.

X reads its own set of tags. The one that matters most is twitter:card: summary shows a small square thumbnail beside the text, and summary_large_image shows a wide image above it. I add twitter:title, twitter:description, twitter:image, and twitter:image:alt too, so nothing depends on how a platform falls back.

Why 1,200 by 630

Meta's documentation asks for images at least 1,200 by 630 pixels for the best display on high-resolution screens, and says to keep them as close to a 1.91 to 1 ratio as you can so the whole image shows in the feed without cropping. Images smaller than 600 by 315 get shown small. Files must stay under 8 MB. LinkedIn and X lay out their large previews as wide rectangles too, so one image at 1,200 by 630 serves all of them.

Declaring the width and height matters more than it looks. Meta says those two tags let its crawler render the image immediately. Without them, the first person to share a new page can get a preview with no picture while the platform downloads and measures the file.

The square artwork trap

Square images are everywhere: podcast covers, product photos, logos, album art. Put a square image in a large card, and every platform crops it to a wide strip from the middle. The top and bottom are gone, and on cover art that's usually where the title is.

I found exactly this on a podcast site I built. Every page had complete Open Graph and X tags, and every image existed at the declared size, so a tag audit passed. But 458 episode pages pointed at square cover art inside large cards, so every shared episode lost the top and bottom of its cover. More than two hundred episodes shared the same default cover, so their previews were also identical. The fix was a generated card for each episode, 1,200 by 630, with the cover art on one side and the episode title in large type on the other. The build makes the card once, reuses it on every later build, and makes a new one when an episode is renamed.

If you can't generate cards, switch square images to the summary card on X, which shows a square thumbnail uncropped, and accept a smaller preview elsewhere.

Making the image work as a preview

  • Put the page's own title in the image when pages share artwork, so each preview is distinct.
  • Keep important content near the center. Some apps trim the edges or round the corners.
  • Use large type. Most previews are seen on phones, at a fraction of full size.
  • Use JPEG for photos and artwork and keep files in the low hundreds of kilobytes.
  • Write alt text that describes the image, since some apps read it aloud.

Checking your pages

View the source of a page and confirm every tag is present, every image address is absolute and loads, and every declared size matches the real file. On a large site, crawl it with Screaming Frog and extract the og:image value from each page, then check the images in bulk; the method is in my guide to custom extraction. Group the results by image. A single image behind hundreds of pages is a sign your previews all look the same.

Refreshing previews that are already out there

Platforms cache what they fetch. Meta notes that changing the image for a URL doesn't update the preview on old shares. After fixing a page, paste its address into Meta's Sharing Debugger and ask it to scrape again, and do the same in LinkedIn's Post Inspector. Other platforms refresh on their own schedule.

Where this fits

Share cards don't move rankings directly. They decide whether a shared link gets clicked, and clicks bring the visits, links, and mentions that do matter. I check them in every audit and build them into every site I make; see static websites built for search and podcast website SEO.

item.title: How to load Google Analytics 4 without hurting PageSpeed
item.description: On a fast static site, gtag.js caused most of the blocking time. Loading it after the first scroll or tap took mobile Lighthouse to 100. How, and the cost.
item.content:encoded:
How to load Google Analytics 4 without hurting PageSpeed

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 14, 2026

On a lean site, the Google Analytics tag can be the heaviest thing on the page. When I tested this site in October 2026, gtag.js accounted for most of the main-thread work during load on mobile, about twice what the site's own code used. Loading the tag after the visitor's first scroll, tap, or key press, or four seconds after the page finishes loading, took the home page from a mobile Lighthouse score of 73 to 80 up to 100. Pageviews still count. The cost is the visitors who leave within a few seconds without touching the page.

What the tag costs

The standard GA4 snippet loads gtag.js asynchronously, which keeps it from blocking the HTML parser. It still runs on the main thread once it arrives, and the script is large: about 176 KB on my pages. On a phone, parsing and running it lands in the same window as the page's first paint, and Lighthouse counts every long task in that window toward Total Blocking Time. On my home page, Total Blocking Time ran from 700 to 1,760 milliseconds, depending on the run.

Total Blocking Time is a lab measure. Google's ranking signals use field data, and the field measure for responsiveness is Interaction to Next Paint. Real phones on real networks still pay the cost of a large script parsed during load, so a lab fix that removes that work tends to show up in the field too, a month or so later, once enough visits have been recorded.

Load the tag after the visitor acts

The fix keeps every analytics command and moves only the script download. The page defines dataLayer and the gtag function as usual, queues the consent defaults, the js timestamp, and the config call, and then waits. The first scroll, pointer press, touch, or key press loads gtag.js. If none comes, a timer loads it four seconds after the page's load event. When the script arrives it reads the queued commands in order, so the pageview is recorded with the right consent state.

<script>
  window.dataLayer = window.dataLayer || [];
  function gtag(){dataLayer.push(arguments);}
  gtag('js', new Date());
  gtag('config', 'G-XXXXXXXXXX');
  (function () {
    var done = false;
    function load() {
      if (done) return;
      done = true;
      var s = document.createElement('script');
      s.async = true;
      s.src = 'https://www.googletagmanager.com/gtag/js?id=G-XXXXXXXXXX';
      document.head.appendChild(s);
    }
    ['pointerdown', 'keydown', 'scroll', 'touchstart'].forEach(function (e) {
      addEventListener(e, load, {once: true, passive: true});
    });
    addEventListener('load', function () { setTimeout(load, 4000); });
  })();
</script>

Keep your consent mode defaults above the config line, exactly where they were. They are commands in the same queue and run before anything is sent.

The result

I tested the original and the deferred version of the same page side by side, twice each, with Lighthouse in mobile mode on the same machine. The original scored 73 and 80, with 1,760 and 890 milliseconds of blocking time. The deferred version scored 100 both times, with 40 and 30 milliseconds. The two pages I measured on this site afterward scored 98 and 100.

The cost, stated plainly

A visitor who opens a page and leaves within about four seconds without scrolling, tapping, or typing is never counted. On most sites that group is small and includes a share of bots, but it is real, and a client should hear it before the change ships. Bounce rate and short-session counts will shift on the day you deploy, so annotate the change in GA4 and compare like with like afterward.

Two cases call for the standard snippet instead. A site whose business depends on counting single-page visits exactly, such as a landing page measured by paid campaigns, should keep the tag loading immediately. So should any page where the tag fires conversion events the moment it loads.

Check the rest of the page first

Deferring analytics is the right first move only when analytics is the problem. Run Lighthouse, open the diagnostics, and read which scripts take the main-thread time. If a theme, a page builder, or a chat widget is the larger cost, fix that first. My guide to Core Web Vitals covers the other common causes.

item.title: How to measure your share of voice in AI answers
item.description: Track how often ChatGPT, Claude, and Google's AI name you beside competitors, in what tone, and from which sources, with a fixed question set and a monthly run.
item.content:encoded:
How to measure your share of voice in AI answers

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 14, 2026

Share of voice in AI answers is the share of relevant questions where an assistant names you, measured against the competitors it names instead. You get a number you can track by asking the same set of buyer questions every month, with web search turned on, and recording four things from every answer: who it names, where you rank among them, the tone toward you, and the sources it cites. I run this on my own name, and the first run told me more than a year of guessing would have.

Why a fixed question set beats screenshots

AI answers change from run to run. Ask ChatGPT the same question twice and the list of names shifts. A screenshot someone sends you on a Tuesday proves only that the answer looked that way once. A fixed set of questions, asked on the same schedule with the same settings, turns that noise into a trend: one run is a reading, and three monthly runs show a direction.

The set stays stable from month to month. New questions go on the end so earlier months still compare. Change the wording of an old question and you have started a new series.

Build the question set from three kinds of question

I split every set into three groups, because they measure different things and a single blended number hides the gap that matters.

  • Branded questions name you: "Who is this company?" "Is this consultant any good?" They test whether assistants know you and describe you correctly.
  • Open questions are the ones buyers ask before they have a name: "Who should I hire to fix my JavaScript indexing?" "Recommend an agency for a B2B AI search program." These measure whether you are in the consideration set at all.
  • How-to questions ask for an answer your content provides: "How do I fix Crawled, currently not indexed?" They show whether your guides get cited as a source.

Pull the wording from places buyers speak in their own words: Search Console queries, sales call notes, the first lines of inbound emails, and the questions clients ask on a first call. Sixteen questions is a workable start for one person or a small firm. A client program usually runs forty to a hundred.

Record four things from every answer

For each answer, I record the providers it names in the order they appear, my position in that list, the tone toward me (positive, neutral, negative, or mixed), and every URL it cites. I also copy out each factual claim it makes about me, word for word, because tone and accuracy are separate questions. A warm answer with the wrong founding date still needs fixing.

Share of voice for a group is the number of answers that name you divided by the number of answers in that group. Report it per group, beside the names that appear most often in the answers where you are missing. Those names are your real competitors in AI search, and they are often different from the ones your sales team worries about.

What my own first run showed

In October 2026 I asked Claude, with live web search, sixteen questions a prospect of mine might ask. It named me in all three branded answers and cited my sites in each. It named me in none of the nine open hiring questions and cited none of my guides on the four how-to questions. The answers about me were mostly accurate, with two dated facts and one sentence that had merged two of my companies into one founding year.

The sharpest line came from the answer to "Is Chris Abraham a good SEO consultant to hire?" It noted that almost everything it found about me was written by me. That is the finding that sets the work: the sites are readable and current, and the rest of the web hasn't caught up with them.

The run cost $1.88 in API fees. Web search on both Anthropic's and OpenAI's APIs is billed at $10 per thousand searches plus tokens, so a monthly run of this size stays in the single dollars.

Read the competitors from the answers

The names that appear when you are absent tell you what the assistants are working from. In my run, the hiring answers drew names from marketplace listing pages and "best consultants" roundups, and the how-to answers cited vendor blogs. Each pattern points at a different fix: listings and roundups are an outreach problem, and how-to citations are a content problem. My guide to earning mentions that last covers the first.

Know the limits before you report the number

An API call with web search is close to what a person sees in the assistant's app, and the two are not identical. The app adds memory, personalization, and the user's location. Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode use different models and techniques, so their answers and links vary between the two features as well. Report the trend across runs, name the engine and the date on every figure, and keep the raw answers so anyone can check a number against the words behind it.

Bing Webmaster Tools now reports citations of your pages in Copilot answers, and Search Console includes AI features in its performance data. Use both beside the question set: they count what actually happened on those platforms, and the question set shows what you would see if you asked.

item.title: Reddit and AI answers: what a moderator wants brands to know
item.description: Why Reddit threads now shape Google and ChatGPT answers about your business, what moderators remove on sight, and the honest ways a brand can take part.
item.content:encoded:
Reddit and AI answers: what a moderator wants brands to know

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

Ask Google or ChatGPT which running shoes, accountants, or project tools people actually like, and the answer often leans on a Reddit thread. Brands have noticed, and a lot of them are now trying to plant themselves in those threads. I've moderated a Reddit community of more than 16,000 runners for nine years, so I see that effort from the other side, every week. Here is what works, what gets removed, and why the honest route is also the one that lasts.

Why Reddit carries so much weight right now

Three things happened in 2024. On February 22, Google announced an expanded partnership that gave it access to Reddit's Data API, the structured feed of posts and comments. In May, OpenAI announced its own Data API deal with Reddit. In December, Reddit launched Reddit Answers, its own AI search that summarizes discussions from across the site. Google's announcement also said the deal doesn't change how it uses public, crawlable content, which Reddit threads have always been.

The result is simple to state. When someone asks an AI assistant a question that real people have argued about, the argument on Reddit is one of the places the answer comes from. A thread where three strangers say your product broke after a month can matter more than your entire product page.

What moderators remove on sight

Every community writes its own rules, and Reddit's sitewide content policy sits underneath them. Rule 2 asks people to post authentic content in communities where they have a personal interest, and it bans content manipulation, including spam and vote manipulation. Moderators enforce that with pattern recognition. These are the patterns I see most:

  • The fresh account with a recommendation. Two days old, no history, and its first comment names a product with enthusiasm no customer has ever felt.
  • The fake question. "Has anyone tried this brand?" posted by an account that then answers itself from a second account. Moderators can see posting history, and sock puppets tend to share habits.
  • The link drop. A comment that exists to carry a URL, often to a blog post that barely relates to the thread.
  • The agency voice. Polished, upbeat, slightly too complete. Reddit readers recognize marketing copy instantly, and they report it.
  • The pile on. A sudden run of upvotes on one comment from accounts that never visit the community. That one gets reported to Reddit's own safety teams, and it can take the whole account network down.

Removal is the mild outcome. The worse one is a top comment that says "this is an ad," which then becomes the thing people, and AI summaries, remember about you.

The legal line in the United States

If an employee, contractor, or paid agency posts about your product without saying so, that is an endorsement with an undisclosed connection. The FTC's Endorsement Guides, revised in 2023, say material connections must be disclosed clearly, and the revision says intermediaries, including advertising agencies, public relations firms, and reputation management companies, can share responsibility for endorsements they know or should know are deceptive. Handing the posting to an agency doesn't move the responsibility off your brand. A plain "I work for the company" is all it takes to stay on the right side of that line.

What honest participation looks like

  • Use a named account. "Jane from the Acme support team" can answer questions in a thread about Acme, and most communities welcome it, because it's useful. Read each community's rules first; some require you to message the moderators before posting as a company.
  • Show up where you're already discussed. Search Reddit for your brand name and your product names. Answer the unanswered questions, correct factual errors politely, and say thank you for criticism you plan to act on.
  • Fix what people complain about. Then say so in the thread where they complained. A reply that says "you were right, the return policy is now 60 days" does more than any campaign.
  • Ask before you host anything. Ask Me Anything sessions, giveaways, and surveys belong in communities whose moderators have agreed in advance.
  • Give more than you take. Help in threads that have nothing to do with your product. That history is what makes the occasional mention of your own work believable.

Use Reddit as research, then answer on your own site

The most underused value of Reddit isn't posting at all. Threads about your category are a free record of the exact questions customers ask, in their own words, and the objections they raise before buying. Collect them, then answer each one properly on your own site: a clear page, a real FAQ, a comparison that admits where you're weaker. Those pages are what AI assistants can quote alongside the thread, and they're the ones you control. My AI search readiness checklist covers how to make them readable to the answer engines.

Check what the threads are teaching the machines

Once a month, search Reddit and Google for your brand with "reddit" added, then ask ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity the questions customers ask about your category. Note which threads get cited and what they say. If an AI answer repeats a complaint you've already fixed, the fix belongs in the thread and on your site, and my guide to correcting what AI search says about you walks through tracing each claim to its source.

Where I fit

My own community has nothing for sale and never has; I explain why on off the clock. That's exactly why I'm useful to a brand that wants to take part properly: I can review how Reddit and the AI answers built from it describe you, tell you which threads matter, and write a participation plan your team can follow without getting banned. item.description: Proof that an SEO fix shipped: compare before-and-after crawls in Screaming Frog, check change detection, then confirm in Search Console with validation.
item.content:encoded:
How to prove an SEO fix actually worked

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

"Done" is the most dangerous word in SEO. A developer marks the ticket closed, the CMS shows the new titles, and three months later a crawl finds the old ones still live on half the site. A cache never cleared, a second template was missed, or the change only applied to new pages. I don't call a fix finished until two crawls and Search Console agree that it is. Here is the routine.

Step 1: crawl before you change anything

The baseline is the step people skip, and without it there's nothing to compare. Before any fix ships, crawl the site with the settings you'll use afterward: the same start URL, the same rendering mode, the same exclusions, the same custom extractors. Save it.

In Screaming Frog, comparison needs a licence and database storage mode, which you switch on under File > Settings > Storage Mode. Database storage saves every crawl automatically and lists it under File > Crawls, and it copes with large sites far better than memory storage. Crawls saved in the old file format can be imported and converted.

Step 2: crawl again after the release

Once the fix is live and caches have cleared, crawl again with identical settings. Then switch to Mode > Compare, pick the two crawls, and run the comparison. The newer crawl becomes Current and the older one Previous.

Step 3: read the four change columns

For every tab and filter, the comparison sorts URLs into four groups, and the difference between them is the whole point:

  • Added: URLs present in both crawls that have moved into this filter. If the filter is an error, these are new problems on existing pages.
  • Removed: URLs present in both crawls that have left this filter. For an error filter, these are your fixes.
  • New: URLs found only in the current crawl.
  • Missing: URLs found only in the previous crawl.

If you fixed duplicate titles on 600 product pages, you want to see roughly 600 in Removed under Page Titles > Duplicate, and close to zero in Added. A large New count after a fix that wasn't supposed to create pages tells you something else changed, often a parameter or a pagination pattern now exposed to crawlers.

Step 4: turn on change detection

Filters only notice changes that move a URL between filters. A title rewritten from one acceptable wording to another triggers nothing. For that, open Config > Compare before you run the comparison and select the elements you changed: page titles, meta descriptions, H1s, word count, crawl depth, internal links, structured data, or content. A Change Detection tab then lists every URL where those elements differ between the crawls.

This is how I answer the question every client eventually asks: did the new titles actually go live everywhere? The tab gives a URL by URL answer, and the pages that didn't change are the ones to chase.

Step 5: check structure and internal links

The Site Structure tab in a comparison shows the directory tree with URLs added and removed, and how crawl depth shifted. The lower window's inlinks view can filter to links added or removed. When a menu change quietly pushes a section of pages one click deeper, this is where it shows up, along with the exact links that went away.

Comparing staging with live

Before a migration or a redesign launches, URL Mapping under Config > Compare lets you compare crawls whose URLs differ. A regex maps the previous crawl's URLs onto the current crawl's, so a staging hostname can be compared page for page with the live site. Run it before launch and you'll catch missing titles, dropped schema, and lost internal links while they're still cheap to fix.

Step 6: confirm with Google

A clean crawl proves what your site serves. Search Console shows what Google has noticed.

  • URL Inspection on a handful of representative URLs. The live test shows whether Google can index the page as it stands now, and the indexed result shows the version Google currently holds, including its chosen canonical.
  • Validate fix in the Page indexing report, once every instance of an issue is fixed. Google rechecks the affected URLs and emails you when the fix is confirmed or when it finds one still broken, which stops the validation. Google says this typically takes up to about two weeks and sometimes longer.
  • A smaller sitemap for speed. Google suggests submitting a sitemap of your most important affected pages and filtering the report to it before validating, since a smaller set can finish sooner.

Write it down

A verification note after each release can be short: the two crawl dates, the counts in Removed and Added for each targeted issue, a list of any URLs that didn't change and why, and the Search Console validation status with its date. It turns "fixed" into a record anyone can check, and it catches the missed template before Google does.

Verification is built into my sitewide technical SEO work and every site migration. The extractors I use for before-and-after comparisons are in Screaming Frog custom extraction recipes.

item.title: How to find near-duplicate pages and multiple H1s across a whole site
item.description: Find near-duplicate pages and heading problems across an entire site with Screaming Frog, then decide which pages to rewrite, merge, redirect, or canonicalize.
item.content:encoded:
How to find near-duplicate pages and multiple H1s across a whole site

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

Two findings turn up in almost every full crawl I run: clusters of pages that say nearly the same thing, and headings that don't describe the page. Neither can be judged one URL at a time. Here is how I find both across every page, and how I decide what to do about each.

Crawl the rendered page, not only the source

Set Screaming Frog to JavaScript rendering under Configuration > Spider > Rendering before you start. On sites built with React, Next.js, or a page builder, the H1 a browser shows can differ from the one in the raw HTML. A component may replace it after load, or a script may inject a second one. If you crawl only the source, you're auditing a page nobody sees.

Turn on near-duplicate detection

Screaming Frog finds exact duplicates by default. Near duplicates need switching on, under Configuration > Content > Duplicates, which tells the crawler to store each page's text. The default similarity threshold is 90%, and you can lower it to cast a wider net. By default it compares only indexable pages, which is usually what you want.

Before crawling, open Configuration > Content > Area and exclude the navigation, header, and footer elements. Otherwise every page shares hundreds of words of menu text, and pages that differ in their main content can still score as near twins. You can adjust the content area and threshold after a crawl without crawling again.

One step trips people up: the Near Duplicates filter stays empty until you run Crawl Analysis at the end of the crawl. The overview pane marks the filters that are waiting on it. Once the analysis finishes, the Content tab lists each page's closest similarity match and how many near duplicates it has, and the Duplicate Details tab shows the matching text and highlights where the pages differ.

Count headings with custom extraction

The crawler's H1 columns show you the heading text page by page. A custom extraction gives you a number you can sort by. Under Configuration > Custom > Custom Extraction, add an XPath rule in Function Value mode with count(//h1). Every URL gets a column with its H1 count. Add count(//h2) alongside it if you want to see which templates skip a level. Group the results by URL pattern and the template behind each problem usually becomes obvious.

What multiple H1s actually cost you

Less than most audit tools suggest. Google's SEO Starter Guide says headings in semantic order are fantastic for screen readers, and that from Google Search's perspective it doesn't matter if they're out of order. There is no ranking penalty for two H1s. The W3C's accessibility tutorial explains why order still matters: people using screen readers move through a page by its headings, so the ranks should describe how the page is organized.

So I treat headings as a clarity and accessibility problem. The cases worth fixing are:

  • No H1 at all, often because a theme styles the page title as a div.
  • The logo wrapped in an H1 on every page, so the site name is the main heading of every URL.
  • An H1 split across styled elements, such as two spans with no space between them, so extracted text reads "BestPrices" instead of "Best Prices."
  • The same H1 sitewide, usually from a layout that hard codes it.

Each of these is one template fix. That's the payoff of finding them by count rather than by spot checking.

Where near duplicates come from

When I group near-duplicate clusters by URL pattern, the same handful of causes come up again and again:

  • City swap location pages, where the only difference is the town name.
  • Tag and category archives that list the same posts under different labels.
  • Parameter URLs for sorting, filtering, or tracking that serve the same content.
  • Printer friendly versions of articles and recipes.
  • Quiz or calculator variants that share an explanation and change a few inputs.

Decide, cluster by cluster

Every cluster gets one of three decisions:

  1. Differentiate. If each page has a real reason to exist, such as location pages for offices that actually differ, rewrite them so each carries information the others don't: staff, services, directions, local proof.
  2. Merge and 301. If the pages serve the same purpose, keep the strongest, fold in anything useful from the rest, and permanently redirect the others to it. Google's documentation calls a redirect a strong signal, and recommends redirects when you want to get rid of duplicate pages.
  3. Canonicalize. If the duplicates have to stay reachable, as parameter and printer versions usually do, point them at the main version with rel="canonical." Google treats that as a strong signal too.

Noindex is rarely the right tool here. Google specifically advises against using noindex to steer canonical selection within a site, since it removes the page from Search entirely. I reserve it for pages that should never appear in results at all.

Check the fix with a second crawl

After the changes ship, crawl again with the same settings and compare the two crawls. The clusters you merged should now show redirects, the canonicalized URLs should point where you meant, and the H1 count column should read 1 across the templates you fixed. Then give Google a few weeks and check the Page indexing report in Search Console for duplicates it has resolved.

item.title: Digital PR for AI search: how to earn mentions the answer engines repeat
item.description: AI answers repeat what other sites say about you. How to earn honest mentions in the press, newsletters, and niche sites, plus the FTC and Google rules on pay.
item.content:encoded:
Digital PR for AI search: how to earn mentions the answer engines repeat

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

When an AI assistant describes your company, it isn't reading your About page alone. It's drawing on what other people have written: trade press, local news, newsletters, review roundups, niche sites, interviews. Those mentions used to be valued mostly for the links they carried. Now the words themselves travel into the answers. I've been earning that kind of coverage for clients since I helped develop long-tail blogger outreach in 2006, and the fundamentals have barely changed. The stakes have.

Why mentions matter more than they used to

A link tells a search engine that one page points to another. A mention tells a reader, and a language model, what you are: "the neighborhood bakery known for its sourdough," "the accountant who specializes in restaurants." AI answers are built from sentences like those, gathered across many sources. If ten independent sites describe you the same accurate way, that description tends to become the answer. If the only sentences about you are your own, the machines have little to confirm them with.

Aim at the long tail

Everyone wants the national newspaper. Far fewer people pitch the newsletter with 4,000 devoted readers in your exact niche, the trade association's blog, the local business journal, or the hobbyist site that has covered your category for a decade. Those outlets are easier to reach, their writers know the subject, and their coverage is usually more specific, which is exactly what makes a mention useful to an AI answer. Twenty small, accurate mentions beat one big vague one.

Give writers something worth using

  • Original numbers. A small survey, a count from your own records, a price index. Writers need facts nobody else has. My guide to original research on a small budget shows how to produce them honestly.
  • A quotable expert. A founder or specialist who answers a reporter's question in two clear sentences, on deadline, gets quoted again.
  • Real access. A product to test, a behind the scenes visit, a straight answer about a mistake. Writers remember who was easy to work with.
  • A pitch about them. Read what the writer has published, and explain in three sentences why this fits their readers. A personal note to one writer outperforms a blast to five hundred.

Say your name the same way every time

A mention only helps if machines can connect it to you. Use one consistent business name, one description, and the same founder name everywhere, and make sure your own site states those facts plainly, with structured data that ties your profiles together. If you trade under two names, my guide to connecting two names into one entity covers the method.

The rules on paying

Paying for coverage isn't forbidden, but it changes what you must disclose. In the United States, the FTC's Endorsement Guides, revised in 2023, require clear disclosure of any material connection between a brand and the person talking about it: payment, free product, or employment. The revision also says agencies, PR firms, and reputation management companies can share liability for deceptive endorsements they help create. In August 2024 the FTC announced a separate final rule banning fake reviews and testimonials, including ones attributed to people who don't exist, which took effect that October.

Google has its own rule. Its spam policies treat buying or selling links that pass ranking credit as link spam, and it asks that paid placements carry rel="sponsored". A sponsored article can still describe you well; it just shouldn't pretend to be editorial or pass link value.

Measure mentions, not only links

Keep a simple log: outlet, date, the sentence that describes you, and whether it's accurate. Then, monthly, ask ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity the questions your customers ask and see which of those sentences come back. When an answer is wrong, trace the claim to its source; my guide to correcting AI answers explains how.

Where I fit

I've taught influencer marketing as a guest lecturer at Georgetown, run outreach teams, and spent years on both sides of the pitch: as the person asking for coverage and as an editor deciding what to run. item.title: Screaming Frog custom extraction recipes for sitewide SEO audits
item.description: XPath and regex recipes for Screaming Frog custom extraction to audit a site: heading counts, canonicals, robots tags, schema types, alt text, and tag IDs.
item.content:encoded:
Screaming Frog custom extraction recipes for sitewide SEO audits

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

The standard Screaming Frog tabs answer the standard questions. Custom extraction answers yours. With a few lines of XPath or regex, every URL in a crawl gets a new column holding exactly the fact you need, and a question like "which templates are missing a canonical?" becomes a sort and a filter. These are the extractors I load into almost every audit.

Setting it up

Custom extraction needs a paid licence. Open Configuration > Custom > Custom Extraction and click Add. Each extractor gets a name, which becomes its column heading, a type, and an expression. You can run up to 100 extractors in one crawl.

There are three types:

  • XPath, which selects elements and attributes from the HTML. Most of my recipes use it.
  • CSSPath, the same idea using CSS selectors, often the quickest to write.
  • Regex, for anything that isn't an HTML element, such as JSON inside a script tag or an ID in inline JavaScript.

For XPath and CSSPath you then choose what to return: the whole element, its inner HTML, its text, or, with Function Value, the result of a function such as a count. If you'd rather not write expressions at all, the visual extraction browser lets you click an element on a sample page and suggests the expression for you.

One setting matters more than any recipe. Screaming Frog extracts from the raw HTML unless JavaScript rendering is on, in which case it reads the rendered page. On a React or Next.js site, run the same extractors in both modes and compare. Any column that fills in only after rendering is content that depends on JavaScript to exist.

Heading recipes

  • H1 count (XPath, Function Value): count(//h1). Sort descending to find templates with two or more, ascending to find pages with none.
  • All H1 text (XPath, Extract Text): //h1. Shows when a logo or a hidden mobile heading is the H1.
  • H2 count (XPath, Function Value): count(//h2). A zero on a long page usually means the template styles its subheads as plain text.

Indexing and canonical recipes

  • Canonical count (XPath, Function Value): count(//link[@rel='canonical']). More than one canonical tag on a page is a conflict worth fixing at once.
  • Canonical target (XPath, Extract Inner HTML): //link[@rel='canonical']/@href. Screaming Frog reports canonicals already; I extract it anyway when I need it beside other custom columns in one export.
  • Robots meta (XPath, Extract Inner HTML): //meta[@name='robots']/@content. Catches noindex left behind from a staging site.
  • Hreflang values (XPath, Extract Inner HTML): //link[@rel='alternate'][@hreflang]/@hreflang. A quick check that every language version lists the same set.

Structured data recipes

JSON-LD lives inside a script tag as JSON, so element selectors can't reach the fields inside it. Screaming Frog's own guidance is to use regex for any JSON in the code.

  • JSON-LD block count (XPath, Function Value): count(//script[@type='application/ld+json']). Zero on a template that should carry schema is the first thing to fix.
  • Schema types (Regex): "@type"\s*:\s*"(.*?)". Lists every type declared on the page, so you can see which templates emit Product, Article, or nothing at all.
  • The whole block (Regex): <script type="application/ld\+json">(.*?)</script>. Useful for exporting and validating a sample per template.

Content and authorship recipes

  • Published date (XPath, Extract Inner HTML): //meta[@property='article:published_time']/@content. Finds articles with no machine readable date.
  • Author meta (XPath, Extract Inner HTML): //meta[@name='author']/@content. Many themes leave this blank or set it to the site name.
  • Images with no alt attribute (XPath, Function Value): count(//img[not(@alt)]). Counts per page, so you can see which template is the repeat offender.
  • Links inside the main content (XPath, Function Value): count(//main//a). Separates contextual internal links from the menu and footer, assuming the template uses a main element.

Tracking recipes

  • Google Tag Manager container (Regex): ["'](GTM-.*?)["']. Shows pages with no container, or two different ones.
  • GA4 measurement ID (Regex): ["'](G-[A-Z0-9]+)["']. Same idea for sites that load GA4 directly.

Reading the results

A column of numbers is only useful once it's grouped. Export the crawl, add a column for the URL pattern or template, and pivot. When every product page reports two H1s and every blog post reports one, the cause is in the product template, and one change fixes thousands of URLs. That is the habit that turns a crawl from a list of warnings into a short list of causes.

Check a few rows by hand before you trust a recipe. View the source of one page, confirm the extracted value matches, and adjust the expression if a theme uses different markup from the one you expected.

item.content:encoded:
I turn down backlink work. Here's the one agency I recommend instead

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

I hate backlink campaigns, and I refuse every one I'm offered. That's my choice, and it isn't a verdict on anyone who buys links. Plenty of businesses want them, and they deserve a vendor that won't burn them. So whenever I turn a backlink gig down, I give the same referral, every time: FatJoe. Nobody asked me to say so, and I'm not carrying anyone's water. I'd simply be a hypocrite to stay quiet, because I've been one of their publishers for more than a decade, and my experience with them has been good from start to finish.

Why I won't do backlink campaigns

A backlink campaign is pitching strangers, haggling over fees, collecting PayPal addresses, chasing posts that were promised and never went live, and checking every month that the links are still there. It's a full-time job of follow-up, and it's the opposite of the work I'm good at. I diagnose why sites lose traffic, fix how they render and get indexed, and make them readable to search engines and AI answers. That's what my services cover, and links aren't on the list.

There's also Google's rule, covered below, which puts every paid link in a gray zone I'd rather leave to the people who specialize in it.

What a decade as a FatJoe publisher has shown me

I see FatJoe from the side most buyers never see: the publisher's. They send me articles for my own site, chrisabraham.com, and here is what that has been like.

  • I get first refusal on everything. Every article they offer me, I read first, then publish or turn down. Nothing appears on my site without my say so. A vendor that respects the publisher's editorial control is a vendor whose placements land on sites that still have some.
  • They pay right away. When an article goes live and I confirm it, payment follows within hours. Writers, publishers, and influencers who get paid promptly keep working with a service, and that keeps its network full of real sites.
  • They tee everything up. The article arrives written, the link and its placement are spelled out, and the confirmation is one reply with the live URL.
  • They're professional. A real support team, consistent processes, and no surprises.
  • They don't do shady things. In more than ten years, I've never seen them ask for anything that would make me uncomfortable as a site owner.

What FatJoe offers buyers

FatJoe has operated since 2012 and reports more than 260,000 orders delivered. It sells blogger outreach and placed articles, niche edits, digital PR, press release distribution, local citations, and content writing. It also says every service is white label, which makes it a clean option for an SEO or agency that wants to offer links to its clients without running outreach itself.

Be clear about what you're buying: placed articles on real sites, paid for. That's a different thing from a link a writer gives you because they admire your work. Within the paid category, FatJoe is the only agency I recommend.

Another name I keep hearing

Rhino Rank, a UK link building agency based in Shrewsbury, gets praised by colleagues whose judgment I trust. It sells curated links on existing articles, guest posts, and a managed service, and it calls itself the original white-label link-building agency. I have no experience with it at all, so this is secondhand: worth a look, and worth judging by the same tests below.

Google's rule on paid links

Google's spam policies treat buying or selling links that pass ranking credit as link spam, and Google asks that paid links carry rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow". That applies to every vendor and every hand-built campaign alike. Placed articles still bring readers, referral visits, and brand mentions that AI answers can pick up; my guide to digital PR for AI search explains why mentions matter. Decide with your eyes open how much risk you'll accept, and ask any vendor how its placements are marked.

Five questions for any link vendor

  • Can I see the sites before I pay? Real publications with an editorial voice, never a network of identical blogs.
  • Do those sites have readers? Estimated search traffic, a publishing history, people who comment or share.
  • Would I be glad for a customer to read the article? If not, don't buy it.
  • What happens if a link disappears? Ask about replacements before ordering.
  • Do the publishers get paid promptly? A vendor that pays late soon has no publishers worth having.

Disclosure

I've been a publisher in FatJoe's network for more than a decade. FatJoe pays me for articles it places on chrisabraham.com, each of which I approve or decline before it runs. It pays me nothing for this recommendation, and I have no referral or reseller link. I don't buy links from FatJoe or anyone else, for myself or for clients.

item.title: When to keep your brand name in your page titles, and when to let it go
item.description: Where a brand name belongs in a title tag, how to write it into the sentence instead of a pipe suffix, and how to test the change after a site migration.
item.content:encoded:
When to keep your brand name in your page titles, and when to let it go

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

Most site templates finish every title the same way: the page topic, a pipe, and the company name. I take that suffix off almost every page I work on and keep the name only where it earns the space. Google allows either choice, so this is an editorial decision, not a rule. Here is how I make it, how I write the name into a title when it stays, and how I test the change instead of trusting it.

What Google says about site names in titles

Google's documentation on title links suggests that a site with many pages can include its name at the beginning or end of each title. It also says Google may leave the site name out of the displayed title when it repeats the name already shown in the result. The title element has no maximum length; Google shortens the displayed title to fit the screen.

Two things follow from that. A suffix is not a penalty, and removing one will not lift rankings by itself. And on most results the searcher already sees your site name and icon directly above the title, so a suffix repeats information inside the same result.

Part of my position is plain taste. A pipe and a company name stamped on every page reads unfinished to me. Taste is a fair reason to propose a change. It is not evidence that the change will bring more visitors, which is why I test it.

Three questions I ask about every page

  • Is the organization the subject? Home, About, Contact, booking, and team pages are about the business itself. The name belongs on those.
  • Would the name persuade a stranger to click? For a household brand, perhaps. For a practice or consultancy most searchers have never heard of, the topic does the persuading.
  • Does the topic need the room? If the subject of the page fills the visible width, the subject wins.

When the organization is not the subject, I drop the name and spend those characters on what the page answers.

Write the name into the sentence

Where the name stays, I write it into the title as part of the sentence instead of bolting it on after a separator. Using a made-up practice:

  • Template: Couples Counseling in Portland & Online | Harbor Counseling Group
  • Written: Couples Counseling at Harbor Counseling Group in Portland and Online
  • Template: Book a Session | Harbor Counseling Group
  • Written: Book a Free Consultation with Harbor Counseling Group

The written versions read like headlines. I spell out “and” instead of using an ampersand, and I keep separators out of the topic as well. A title stitched together from three phrases with pipes between them looks like a keyword list. Choose the one idea the page is about and say it plainly.

Compare titles before and after a migration

A new theme, plugin, or site generator often arrives with its own title template, and that template can quietly overwrite titles someone tuned by hand. On a recent recovery project, a therapy practice moved off WordPress and the share of indexable pages ending in the site name rose from 83 percent to 96 percent. About 95 pages that had carefully written titles without a suffix gained one, including articles that had been earning a large share of the practice's search clicks.

The check is simple. Crawl the old site before launch and the new site after it, export both sets of titles, and compare them by URL. Every page whose title changed during the move deserves a look before anyone writes new titles.

Roll the change out as a test

  1. Restore titles that were working before a migration. That is a return to known performance, not an experiment.
  2. Protect titles that already match their main query. If a page's most searched phrase opens its title, edit around those words or leave the page alone.
  3. Remove the suffix from one section first, such as the blog, and leave comparable sections unchanged.
  4. Compare the two groups in Search Console for three to four weeks, looking at clicks and click-through rate. Updates and seasonal swings hit both groups, which makes the comparison fairer than a before-and-after view of one group.
  5. Expand only if the changed section held steady or improved.

Keep every change reversible. Export the current titles or keep them in version control before editing, so any page can go back in minutes.

What a title cleanup can and cannot fix

A cleaner title gives a searcher a clearer reason to pick your result and gives Google less boilerplate to rewrite. It cannot repair thin pages, broken redirects, or a missing image library. Treat it as one tidy, measurable improvement. If traffic has fallen, keep looking for the larger cause; my guide to recovering from a 2026 Google update walks through finding it, and the ten rules for 301 redirects cover the migration mistakes that cost the most.

item.description: AI app builders ship a site in an afternoon. Here is how to check that Google and AI crawlers can read it: rendering, links, titles, status codes, and sitemaps.
item.content:encoded:
SEO for websites built with AI app builders: what to check before you launch

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

Describe a business to Lovable, Bolt, v0, or a coding assistant, and an afternoon later there's a good looking website. Plenty of founders now launch exactly this way, and I'm all for it. The catch is that a site can look perfect in your browser while search engines and AI crawlers receive something close to an empty page. These are the checks I run on every AI-built site, in the order I run them.

Know how your site renders

Everything else depends on one question: does the server send finished HTML, or does it send a script that builds the page in the visitor's browser? The second approach, client-side rendering, is how many React single page apps work. Google can render JavaScript, but its own documentation describes rendering as a separate step after crawling, and recommends server-side rendering or prerendering because it's faster for everyone and because not every bot runs JavaScript. Many AI crawlers fetch the raw HTML and stop there.

Defaults change quickly, so check rather than assume. Lovable is a good example. Its documentation says apps created from May 13, 2026 (June 22, 2026 for Enterprise workspaces) use TanStack Start, which renders pages on the server. Older Lovable apps are React and Vite apps that render in the browser; for those, Lovable serves prerendered copies of published pages to verified search engines, social preview bots, and AI crawlers, and it offers an upgrade path to the newer stack. If your site was built before the change, find out which one you have.

The two minute test

Open a page, then open its source with View Source (not the inspector, which shows the page after scripts run). Search the source for a sentence from the middle of the page. If it's there, crawlers that don't run JavaScript can read it. If the source is mostly a single empty div and a script tag, your content exists only after rendering. For a fuller picture, run the URL through Search Console's URL Inspection tool and look at the rendered HTML Google captured. My text browser test is another quick way to see a page the way the simplest bots do.

Check that every page has its own address

Search engines index URLs. If the "Services" and "About" sections are views inside one page, or live behind a # in the address, they may never be indexed as pages at all. Each page you want found needs its own clean path, such as /services/, that loads that page directly when someone pastes it into a new tab.

Check the links are real links

Generated code often moves between pages with a button and a click handler. It works for people and is invisible to crawlers. Google says plainly that it can follow links only when they're <a> elements with an href. Crawl the site with a crawler such as Screaming Frog; if it finds only the home page, your navigation is the reason. Ask the builder to change navigation to its router's link component, which produces real anchors.

Check titles and descriptions per page

A common result of a fast build is one title, written for the home page, on every URL. Look at the browser tab on five different pages. Each needs its own title and meta description, present in the HTML the server sends. The same goes for the canonical tag: one that points every page at the home page tells Google to ignore the rest.

Check what a missing page returns

Type a nonsense address on your site. Single page apps often show a friendly "not found" message while telling crawlers everything is fine, with a 200 status code. Google calls these soft 404s, and a site with many of them wastes crawling on pages that don't exist. A missing page should return a real 404, and a moved page a 301 redirect.

Give crawlers a map and an open door

  • A sitemap. An XML sitemap listing every real page, submitted in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.
  • A robots.txt that allows the bots you want. Check it by hand; generated files sometimes block everything, a leftover from a staging setup.
  • Structured data. Organization or LocalBusiness markup in the server HTML, matching what the page says. My small business schema guide has examples.

Own the code

Most AI builders can sync a project to GitHub. Do it on day one, in an account your business controls. A repository means any developer, or any SEO who works in code, can fix problems at the template level instead of patching pages through a chat window. item.title: How to publish useful original research without a big budget
item.description: Turn a small, repeatable investigation into useful original research with a clear question, honest sample, documented method, and evidence readers can check.
item.content:encoded:
How to publish useful original research without a big budget

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 12, 2026

You do not need a national survey to contribute something worth reading. A carefully documented investigation of twenty pages can answer a practical question that a thousand recycled articles leave unresolved. The valuable part is the discipline: explain what you examined, make the method inspectable, and keep the conclusion within the evidence. I would rather publish a modest finding with clear boundaries than a sweeping statistic nobody can reproduce.

Start with a question small enough to finish

“What makes websites successful?” is too broad for an afternoon. “Do these twenty public appointment pages expose their booking link in the initial HTML?” is manageable. It names the population, the thing being tested, and a result someone can check. The example is hypothetical; it is a research plan, not a claim about a completed study.

A useful question has a consequence. If the booking link only appears after a particular interaction, a publisher has something concrete to investigate. If the page exposes it immediately, that rules out one possible explanation for an access problem. Either result helps a reader decide what to test next.

Before collecting anything, write a sentence describing the decision the investigation could inform. Then list what it cannot establish. A check of visible links cannot measure appointment completion, prove crawler behavior, or explain a business's revenue. Those would require different evidence.

Choose your sample before seeing the results

Write down how the pages enter the sample. Perhaps they are every appointment page in one public directory, or every qualifying page in a saved list. Record the selection date and the inclusion rule. Do not quietly replace awkward cases with examples that support the story you hoped to tell.

A convenient sample can still be informative, provided it is described honestly. Twenty websites chosen from your own bookmarks do not represent an industry. A test of your own archive describes that archive. Avoid dressing either one up as a random survey.

Keep a record of exclusions as well. If a site is unavailable, distinguish that from a site that fails the actual test. Report the denominator whenever you publish a proportion. Three failures among fifteen successfully tested pages is a different statement from three among twenty selected pages.

Write a method another person could repeat

Decide what counts as a pass before starting. For the appointment example, the rule might require a normal link to a booking destination in the HTML response. Record whether redirects are followed, whether authentication is excluded, and whether a browser comparison is part of the procedure.

A method note should identify the tool and relevant version, the date, and any setting that could alter the result. Mobile and desktop rendering can differ. A consent choice can change loaded resources. An authenticated editor session can reveal content that a public visitor cannot see.

Save the observations in a simple ledger:

  • Sample identifier: a stable label for each selected case.
  • Tested address: the requested URL and final destination.
  • Observation time: when the response or interaction was checked.
  • Result: pass, fail, unavailable, or unresolved, using defined criteria.
  • Evidence: the relevant response excerpt, output, or screenshot.

A screenshot can illustrate an observation, but it should not carry the whole method. Publish the important information as text so readers can inspect it without interpreting a tiny image. Remove credentials, personal information, and irrelevant private material before sharing any artifacts.

Separate counting from explaining

Once the observations are recorded, calculate the result and check it against the ledger. Describe the count in ordinary language. If the sample is small, the exact numerator and denominator are often more informative than a percentage with several decimal places.

Then explain the limits. You might have established that some pages expose a link only after rendering. You have not established that this caused a search decline. Correlation between two observations does not identify the mechanism connecting them. A plausible explanation belongs in a clearly labeled interpretation section.

For a comparison, keep the environments as similar as possible and state what changed. If you test a page before and after a repair, retain both versions and the test settings. When several changes happen together, acknowledge that the result cannot isolate the contribution of each one.

Publish the finding and its working notes together

The article should answer the research question near the top, then show how the answer was obtained. Include the selection rule, the method, the results, and the limitations. A downloadable table can help, but its definitions and main finding should remain on the page.

Use a permanent address and a descriptive title. Give the investigation a named author and an actual publication date. If you revise the method or correct a count, explain the correction and keep a visible revision note. Silent replacement makes it difficult for someone who already cited the finding to understand what happened.

Google's helpful content guidance asks publishers to consider originality, sourcing, and how material was produced. That supports making the work inspectable; it does not promise rankings for a small study. My guide to becoming a useful AI search source explains where this kind of evidence fits into a broader publishing strategy.

Use AI to assist the work, then check its output

An assistant can suggest a ledger structure, help write a test script, or identify inconsistent labels. Treat those contributions as drafts. Confirm that a script measures the stated condition, inspect a few cases manually, and reconcile every published number with the actual observations.

Do not ask a model to invent missing measurements or supply plausible quotations. If the evidence is incomplete, narrow the claim or repeat the test. If AI materially helped produce the research, describe its role where that context would help the reader evaluate the work.

A first project worth attempting

Pick one recurring technical question and a small public sample. Reserve one session for defining the method, another for collecting observations, and a final session for checking the draft against the evidence. Publish only when the numbers, examples, and limitations agree.

The result may be a short, useful reference rather than a headline announcement. That is enough. A reader who can repeat your test has something more valuable than an unsupported prediction. For the credibility surrounding the author, see how to document expertise with independent sources.
