item.title: AI catnip for fall 2026: become the source worth citing
item.description: Make your expertise easier to discover and cite in AI search this fall with original evidence, clear answers, accessible pages, and honest measurement.
item.content:encoded:
AI catnip for fall 2026: become the source worth citing

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 12, 2026

If I wanted to attract AI search attention this fall, I would publish something a reader could use and another writer could verify. Think of catnip as a memorable description of useful source material: a documented test, a precise explanation, a comparison with stated limits. Clever instructions aimed at a model do not create expertise. A page needs a reason to exist before it needs a distribution strategy.

Choose a question you can answer better

Start with a decision, rather than a keyword variation. A business owner might ask whether a migration preserved old image addresses. A developer might need to distinguish an unavailable resource from a harmless browser warning. A buyer might want to know what an audit actually delivers. Each question suggests a bounded article with evidence, a method, and an answer.

I would keep a notebook of the questions that required investigation, then choose one where the explanation can stand without private client data. Describe the setting, show the test, and explain how the result changes the decision. An anonymized example should say it is anonymized. A hypothetical scenario should be labeled as such. Invented experience is a poor foundation for a public reference.

Give the answer a useful shape

Put the direct answer near the beginning. Follow it with the conditions under which it holds. If the answer is “keep the existing URL,” explain which signals make that sensible and what would justify changing it. A reader should not have to cross a sales pitch to discover the conclusion.

Use headings that describe the next practical question. Define unfamiliar terms where they first appear. A comparison belongs in a table when the rows genuinely share the same criteria; a sequence belongs in a numbered list. Formatting should reveal the reasoning rather than manufacture dozens of nearly identical questions.

My preferred evidence package has four parts:

  1. The observation: what was measured, including the date and relevant environment.
  2. The method: enough detail for someone else to repeat the check.
  3. The interpretation: what the result supports and what remains uncertain.
  4. The next action: what a reader should do with that information.

For example, a successful HTTP response proves availability at the time of testing. It does not establish that a search engine indexed the resource, selected it for an answer, or credited a conversion to it. Keeping those distinctions visible makes an article more useful than a confident claim assembled from unrelated screenshots.

Make your identity and evidence easy to check

A named author, a relevant biography, and a clear way to contact the publisher help readers assess responsibility. Link technical assertions to their primary documentation. Explain which parts are your recommendation. Keep a publication date separate from a substantive revision date, and record what changed when the advice changes.

On your own site, link a new explanation from the appropriate topic hub and from an older article that actually needs it. Avoid orphaned material and generic anchor text. My guide to independent evidence of expertise covers corroboration beyond an author's own biography.

Access comes before attraction

Google's documentation says existing SEO practices apply to its AI search features. A supporting page needs indexing and snippet eligibility; a special AI file is not an admission ticket. That makes a technical check worthwhile before rewriting successful content.

Open the page without signing in. Inspect the returned HTML, then compare it with the browser's rendered view. Confirm the main explanation is present, the canonical identifies the intended page, and crawler requests are not caught by a challenge. Check both robots rules and response headers. An attractive design can coexist with straightforward text, descriptive links, and accessible navigation.

Different crawler purposes also deserve separate decisions. OpenAI documents OAI-SearchBot for search and GPTBot for training. Allowing one is not the same policy choice as allowing the other. Consult the current provider documentation before changing access, and do not treat a copied user agent string as proof that a real provider visited.

Use IndexNow without confusing notification with a citation

IndexNow tells participating search engines that a URL was added, changed, or removed. It can improve discovery of a meaningful update. Bing is a participant; Google is not listed among the participating endpoints in the documentation checked for this guide. An accepted notification is not a promise to index or recommend the page.

The useful connection to AI search is indirect: fresher search indexes can help products that retrieve from those indexes. IndexNow does not deliver every article to every AI crawler. I would pair it with a valid sitemap, ordinary internal links, and Bing Webmaster Tools rather than describe it as a universal AI feed.

Keep a small measurement journal

Choose a handful of realistic questions and record the wording, date, product, cited URLs, and any factual errors. Repeat the same checks periodically. Answers vary, so one favorable screenshot is an observation rather than a ranking report. Separately record search impressions, referred visits, and inquiries. Those are different outcomes.

Give a revision time to be discovered before changing the next variable. If you replace the title, illustrations, introduction, and URL together, you make the outcome harder to interpret. Keep a short change log so a future traffic movement can be compared with actual releases rather than memory.

A realistic afternoon of work

Select one strong article. Improve its opening answer, add one verifiable example, repair its references, and link it from a relevant guide. Test the published page and notify the participating engines after the change is live. Then write down what you changed and when you will review it.

That is my version of AI catnip: material someone can confidently build on, delivered through a site that works. For a broader technical review, use the AI search readiness checklist. New Guides also appear in the full-text RSS feed, which can be imported into a feed reader or publishing system.

item.title: Is a Screaming Frog licence worth $279 a year? Mine was
item.description: Why I finally paid for the Screaming Frog SEO Spider, what the free 500 URL version leaves out, and everything a $279 a year licence can do in 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Is a Screaming Frog licence worth $279 a year? Mine was

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 11, 2026

For years I was too cheap to pay for the Screaming Frog SEO Spider. I ran the free version, slurped up 500 URLs at a time, and got a tip of the iceberg view of what was going on with a site. I wasn't using a ten thousandth of what the tool can do. This year I finally bought a licence. Paying $279 stung. It also leveled me up more than any tool purchase I've made, and I should have done it a decade ago. It's legit my secret weapon now. Don't make my mistake. Here is what the free version leaves out and everything the paid version can do.

What it costs, as of October 2026

The SEO Spider is a desktop program for Windows, macOS, and Linux. The free version needs no sign up. A licence costs $279 (£199) per user per year, and Screaming Frog discounts bulk purchases:

Licences bought at oncePrice per licence, per year
1 to 4$279
5 to 9$265
10 to 19$249
20 or more$235

Licences are per person, so two people need two licences, and each one lasts a year before it needs renewing. There's no per page or per project metering: the only ceiling on crawl size is your computer's memory and storage.

What the free version gives you

The free version is genuinely useful, which is exactly how it kept me from paying. It crawls up to 500 URLs and will:

  • Find broken links, server errors, and redirects.
  • Check page titles and meta descriptions.
  • Show meta robots and other directives.
  • Audit hreflang attributes.
  • Find exact duplicate pages.
  • Generate XML sitemaps.
  • Draw site visualisations.

For a ten page brochure site, that's plenty. For anything bigger, 500 URLs runs out fast, because every image, script, and stylesheet the crawler finds can count toward the limit, and you can't change the crawl settings to leave them out.

My defense: the Rumsfeld

When anyone asks why I waited so long, I plead the Rumsfeld:

"There are known knowns; there are things we know we know. We also know there are known unknowns; that is to say we know there are some things we do not know. But there are also unknown unknowns, the ones we don't know we don't know."

Donald Rumsfeld, U.S. Secretary of Defense, Pentagon news briefing, February 12, 2002

That was me and the free version. The 500 URL cap was a known unknown: I knew there were pages past it I wasn't seeing. Everything in the next section was an unknown unknown. I never saw most of it, so I never missed it, and I never knew what it would have caught. You can't price a tool by the features you've never seen.

And when I couldn't plead ignorance, I pleaded his other famous line, from a town hall with troops in Kuwait on December 8, 2004:

"As you know, you go to war with the Army you have. They're not the Army you might want or wish to have at a later time."

Donald Rumsfeld, U.S. Secretary of Defense, town hall meeting, Camp Buehring, Kuwait, December 8, 2004

The free version was the army I had, and I made do with it. Five hundred URLs at a time, I patched together a picture of each site from slices. The difference is that I never had to wait for anyone's production line. The army I wanted was one $279 purchase away the entire time.

What the licence unlocks

Here is the part I spent years ignoring. According to Screaming Frog's own comparison, everything below is paid only.

Crawl the whole site, your way

  • No 500 URL limit. Crawl sites with hundreds of thousands of pages; the tool can store crawl data on disk instead of in memory.
  • Full crawl configuration. Include or exclude sections, set speed, change the user agent to Googlebot, Bingbot, or an AI crawler, and decide which resources to check.
  • Save and reopen crawls. In the free version, closing the window throws the crawl away.
  • Forms based login. Crawl staging sites and member areas that sit behind a login page.
  • Custom robots.txt. Download, edit, and test a site's robots.txt rules against the crawl before you change the live file.

See what Google sees on JavaScript sites

The licence turns on rendering with built-in headless Chromium, so the crawler runs the JavaScript on React, Angular, and Vue sites and reads the finished page. Crawl the same pages with rendering off and then on, compare word counts by template, and content that only exists after scripts run stands out immediately. Rendered screenshots and stored rendered HTML let you see exactly what the crawler saw.

Catch the problems that cost rankings

  • Near-duplicate content. Beyond exact copies, it finds near duplicates and semantically similar pages using algorithmic checks and vector embeddings.
  • Structured data validation. Extracts schema markup and checks it against Schema.org and Google's rich result features.
  • Accessibility auditing. Runs the open-source axe rules against WCAG on every page.
  • Spelling and grammar checks in more than 25 languages.
  • Mobile usability checks using Lighthouse.
  • AMP crawling and validation with the official AMP validator.
  • Uncrawlable links. Since version 24.0, a filter shows pages whose internal links don't follow Google's link best practices, such as a link that only works through an onclick handler.

Pull any data off any page

  • Custom search looks for anything in the source code: a missing analytics tag, an old phone number, a retired product name.
  • Custom extraction scrapes any element with XPath, CSS selectors, or regex: prices, SKUs, authors, publish dates, stock notices.
  • Custom JavaScript runs your own snippets during the crawl, so you can scroll pages, trigger events, or extract nearly anything you could in the Chrome console.

Layer real data on top of the crawl

  • Google Search Console: clicks, impressions, and index status in bulk through the URL Inspection API.
  • Google Analytics: users and conversions for every crawled URL.
  • PageSpeed Insights: Lighthouse scores, diagnostics, and Chrome UX Report field data for every page at once.
  • Link metrics: Ahrefs, Majestic, and Moz data next to each URL, useful for content audits and deciding which pages deserve redirects.

Put those side by side and the crawl answers the question that matters: which pages earn traffic and have a technical problem? Fix those first.

Use AI inside the crawl

The licence connects the crawler to OpenAI, Gemini, Anthropic, and Ollama, so you can run your own prompt against every page as it's crawled: draft missing meta descriptions, write alt text, classify page intent, or flag thin content. Any AI-written metadata still needs a person to check it before it goes live.

Version 24.0, released May 19, 2026, also added an MCP server, so you can run crawls and analyze, export, and reshape the data from inside AI assistants such as Claude, in plain English. Screaming Frog says plainly that it isn't a replacement for an experienced SEO, and not every feature is available through it yet.

Put audits on autopilot

  • Scheduling: crawls run on their own at set intervals and export to a folder or Google Sheets.
  • Command line: run the whole thing from a script on a server.
  • Crawl comparison: see what changed between two crawls, and map staging URLs to production URLs to check a redesign before launch. Since version 24.0, scheduled crawls can compare the last two crawls automatically.
  • Email alerts: get a summary of issues when a crawl finishes, including what changed, and send a chosen export (say, weekly broken links) straight to a developer.
  • Data Studio crawl reports for site health dashboards over time.
  • Segmentation to report on sections of a site, such as products versus articles, separately.

Support from the people who build it

Licence holders get free technical support. Free users don't.

Who should buy a licence

  • Buy it if you do SEO for a living, look after any site over a few hundred pages, run a JavaScript framework, or are planning a migration or redesign.
  • Skip it, for now, if you own one small site that stays under 500 URLs and you only need to find broken links once in a while.

Screaming Frog is a technical crawler. It doesn't track rankings or research keywords and competitors, so it complements a keyword tool rather than replacing one.

What I'd tell my younger self

The math is embarrassing in hindsight. $279 a year is about 76 cents a day. One recovered redirect, one page that was quietly invisible to Google, or one launch that didn't break pays for years of licences. I spent a decade reading the first 500 URLs of every site and guessing at the rest, when the whole iceberg was right there the whole time.

If you want to see what a properly configured crawl turns up on your own site, that's where my audits start. For what the finished audit should look like, see what a technical SEO audit should give you.

item.content:encoded:
WordPress SEO 101: the settings and habits that matter most

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 9, 2026

WordPress runs a huge share of the web, and it is a genuinely good platform for search right out of the box. Most WordPress SEO problems I'm hired to fix come from a handful of settings nobody changed, a few plugins that fight each other, and habits like linking the words "read more" a thousand times. Here is what a beginner should do, in order, on a new site or an old one.

Day one: five settings to check

  1. Settings, then Reading: find "Discourage search engines from indexing this site" and make sure it is unchecked. Developers tick it while building and forget it at launch more often than you'd believe. One checkbox can keep an entire business out of Google.
  2. Settings, then Permalinks: choose "Post name," so addresses read /kitchen-remodeling/ instead of /?p=123. On an established site, change this only with redirects in place.
  3. Settings, then General: set a real Site Title and a tagline that says what you do. Many themes print them on every page.
  4. HTTPS: both addresses in General settings should start with https://. Your host can install a free certificate.
  5. Users: give every author a real display name and a short bio. Pages signed by an actual person are easier to trust.

The plugins I recommend

These are my personal picks after years of building and fixing WordPress sites. Install one SEO plugin only; two will fight over your titles and sitemaps.

  • Yoast SEO Premium. The free version handles titles, meta descriptions, XML sitemaps, schema, and archive settings well. Premium adds a redirect manager, so changed or deleted pages never strand a visitor, and internal linking suggestions that help you connect related posts as you write. It pays for itself the first time you rename a page.
  • WPCode, and WPCode Pro for schema. The safe way to add snippets: a verification tag, a tracking code, a small PHP tweak. It keeps them in one place, survives theme changes, and spares you from editing functions.php, where one typo can take the site down. I use the paid Pro version for structured data: it lets me add bespoke schema to any individual page or post, so a service page, an event, or a case study can each carry markup written for exactly what that page says. Keep it consistent with what Yoast already outputs, and test every page in Google's Rich Results Test.
  • Site Kit by Google. Google's own plugin connects Search Console, Analytics, and PageSpeed Insights to your dashboard and verifies site ownership for you. It hardwires your site into Google's tools in a few clicks, and puts the numbers where you'll actually see them.

Archive pages: keep the duplicates out of search

WordPress automatically makes extra pages that list your posts by tag, category, date, and author. On most small sites those pages repeat content that already lives on the posts themselves. In Yoast's settings I set tag archives, date archives, and author archives on single-author sites to stay out of search results, and leave categories indexed only when each one has a real introduction of its own. Media attachment pages, which give every uploaded image its own thin page, have been off by default for new sites since WordPress 6.4; on older sites, Yoast can redirect them to the image itself.

Writing a post that ranks

  • The post title is your H1. Use Heading 2 and Heading 3 blocks for sections, in order. Never pick a heading level for its size.
  • Fill in the SEO title and meta description in the Yoast box under every post: a unique title around 50 to 60 characters and a description around 150.
  • Edit the slug to a short, readable phrase before you publish.
  • Answer the question early, in plain words, and add what only you know: prices, photos of your work, your process, your results.

Alt text in the media library

Every image block and every media library item has an "Alternative text" field. Describe what the image shows in a short sentence, including any words visible in it. Leave out "image of," because screen readers already say that. Leave the field empty only for purely decorative images, so screen readers skip them. Fill it in once in the media library and WordPress reuses it wherever you insert that image.

Kill "read more" for good

Many themes end every excerpt with a "Read more" or "Continue reading" link. On a blog page with twenty posts that's twenty identical links, each one telling crawlers and screen reader users nothing about where it goes. Link the post title instead, or change the theme's excerpt link to include the post's name. In your own writing, put links on words that describe the destination: "my guide to accessible websites," never "click here." Link new posts to your older related posts, and older posts forward to new ones; this is the internal linking that helps both readers and crawlers find your best pages.

Put Cloudflare in front of WordPress

After the plugins, my strongest advice is to move the domain's DNS to Cloudflare and route the site through it. Even the free plan speeds up WordPress, manages certificates, and fends off attacks, and the paid features are worth their price on most WordPress sites. My guide to Cloudflare for WordPress walks through the setup, the plan I'd choose, and the budget.

Tell the search engines

  1. Verify the site in Google Search Console (Site Kit can do it for you) and submit the sitemap Yoast creates at /sitemap_index.xml.
  2. In Bing Webmaster Tools, use the import from Google Search Console option. It copies every verified site and sitemap across in a few clicks.
  3. Make sure IndexNow is on. Yoast SEO Premium includes it and pings Bing and the other participating engines every time you publish or update a post.
  4. Check both consoles every few weeks for sitemap errors and pages that aren't indexed.

Speed

  • Hosting matters most. A good managed WordPress host beats any plugin on cheap shared hosting.
  • Use fewer plugins. Each one can add scripts to every page. Remove what you don't use.
  • Upload sensible images. WordPress already creates smaller sizes and lazy loads images below the fold, but a 6 MB photo straight from a phone still slows the first view. Resize before uploading, or use an image optimization plugin.
  • Add caching if your host doesn't provide it, and test in PageSpeed Insights. My Core Web Vitals guide covers what the scores mean.

Accessibility

Choose a theme tagged "accessibility ready" in the WordPress theme directory; those themes have passed a review for keyboard navigation, contrast, and structure. Then keep your content accessible with real headings, alt text, descriptive links, and captions on video. Accessibility and SEO reward the same work; see the SEO dividends of accessibility.

Updates and spam

Keep WordPress, your theme, and your plugins updated; hacked sites get spam pages injected and drop out of search fast. Turn off comments if you don't moderate them. And treat any offer of cheap backlinks, guaranteed rankings, or "AI content at scale" as the spam it is.

item.title: Hit by a 2026 Google update? A recovery checklist that works
item.description: How to tell whether a 2026 Google core or spam update hit your site, rule out reporting quirks, find the pages that lost, and fix them in the right order.
item.content:encoded:
Hit by a 2026 Google update? A recovery checklist that works

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 9, 2026

Google confirmed two core updates and four spam updates between March and October 2026. When traffic falls in a year like that, the first instinct is to change everything at once. Resist it. Recovery starts with knowing which update, if any, actually touched you, and which pages took the loss. Here is the order I work in when a client calls with a graph that points down.

1. Line the drop up with the calendar

Open Google's Search Status Dashboard and note this year's ranking updates: a spam update on March 24, the March core update from March 27, the May core update from May 21, and spam updates starting June 24, August 18, and September 24. Then open Search Console, set the date range to sixteen months, and compare. A drop that begins within a few days of a rollout's start is a strong lead. A drop that began weeks before one, or on the day a redesign launched, points somewhere else.

2. Rule out the reporting quirks

  • The num=100 change. In September 2025 Google stopped serving a hundred results per page to rank trackers, and desktop impressions in Search Console fell for most sites while average position rose. If your comparison spans that month and clicks held steady, nothing happened to real visitors.
  • Seasonality. Compare against the same weeks last year before blaming an algorithm.
  • Tracking breaks. If analytics fell but Search Console clicks didn't, a broken tag or consent banner is the suspect.

3. Decide which kind of update it was

The two kinds behave differently. A core update re-ranks pages against each other; losses tend to spread across many queries and pages, often by moderate amounts. A spam update applies detection systems for policy violations; losses are usually steep, fast, and concentrated in the sections that triggered them. Also check Search Console's Manual actions report. Algorithmic hits stay off that report, so an empty report plus a cliff on a spam update date tells you an automated system made the call.

4. Find the pages that lost

In the Performance report, compare the two weeks after the update with the two weeks before, by page. Sort by lost clicks. Usually a minority of pages accounts for most of the loss, and they share something: the same template, the same author, the same type of content, or the same section of the site. That shared trait is the real finding.

5. Match the losers against the spam policies

Read Google's spam policies with that list of pages open. The ones that matter most this year:

  • Scaled content abuse: lots of pages made mainly to rank, by AI, by people, or both. Programmatic city pages, mass "best of" lists, and unreviewed AI articles are the usual suspects.
  • Site reputation abuse: third-party content hosted in your subfolder or subdomain to borrow your site's standing.
  • Expired domain abuse: an old domain repurposed for unrelated, low-value content.
  • Manipulating AI answers: since May, hidden text or instructions aimed at AI Overviews and AI Mode count as spam too.

If any of these describe the losing pages, remove or rewrite them before anything else. A policy problem outweighs every improvement elsewhere.

6. Fix in order of value

  1. Delete or consolidate thin and duplicate pages, redirecting any with links or traffic to the closest strong page.
  2. Rewrite the pages worth keeping with what only you can add: real examples, photos, numbers, procedures you follow, and the name of the person who knows the subject.
  3. Check access for every crawler you care about, Googlebot, Bingbot, and the AI search crawlers, at the robots.txt, CDN, and firewall levels.
  4. Make structured data honest: every claim in the markup should be visible on the page.

7. Set the right expectations

Google describes core updates as broad changes that don't target specific sites, and says it can take several months for its systems to confirm that improved content is helpful; if nothing moves after a few months, the next core update is the one to watch. Spam systems reassess too, after the problems are gone. Keep a dated change log so each later movement can be tied to a specific fix. Avoid the panic moves: buying links, mass-deleting pages that performed well, or rewriting the whole site in a week.

What I'd watch next

Expect another core update before the year ends, and more enforcement against manipulation of AI answers. Sites built on original work have done well through all of 2026; sites built on volume have struggled. Where to get reliable SEO and AI search news in 2026

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 9, 2026

Search the phrase "best SEO news sites" and the first things you see are ads for AI visibility audits, then an AI summary, then lists of lists. Most of it is marketing for whoever wrote it. Staying current takes a short reading list, an order to read it in, and the habit of checking the claim before repeating it. Here is mine, built over decades of doing this work and refreshed for the AI search era.

Start with the people who make the rules

  • Google Search Central Blog. Official announcements: core updates, policy changes, new Search Console reports. Recent posts covered the site reputation policy update on August 28 and new multimodal performance reporting on September 24.
  • Google Search Status Dashboard. The authoritative record of every ranking update, with start dates and durations. When an article and the dashboard disagree, the dashboard wins.
  • Google's documentation changelog. Quiet but important. On October 1, Google's guidance on AI-generated content began calling manual fact checking and review of AI output critical before publishing.
  • Bing Webmaster Tools and its blog. Bing's AI Performance report is the closest thing to a first-party view of AI citations.
  • The AI companies' own policies. OpenAI's crawler documentation, and usage policies like the one Anthropic updated on October 8, change what is allowed faster than any trade article can summarize.

Then the daily trade press

  • Search Engine Roundtable. Barry Schwartz's site is the fastest on tests, volatility, and small interface changes, often within hours.
  • Search Engine Land. Broad daily coverage and analysis from many contributors. Its footer notes that it is a trademark of Semrush, the SEO software company, which is worth knowing when a story touches SEO tools.
  • Search Engine Journal. News plus long columns from practitioners, published by Alpha Brand Media.

Read at least two for anything big. They often break the same story with different details.

A weekly digest

Aleyda Solis' SEOFOMO newsletter arrives every Sunday with the week's news, guides, tools, and events. If you read only one thing a week, make it this.

Research, with a grain of salt

The big tool makers, Ahrefs and Semrush among them, publish large studies on AI Overviews, citations, and click rates. They are valuable and they are also marketing for the tools that produced the data. Independent practitioners who publish their own tracking, such as Lily Ray and Marie Haynes, are worth following for the same reason: you can see their method and their sample.

Three habits that keep you from repeating mistakes

1. Check dates against the primary record

This month a widely read write-up gave the start of Google's September spam update as "Thursday, September 28." The dashboard says September 24, which was the Thursday. Small slip, easy check, and the kind of error that spreads when everyone copies everyone.

2. Compare studies before quoting one

Three studies this fall measured how often AI Overviews appear for brand searches. Ahrefs reported 83 percent of branded searches; DemandSphere data reported in Search Engine Land showed a jump from 26 to 80 percent; a third found summaries for 93 of 100 brands. Different samples, different methods, same direction. The direction is the finding. The exact number belongs to its study.

3. Read the footnote on every bold claim

One agency's ad this month promises a 100 percent success rate at increasing AI visibility. The footnote defines success as an increase in any one of several visibility metrics from the start of a campaign to its latest measurement. Another vendor reports a "100% client success rate" for making reviews crawlable. Neither claim is false. Both describe something much smaller than the headline suggests.

What to skip

  • "Best agency" lists written by an agency that ranks itself first.
  • Statistics with no named study, sample, or date, especially round ones repeated by AI summaries.
  • Anyone claiming a secret formula for AI Overviews. Google's own documentation says there are no special requirements beyond ordinary search eligibility.

item.title: Cloudflare for WordPress: setup, plans, and what to budget
item.description: How to put a WordPress site behind Cloudflare: moving DNS, what the free plan already does, APO and Polish on paid plans, HTTPS settings, and a monthly budget.
item.content:encoded:
Cloudflare for WordPress: setup, plans, and what to budget

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 9, 2026

If I could make one change to most of the WordPress sites I'm asked to look at, it would be putting them behind Cloudflare. It makes them faster, safer, and cheaper to run, and the free plan alone covers a lot of ground. My own experience and every AI assistant I've put the question to agree. For the record, Cloudflare pays me nothing for saying so, which, given how often I say it, is a little sad.

Two ways to use Cloudflare

Every DNS record in Cloudflare shows a cloud. A gray cloud means DNS only: Cloudflare tells browsers where your server is, then steps aside. An orange cloud means proxied: visitors reach Cloudflare's network first, and it serves what it can from the data center nearest them before passing the rest to your host. The speed and protection only apply to orange records.

  • Gray, DNS only: if Cloudflare just registers the domain and answers DNS, the free plan is all you need.
  • Orange, proxied: this is where WordPress gains the most, and where the paid features become worth considering.

What the free plan does once you're proxied

  • Caches your images, scripts, and stylesheets close to visitors. HTML pages aren't cached by default; that takes APO or a cache rule, below.
  • Compresses files on the way out.
  • Provides HTTPS certificates at no cost.
  • Absorbs denial of service attacks before they reach your host.
  • Tells Bing and other engines that support IndexNow when your content changes, through a free feature called Crawler Hints.

The paid features that matter for WordPress

  • Automatic Platform Optimization (APO): caches whole WordPress pages at Cloudflare's edge, so even the first byte arrives fast from anywhere. It works with the official Cloudflare WordPress plugin, comes included with the Pro plan and above, and costs $5 a month on the free plan.
  • Polish: compresses images and can convert them to WebP automatically. Available on Pro and above.

Even though Cloudflare can cost nothing, when a WordPress site runs through it I recommend budgeting about $50 a month for Cloudflare's paid services, starting with Pro. WordPress almost always benefits. I pay for Pro on my own main site.

Setting it up

  1. Add the site in a free Cloudflare account. Cloudflare scans your existing DNS records; compare them against your current DNS provider line by line, especially mail records, before going further.
  2. Change the nameservers at your registrar to the two Cloudflare gives you. Or transfer the domain to Cloudflare Registrar, which charges the registry's wholesale price with no markup on renewals.
  3. Turn the website records orange. Leave mail records gray.
  4. Set SSL/TLS to Full (strict), which requires a valid certificate on your host; most hosts provide one free. Flexible mode can trap WordPress in an endless redirect loop.
  5. Switch on Always Use HTTPS, then HSTS once every page loads securely.
  6. Install the official Cloudflare WordPress plugin, connect it, and turn on APO if you have it, so your cache clears automatically when you publish or edit.
  7. Check the bot and AI crawler settings. Make sure search engines and the AI crawlers you want, such as the ones behind ChatGPT search and Perplexity, aren't blocked. I let them in; being cited by AI assistants is part of being found.
  8. Turn on Crawler Hints under Caching.
  9. Test your home page and a post in PageSpeed Insights before and after.

What to leave alone

  • Rocket Loader rewrites how scripts load. It can speed up a simple site and break a complex one, including forms, analytics, and cookie banners. If anything acts strangely, turn it off first.
  • Caching the admin. Never cache /wp-admin/, the login page, carts, checkouts, or account pages. APO is built to skip logged-in visitors and the admin; any cache rule you write by hand has to exclude them too.
  • Under Attack Mode challenges every visitor, search engine crawlers included. Use it during an actual attack only.

When Cloudflare isn't the right layer

If a site runs on a hosted builder such as Shopify, Squarespace, or Wix, the builder already provides a CDN and certificates. Cloudflare can still hold the domain and answer DNS, but keep those records gray and follow the builder's own connection instructions. Some managed WordPress hosts also bundle Cloudflare or their own CDN; ask before stacking two.

item.content:encoded:
Will Google penalize AI-written content? What Google actually says

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 9, 2026

Almost every client asks me some version of this: if I use ChatGPT or Claude to help write my pages, will Google punish me? The short answer is no, Google doesn't punish content for being written with AI. It punishes content for being unhelpful, inaccurate, deceptive, or mass-produced to game rankings, and AI makes all four of those very easy. Here is what Google has said, in its own words, and how to use AI without risk.

What Google said in 2023, and still says

When ChatGPT arrived, Google published its position plainly: appropriate use of AI or automation is not against its guidelines. It defined inappropriate use just as plainly: generating content primarily to manipulate search rankings, which violates its spam policies. Google's ranking systems look for helpful, reliable content, and they don't care whether a person, a tool, or both typed the words.

What changed on October 1, 2026

Google rewrote its page on using generative AI content, and it now says: "It is critical to manually factcheck and review all AI-generated content for accuracy and trustworthiness before publishing." The same review applies to the parts of a page people forget about: title tags, meta descriptions, structured data, and image alt text, all of which can appear in search results. If an AI tool wrote your metadata, a person should check it.

The page also suggests telling readers how content was created, in a way that makes sense for your audience. Sellers using Google Merchant Center have firmer rules: AI-generated product images need embedded metadata saying so, and AI-generated product titles and descriptions must be labeled.

Fake authors are now named as deception

Google's guide to people-first content encourages accurate bylines and warns against "deceptive authorship information." Its examples are exactly what some AI content shops sell: AI-generated headshots, made-up names, and false credentials meant to make a page look written by human experts. Google calls any form of deception a reason to treat a page as untrustworthy. If a real person reviewed the work, put that real person's name on it.

Where AI content really gets sites in trouble

The risk is scale without value. Google's scaled content abuse policy covers producing many pages mainly to rank, whether people, AI, or both made them, and it was the focus of reporting on Google's 2026 spam updates. The pattern that gets hit looks like this:

  • Hundreds or thousands of pages published quickly, often one per keyword or city.
  • Text that summarizes what's already ranking and adds nothing new.
  • No named author, no first-hand detail, and no review before publishing.
  • Factual errors nobody caught, because nobody read it.

What the data shows

In July 2026, Ahrefs examined pages ranking in Google and estimated how much of each was written by AI. In the top three positions, about 5 percent of pages appeared to be entirely AI-generated and roughly 9 percent at least 80 percent AI. Its conclusion was in the title: Google doesn't punish AI content; it punishes bad content. Two cautions: AI detectors produce probabilities, never proof, and the study shows correlation rather than cause. Still, AI-assisted pages clearly can and do rank at the very top.

A safe way to use AI for your site

  1. Use AI where it's strong: research, outlines, first drafts, summaries of your own notes, and variations to choose from.
  2. Add what only you have: your prices, process, photos, customer stories, mistakes, and opinions. This is the part search engines and AI assistants can't find anywhere else.
  3. Fact check every claim, every number, every quote, and every link before publishing. Treat the draft as a confident intern's work.
  4. Review the metadata too: titles, descriptions, structured data, and alt text.
  5. Put a real name on it, the person who knows the subject and stands behind the page.
  6. Publish at a human pace. Ten excellent pages beat a thousand thin ones.
  7. Be open about your process where readers would want to know.

About AI detectors

Clients sometimes run their pages through an AI detector and panic at the score. Don't. Detectors guess, they disagree with each other, and they flag plenty of human writing. Google's question is whether a page helps the person who searched, and no detector measures that.

How I work

I use AI tools every day, for research, drafts, and checking my own work. Every guide on this site is drafted with AI assistance under my direction, checked claim by claim against named sources, and published with those sources listed at the bottom. That is the standard I'd hold any client's site to. item.title: Holiday hours on Google: set them before you need them
item.description: How and when to set special hours on Google for Thanksgiving, December, and New Year, when to mark a business temporarily closed, and what searchers see.
item.content:encoded:
Holiday hours on Google: set them before you need them

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 7, 2026

Every November, someone drives to a shop that Google said was open and finds the lights off. That customer doesn't blame Google. Special hours on your Business Profile take a few minutes to set, and the best time to set them is weeks before the holidays, not the night before.

Special hours, regular hours, and closures

Your regular hours describe a normal week. Special hours override them for specific dates, such as Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve, or a one day event, without touching the normal schedule. Google's help pages draw the line at about a week: special hours cover a business that adjusts its hours or closes for up to six days in a row. Closed for seven days or more, or for an unknown period, and the right tool is marking the business temporarily closed instead.

Confirm the holidays you're open, too

Google suggests confirming your hours for official holidays even when they're the same as usual. It's easy to skip, and it matters: a confirmed holiday tells searchers you thought about that day, and anyone deciding between you and a competitor with the same hours will pick the one that looks certain.

A calendar for the season

  • Early November: decide your hours for Thanksgiving Day and the day after, and set them.
  • Mid November: set Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, New Year's Eve, and New Year's Day while you're thinking about it.
  • Any extended or late night shopping hours: set those as special hours on each date, so your regular schedule stays clean for January.
  • The week before each holiday: look at your listing in Google Search and Maps the way a customer would, and confirm it shows what you intended.

More than one location

Each location has its own profile, so each needs its own special hours, even when the whole company closes on the same day. If you manage many locations, set them as a batch from the dashboard and then spot check a few in Maps. A location that was missed is the one a customer will find.

Departments and service hours

If part of your business keeps different hours, like a pharmacy counter, takeout, or delivery, Google offers additional hour types for those. Use them for the parts that differ, rather than squeezing exceptions into the main hours.

Keep the website in step

Your website should say the same thing as the profile. A short holiday hours note on the contact page, removed after New Year, avoids the mixed message of one schedule on Google and another on your own site. If your hours appear in structured data, update or remove the special dates there as well.

Snow days and other surprises

Winter brings closures nobody can schedule: a storm, a burst pipe, a sick staff. The same tool works. Set special hours for that single date, or mark the day closed, as soon as you know, even if it's early that morning. A listing that says open while the door is locked costs more trust than a short notice ever will. If the closure stretches past six days, switch to temporarily closed and switch back the moment you reopen, because a business left marked closed by mistake quietly loses calls for weeks.

If you're reading this in December

It isn't too late. Set the dates that are still ahead, check the listing in Maps, and add the note to your website. Then put a reminder in next year's calendar for the first week of November, which is the whole trick: decide early, set it once, and stop thinking about it.

Don't forget to come back

Special hours expire on their own after the date passes, which is the main reason to use them instead of editing your regular hours. If you did change your regular hours for the season, put a reminder in your calendar for January to change them back.

What customers see

On the day, Google shows your special hours in place of the regular ones. Searchers who check ahead see the right times, and the ones who call get a business that's actually open. It's the smallest piece of local SEO there is, and one of the few with an immediate, visible payoff.

item.content:encoded:
How to hire an SEO on Upwork: the questions that reveal real skill

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 7, 2026

Post an SEO job on Upwork and fifty proposals arrive within a day, most of them interchangeable. The screening questions you add to the posting are the fastest way to separate people who understand your problem from people who paste the same letter everywhere. I answer these questions for a living, so here is what I'd ask if I were on your side of the table.

Write the problem, not a wish list

The best postings describe a situation: what changed, when, what you've already checked, and what a good outcome would look like. "Service page rankings fell after the March redesign" gives an expert something to reason about. "Need SEO expert for growth" attracts the people least likely to help. A specific posting also lets you judge the replies, because you'll know whether a candidate engaged with your facts or skipped them.

Five questions worth adding

  1. "Based on this posting, what would you check first, and why?" A strong answer names two or three concrete things in a sensible order and explains what each would rule in or out. A weak answer lists every SEO activity in existence.
  2. "Describe one problem like this one: what was wrong, what you changed, and what happened." You want a mechanism and a result, described honestly. Real practitioners can explain a past diagnosis without naming the client.
  3. "What access would you need in the first week?" Search Console, analytics, and some form of access to the site or its developer are normal. Someone who needs nothing is planning to guess.
  4. "How would you know this worked?" Listen for measures you can check yourself: indexed pages, impressions and clicks on the affected pages, calls or form leads. Be wary of measures only the consultant can see.
  5. "What would you not do?" This one is revealing. Experienced people have boundaries: no link packages, no guaranteed positions, no changes without a reason they can explain.

What good answers sound like

Good answers are short and specific to your posting. They use your words, refer to your platform, and propose a first step small enough to test. They separate what is known from what needs checking. They read like a colleague thinking out loud about your site, not a brochure. If a candidate's answers would fit any other job on the platform, they weren't written for yours.

Red flags

  • Guarantees. Nobody controls Google's results, and Google's own hiring advice says so plainly. A promised position is a reason to keep looking.
  • Link quotas. "Fifty high authority backlinks a month" usually means purchased or manufactured links, the kind Google's spam policies describe.
  • Answers that point elsewhere. "See my cover letter" or "check my profile" in a screening box means the question wasn't read.
  • Free audits as bait. A long unsolicited audit in a proposal is either generic or unpaid work that will be recovered somewhere else. Insight is welcome; a fake deliverable isn't.
  • No questions back. Someone who understands your problem will want to know at least one thing you didn't say.

Read the profile like evidence

Job Success Score, hours worked, and repeat clients tell you how a freelancer behaves over time, not how they write. Open the client reviews and look for specifics: what was fixed, how communication went, whether the client came back. One detailed review is worth more than ten five star ratings with no text.

Start with a small paid step

For anything bigger than a quick fix, pay for a defined first step: a diagnosis of one problem, an audit with a prioritized list, or a fixed number of hours. You learn how the person works, they learn your site, and either side can stop cleanly. It also prices the work honestly, because a good diagnosis is real labor and you should own the result.

Fixed price or hourly

Fixed price suits a well-defined deliverable, such as an audit, a migration plan, or a set list of fixes. Hourly suits ongoing work where the next task depends on what the last one found. Either way, agree on what "done" means before work starts, and keep the scope written in the contract rather than scattered across messages.

item.title: How to change a business name without losing your Google reviews
item.description: How to rename a business without losing its Google Business Profile, reviews, or rankings: edit the existing listing, sequence the change, and update the web.
item.content:encoded:
How to change a business name without losing your Google reviews

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 7, 2026

A new name feels like a fresh start, and that instinct is exactly what costs businesses their reviews and rankings. The safest rebrand treats the renamed business as the same business it has always been, because to Google it is. Here is the order I follow when a client renames a shop, a restaurant, a studio, or a practice.

Rule one: edit the listing you have

Your reviews, photos, and history belong to your existing Business Profile, not to your name. If you create a new profile for the new name, you start from zero and leave a second, competing listing behind. Instead, change the name on the profile you already have. Google's help pages say to enter the name exactly as it appears on your real-world signage, stationery, and branding, and they warn that changing a verified name may mean verifying again. Plan for that so it doesn't catch you mid launch.

Rule two: let the real world go first

Google wants the name on the listing to match what customers see. That makes the sequence matter. The new sign, the receipts, the menu or price list, and the website header should carry the new name before or at the same moment the profile changes. If a reviewer at Google, or a customer standing on the sidewalk, sees the old name on the door and the new one online, you've created the kind of mismatch that slows edits down.

Rule three: don't decorate the name

A rename is a tempting moment to add a keyword or a town to the listing name. Don't. The guidelines ask for the business's real name, and stuffed names are a common reason for suspensions. If the town or the specialty matters, it belongs in the categories, the description, and the website.

The website and the old name

Search engines and AI assistants will keep meeting your old name for years, in reviews, articles, and directory listings you can't edit. Help them connect the dots.

  • Say it plainly on the About page: the business was formerly known as the old name, and when the change happened.
  • In your Organization or LocalBusiness structured data, set the new name as name and keep the old one as alternateName.
  • If the domain changes too, redirect every old page to its closest new equivalent with permanent 301 redirects, and keep them in place for the long term.
  • Update titles and headings, but don't erase the old name entirely from the site while people still search for it.

Everywhere else the name lives

Make a list before you start: Apple Maps, Bing Places, Yelp, Tripadvisor or the directories of your industry, booking and delivery platforms, social profiles, and any chamber or association listings. Update the ones you control in the same week as the profile change. For the rest, note who owns them and request corrections. Consistency across these sources is part of how search engines decide that the renamed business is real and the same as before.

Keep the reviews talking

Reviews stay attached to the profile through a rename, and new ones will mention the new name, which helps. Reply to a few recent reviews after the change; a short reply that uses the new name naturally reinforces the connection without sounding like an announcement.

Watch the first month

For a few weeks, check that the profile shows the new name, that searches for the old name still find you, and that Search Console isn't reporting a wave of errors from old URLs. Branded searches are the early signal: if people searching either name reach you, the rename worked.

Tell your best customers yourself

A rename lands better when regulars hear it from you before they notice it on a sign. A short email or a note at the counter, explaining what changed and what didn't, keeps them from wondering whether the business was sold. Those same customers are the ones most likely to leave a fresh review under the new name.

Common mistakes

  • Creating a new profile instead of editing the existing one.
  • Changing the listing weeks before the sign goes up.
  • Dropping the old domain without redirects.
  • Adding keywords to the new name.
  • Updating Google and forgetting the rest of the web.

item.title: One person, two names: entity SEO for pen names and nicknames
item.description: How to make Google and AI assistants see that Christopher and Chris, or a pen name and a legal name, are one person, using schema, sameAs, and consistency.
item.content:encoded:
One person, two names: entity SEO for pen names and nicknames

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 6, 2026

Plenty of professionals work under more than one name: a formal name on a freelance marketplace, a nickname on bylines, a maiden name on old publications, a pen name on fiction. Search engines and AI assistants treat names as clues, not proof. Unless you connect the names deliberately, they may think you're two people, or worse, merge you with a stranger.

How machines decide who you are

Google's Knowledge Graph and the retrieval systems behind AI assistants build an entity: a single record for a person, with facts attached. They assemble it from pages that agree with each other. When one page says "Christopher Abraham, SEO consultant in Arlington" and another says "Chris Abraham, SEO and reputation specialist in Arlington," the overlap in field and place suggests one person. Structured data and links turn that suggestion into something close to certainty.

Pick a primary name for each site

Each website should have one primary name for you, used consistently in its headings, bylines, and title tags. A site built for marketplace clients can lead with the name they know from the marketplace; a writing archive can lead with the byline name. Having different primaries on different sites is fine, as long as each site acknowledges the other names somewhere visible.

Say it in plain words

Put a sentence on your About page that names the connection: "Most people know me as Chris, and nearly two decades of my bylines carry that name." Plain text is the strongest signal because every crawler reads it, including the ones that ignore structured data.

If you have a full legal name with a middle name, list it once. It distinguishes you from namesakes and matches public records, diplomas, and CVs.

Connect the names in Person schema

Schema.org's Person type has properties built for exactly this:

{
  "@type": "Person",
  "@id": "https://example.com/#person",
  "name": "Christopher Abraham",
  "givenName": "Christopher",
  "additionalName": "James",
  "familyName": "Abraham",
  "alternateName": ["Christopher James Abraham", "Chris Abraham"],
  "jobTitle": "SEO consultant",
  "sameAs": [
    "https://www.linkedin.com/in/example",
    "https://www.upwork.com/freelancers/example",
    "https://publication.example/author/example"
  ]
}
  • name is the primary name on this site.
  • alternateName lists every other name you publish under.
  • additionalName holds a middle name.
  • sameAs points to profiles and author pages that are unmistakably you, whichever name they use.
  • @id gives the entity a permanent identifier, so every page on the site refers to the same person.

Choose sameAs links carefully

sameAs says "this other page is about the same person." Use it only for pages about you: your LinkedIn profile, marketplace profile, author pages at publications, a speaker bio, a consultancy team page. Never point it at a page that merely mentions you, and never at a domain you no longer control. If an old company site has lapsed and now redirects somewhere unrelated, remove it.

Old bios on reputable third-party sites are especially valuable. A team page from decades ago, still online, is independent evidence that you are who you say you are.

Make the profiles agree

Go through each profile you list in sameAs and check the basics: field, city, current role, photo. They don't have to be identical, but they shouldn't contradict each other. A headshot used on every profile is a surprisingly strong signal; image search connects them instantly.

Keep your field attached to your name

Namesakes are the biggest risk. Pair your name with your field everywhere it matters: title tags, page headings, social bios, and author lines. "Christopher Abraham, SEO consultant" repeated across consistent sources teaches the systems which Christopher Abraham this is, and keeps you apart from the theatre director and the novelist who share the name.

What not to do

  • Don't create a separate fake persona with its own invented history. Two names for one real person is normal; two biographies is a credibility problem.
  • Don't hide the connection. A name that appears from nowhere, with no link to an established record, looks like a new entity with no history.
  • Don't stuff every variant into titles and headings. Use the primary name in titles and let alternateName and the About page carry the rest.

Check the result

A few weeks after publishing, search each name with your field and city, and ask the major AI assistants who each name is. When they connect the names and describe the same career, the entity has merged. If they don't, look for a profile that contradicts the others.

item.title: Proving expertise with third-party sources
item.description: Your own claims carry little weight with Google and AI assistants. University news, vendor case studies, old bios, and bylines do. How to find and use them.
item.content:encoded:
Proving expertise with third-party sources

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 6, 2026

Anyone can write "twenty years of experience" on their own website. Search engines and AI assistants know it, so they look for confirmation elsewhere. The most persuasive evidence of expertise is written by someone else, ideally years ago, on a site with no reason to flatter you.

Why outside sources matter so much

Google's quality guidelines ask raters to look at what others say about a creator, not just what the creator says. AI assistants behave similarly in practice: when several independent sources agree on a fact, the assistant states it with confidence; when only your own site says it, the assistant hedges or ignores it. Third-party sources are how a claim becomes a fact in the eyes of a machine.

The kinds of evidence worth hunting for

University and alumni news

Alumni profiles in a university's news site are gold: an institution with a strong domain, an editor, and a publication date. A ten-year-old feature about your company in your college's news site is better evidence than anything you could write today.

Vendor case studies

Software companies publish case studies about their customers. If a major vendor once wrote up your firm, quoting you by name and title, that page confirms your role at a specific time, on the vendor's domain.

Old team and associate pages

Consultancies, agencies, and research groups list their people. A bio on a well-known consultant's associates page, written long ago and never updated, is a fossil record of your early career.

Bylines and author pages

Every publication you wrote for keeps an author page. Columns in trade publications, contributor posts on national sites, and media database profiles all count.

Credits in other people's work

Collaborative projects, anthologies, research papers, and art pieces list their contributors. When a pioneer in your field names you in her own history of a project, that's independent testimony.

Recommendations with names attached

A testimonial is stronger when the person giving it is identifiable and credible in their own right.

How to find what already exists

  1. Search your name in quotes with each employer, school, and project name.
  2. Search your name with distinctive terms from your past: product names, community names, event names.
  3. Check the Wayback Machine at web.archive.org for old employer sites, team pages, and project pages that have since vanished.
  4. Search media databases and your old publications' author archives.
  5. Ask old colleagues what they remember; they often know about write-ups you never saw.

How to use it on your site

  • Link to the source, don't just mention it. "GW Today once wrote up some of this story" with a link is verifiable; "I've been featured in the press" isn't.
  • Quote accurately. Use the source's exact words. If you trim, mark the cut with an ellipsis.
  • Put it where it supports a claim. Next to the sentence about running a virtual company, link the vendor's case study about that virtual company.
  • Add profile pages to sameAs. Author pages and team bios that are about you belong in your Person structured data.
  • Skip what doesn't hold up. If a source now redirects somewhere unrelated, or describes you inaccurately, leave it out.

Respect the details

Old sources come with old details. A case study may name clients you can no longer mention, an alumni profile may print your class year, and a team page may describe a role you've long since left. You don't control their content, but you control what you quote and where you link. Weigh each source's value against what it reveals, and decide deliberately.

Keep a file

Save a copy of every source you find, with the URL and the date. Pages disappear. A PDF in your own archive, plus the Wayback Machine's copy, means you can still point to the evidence if the original goes away.

Create new evidence going forward

The best time to collect third-party proof was years ago; the second best is now. Write for publications in your field, speak where talks are published, contribute to projects that credit contributors, and ask satisfied clients for testimonials you're allowed to attribute. Each one becomes a source that confirms you to the next reader, human or machine.

item.description: Which schema types a small business needs, which to skip, and example structured data for local businesses, services, FAQs, and breadcrumbs, kept accurate.
item.content:encoded:
The schema markup a small business actually needs

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 6, 2026

Schema.org has more than 800 types. A typical small business needs about five. This guide covers which ones, shows example code, and lists the rules that keep structured data accurate enough for Google and AI systems to trust.

Why bother

Structured data states your facts in a format machines don't have to guess at. It can earn rich results in Google, such as review stars, FAQs, and breadcrumbs, and it helps search engines and AI assistants connect your business, its location, and its services into one clear entity. It won't rescue a weak page, but it makes a good page unambiguous.

The five you need

1. LocalBusiness or Organization, on the home page

Use the most specific LocalBusiness subtype that fits: Dentist, Plumber, LegalService, Restaurant, HomeAndConstructionBusiness, and so on. If customers never visit you and you don't serve a defined area, use Organization instead.

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Plumber",
  "@id": "https://example.com/#business",
  "name": "Example Plumbing",
  "url": "https://example.com/",
  "logo": "https://example.com/logo.png",
  "telephone": "+1-703-555-0100",
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "streetAddress": "100 Main Street",
    "addressLocality": "Arlington",
    "addressRegion": "VA",
    "postalCode": "22204",
    "addressCountry": "US"
  },
  "openingHours": "Mo-Fr 08:00-17:00",
  "areaServed": ["Arlington, VA", "Alexandria, VA"],
  "sameAs": [
    "https://www.linkedin.com/company/example-plumbing",
    "https://www.yelp.com/biz/example-plumbing"
  ]
}
</script>

The @id is a permanent identifier for the business. Use the same one on every page that refers to it.

2. Service, on each service page

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Service",
  "name": "Water heater replacement",
  "provider": { "@id": "https://example.com/#business" },
  "areaServed": "Arlington, VA",
  "url": "https://example.com/water-heaters/"
}

The provider points back to the business by its @id, connecting each service to the company that offers it.

3. BreadcrumbList, on every page below the home page

Describes where the page sits in your site. Most SEO plugins generate this automatically if breadcrumbs are turned on.

4. FAQPage, only where questions are visible

Mark up FAQs only when the questions and answers are visible on the page. Google shows FAQ rich results for few sites now, but the markup still helps AI systems match your answers to questions.

5. Person, for the owner or practitioner

If customers choose you partly because of who you are, such as a lawyer, therapist, consultant, or chef, add Person markup on the About page with name, job title, image, and sameAs links to professional profiles, connected to the business with worksFor.

Add if they apply

  • Product and Offer if you sell products online.
  • Article or BlogPosting on blog posts, with author and dates.
  • Event for classes, workshops, or performances with dates.
  • Review markup only for reviews that are visible on the page. Self-serving review stars on your own business are ignored by Google.

The rules

  1. Match the page. Everything in the markup should be visible to visitors. Hidden facts in schema get ignored or penalized.
  2. Match the world. Name, address, and phone should match your Google Business Profile exactly.
  3. One source of truth. Don't let a theme, an SEO plugin, and a reviews app each output their own business markup. Pick one.
  4. Keep it current. Hours, prices, and addresses change. Hardcoded markup goes stale; markup generated from your CMS fields stays accurate.
  5. Validate. Test every template in Google's Rich Results Test and the Schema.org validator, then watch Search Console's enhancement reports.

How to add it

On WordPress, Yoast SEO and Rank Math generate Organization, WebSite, Breadcrumb, and Article markup and let you add more. On Shopify, the theme usually outputs Product markup; check for duplicates before adding an app. On Squarespace and Wix, add JSON-LD through code injection or the platform's SEO settings. On custom sites, generate it from the same data that renders the page.

A five-minute self-check

  1. Paste your home page address into Google's Rich Results Test and note every type it detects.
  2. Open the Schema.org validator on the same page and look for duplicates: two Organization or LocalBusiness blocks usually mean a theme and a plugin are both writing markup.
  3. Compare the name, address, and phone in the markup with your Google Business Profile, character by character.
  4. Repeat on one service page and one blog post.
  5. In Search Console, open the Enhancements section and check for errors and warnings on each detected type.

If all five checks come back clean, your structured data is in better shape than most.

Multiple locations

With more than one location, the home page describes the Organization, and each location page describes its own LocalBusiness with parentOrganization pointing to it. Never describe the company and its first location as the same entity.

item.title: What a technical SEO audit should give you
item.description: How to tell a useful technical SEO audit from a tool export: a clear question, evidence for each finding, a ranked plan, developer tickets, and a plain summary.
item.content:encoded:
What a technical SEO audit should give you

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 6, 2026

You can buy an SEO audit for fifty dollars or fifteen thousand. The cheap ones and some of the expensive ones are the same thing: a crawler's warnings pasted into a document. This guide describes what a useful audit contains, so you can judge one before you pay for it and after you receive it.

It starts with a question

A useful audit answers something specific. "Why did organic revenue from product pages fall 30% since May?" "What is at risk in a move to Shopify?" "Why are half the location pages not indexed?" The question decides what gets examined and how deeply. An audit with no question examines everything at the same shallow depth and concludes nothing.

How to judge it: the first page should restate your question. If it opens with a score out of 100, be wary.

Findings come with evidence

Every finding should show how the auditor knows it: a screenshot of the rendered HTML missing the product description, a Search Console export showing which pages dropped, a crawl comparison, server response headers, a log excerpt. Evidence lets your developers verify the finding themselves, and it protects you from fixing things that were never broken.

How to judge it: pick any finding and ask, "How is this known?" The answer should already be on the page.

Findings explain the mechanism

"Product pages have low word count" is a symptom. "Product specifications and reviews are mounted by a script that runs only when a visitor scrolls, so crawlers receive 300 words of a 3,000-word page" is a mechanism. Mechanisms tell you what to fix. Symptoms tell you to go find someone who can explain them.

Separate problems stay separate

Traffic losses often coincide with several things at once: an algorithm update, a plugin change, a backlink spike, a redesign. A good audit treats each as its own line of inquiry and says which ones the evidence actually connects to the loss. Folding everything into one story feels satisfying and leads to fixing the wrong thing.

Confidence is stated

Not every finding is certain. Good auditors say which conclusions are confirmed, which are likely, and which need more data, and they say what data would settle it. An audit that's equally sure of everything has probably not tested much.

The plan is ranked

You should finish the audit knowing what to do first. That means a prioritized list, often P0 through P3, where each item has:

  • the problem, in one sentence;
  • the expected impact, and on which pages;
  • an owner, such as your developer, your content editor, or the consultant;
  • a rough effort estimate;
  • dependencies, if one fix must come before another.

How to judge it: could your team start work Monday morning without another meeting?

Developers get tickets they can build from

For anything that requires code, a strong audit includes developer-ready tickets: what to change, where, exact steps where possible, and acceptance criteria that say how everyone will know it's done. "Event links must be present as anchor elements in the server HTML of /events/" is testable. "Improve crawlability" isn't.

Leadership gets a summary

A one-page plain-English summary: what's wrong, what it's costing, what it will take, and what to expect afterward. The people who approve the budget shouldn't need to read crawl data to make a decision.

What a useful audit leaves out

  • Hundreds of low-priority warnings with no ranking. Missing alt text on a footer logo isn't why traffic fell.
  • Generic best-practice sections copied between clients.
  • Guarantees about rankings. Nobody controls Google's decisions.
  • Proprietary scores that can't be traced back to evidence.

After delivery

The audit's value shows up when fixes ship. Ask whether the auditor will verify the fixes against the acceptance criteria, check the live site after deployment, and watch the relevant reports. An audit followed by verification turns findings into results.

Questions to ask before you hire

  1. What question will this audit answer?
  2. Can I see an anonymized sample?
  3. Who does the actual analysis?
  4. Will findings include evidence and confidence?
  5. Will developers get tickets with acceptance criteria?
  6. Will you verify the fixes?

item.title: Ten rules for 301 redirects that keep your rankings
item.description: Ten rules for 301 redirects in migrations and redesigns: map one to one, avoid chains, keep redirects for years, use 410 on purpose, and test in bulk.
item.content:encoded:
Ten rules for 301 redirects that keep your rankings

By Christopher Abraham · Published October 6, 2026

A 301 redirect tells browsers and search engines that a page has moved permanently and where to find it. Handled well, redirects carry rankings, links, and bookmarks to a new address. Handled carelessly, they quietly erase years of search equity. These are the rules I follow on every migration.

1. Inventory before you redirect

You can't redirect URLs you don't know about. Build the old URL list from several sources: a full crawl, every XML sitemap, Search Console's performance and indexing exports, analytics landing pages over at least a year, and backlink tools. Old campaign pages and PDFs that nobody links from the menu often carry the most external links.

2. Map one to one, to the closest equivalent

Each old URL should point to the new page that best serves the same visitor. A product goes to the same product, a category to the same category, an article to its new address. When the content is merged, point to the merged page.

3. Don't send everything to the home page

Redirecting hundreds of old pages to the home page is easy and almost worthless. Google treats irrelevant redirects as soft 404s, and the equity those pages carried is lost. If there's no real equivalent, use rule 6.

4. Use 301 or 308 for permanent moves

A 301 (or 308, which also preserves the request method) signals a permanent move. A 302 or 307 says "temporarily elsewhere," and search engines may keep the old URL indexed. Meta refresh and JavaScript redirects work in some cases, but server-side redirects are the clear signal.

5. No chains, no loops

Each redirect should go straight to the final destination in one hop. Chains build up over years: http to https, then www to apex, then old path to new path. Every hop adds delay and risks the crawler giving up. When you add new redirects, update the old ones to point at the final URL.

6. Use 410 deliberately

For pages that are gone for good with no replacement, a 410 status says so plainly and gets them dropped from the index faster than a 404. Use it for retired products with no successor, expired events, and spam pages left from a hack.

7. Keep redirects for years

Search engines need time to process a move, and links, bookmarks, and old emails keep sending visitors for years. Keep redirects in place for at least a year, and for valuable URLs, indefinitely. Removing them to "clean up" the configuration is a common way to lose traffic a second time.

8. Update everything that points at old URLs

Redirects are a safety net, not the plan. Update internal links, canonical tags, hreflang annotations, XML sitemaps, structured data, and your Google Business Profile website link to point directly at new URLs. Ask the sites that link to you most to update their links too.

9. Preserve parameters and casing on purpose

Decide how query strings, trailing slashes, and uppercase URLs are handled. Tracking parameters should usually pass through; old filter parameters may need their own rules. Test a handful of odd real URLs from your logs, not just the clean ones.

10. Test in bulk, then watch

Before launch, run the full old URL list against staging and confirm each returns one 301 to the expected destination, which then returns 200. Repeat on launch day against production. Afterward, watch 404 reports in Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, your server logs, and traffic by page group for several weeks.

Where redirects live

  • Apache: .htaccess or the virtual host configuration.
  • Nginx: server blocks with return 301 or map files for large lists.
  • WordPress: Rank Math, Yoast Premium, or the Redirection plugin, or the server for large maps.
  • Shopify: URL Redirects under Navigation, with CSV import.
  • Netlify and Vercel: _redirects files or the platform's configuration file.
  • Cloudflare: Bulk Redirects or Redirect Rules at the edge, useful when the origin can't do it.
  • GitHub Pages and other static hosts: no server redirects, so a page with a meta refresh and a canonical tag is the fallback.

A note on disavow files

Migrations are a common moment to review backlinks. Disavow only genuinely manipulative or spammy links, and keep legitimate ones; disavowing good links throws away the equity your redirects are trying to preserve.
